title: $Z$-sight: Unifying Vision-Language-Action and Latent World Modeling
authors: Junjie Ye,Yiqi Zhao,Muchen Xu,Celina Shiyu Wang,Hao Dong,Ruohai Ge,Rong Xue,Benjamin J Kolligs,Aditya Dutt,Sasanka Nagavalli,Nassim A. Samad,Gaurav S. Sukhatme,Jyotirmoy V. Deshmukh,Yue Wang,Yuliang Guo
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: Project page:this https URL
abstract:
We introduce 𝒵\mathcal{Z}-sight, a unified robot foundation model that couples
vision-language-action (VLA) and generative latent world modeling. Video-based
world action models (WAMs) show the value of joint future-and-action generation
for control, yet inherit the heavy cost of video generators. Recent
latent-space policies avoid pixel generation, yet typically align intermediate
features or rely on frozen target encoders, decoupling future prediction from
the VLM’s native feature space. 𝒵\mathcal{Z}-sight instead predicts the future directly in the visual token space in which its VLM
perceives the present. Coupling a
foresight expert and a continuous action expert with the VLM in a
mixture-of-transformers, 𝒵\mathcal{Z}-sight jointly denoises future spatial tokens and
actions at inference without pixel reconstruction or external encoders. Trained
on human video and robot trajectories, 𝒵\mathcal{Z}-sight achieves 81.9% success on
SIMPLE (+9.6 points over the strongest baseline) and 73.3% across six Unitree
G1 tasks (+20.0 points) at 110 ms per chunk, while remaining competitive on
tabletop benchmarks.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models transfer visual and linguistic knowledge to
robotic control by building policies on pre-trained VLMs (Zitkovich et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2025; Black et al., 2025b). Recent architectures extend this
paradigm by coupling a VLM backbone with a continuous action expert (Black et al., 2025a; Bjorck et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2026a), combining multimodal reasoning with high-frequency
action generation.

In parallel, world action models (WAMs) (Ye et al., 2026; Bi et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026) adapt pre-trained video generators to jointly model future
observations and actions, capturing physical dynamics at the cost of large
video diffusion backbones. Recent methods avoid pixel generation by moving
future supervision into latent space, yet either align intermediate policy
features to compact embeddings (Zheng et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026) without
generating a future stream, or predict features of frozen target
encoders (Zhang et al., 2026b; Sun et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a) that decouple from the
VLM’s native feature space.

We introduce 𝒵\mathcal{Z}-sight, a unified model that brings joint future-and-action
generation into the policy’s co-evolving native visual space
(Figure 1). A VLM encodes observations into spatial visual
tokens. By supervising future predictions against an exponential-moving-average
(EMA) teacher of this same vision encoder, perception and prediction remain
aligned throughout pre-training and downstream adaptation, without introducing
a video generator or an external target encoder.

As shown in Figure 2, 𝒵\mathcal{Z}-sight couples the VLM stream with a
foresight expert and a continuous action expert in a mixture-of-transformers
(MoT) (Liang et al., 2025). Conditioned on the VLM’s instruction,
state, and observation history, the foresight expert predicts future spatial
tokens via flow matching while the action expert attends directly to these
predicted features. During inference, both experts jointly denoise future
visual tokens and actions, informing control with online latent dynamics at
high efficiency.

We train 𝒵\mathcal{Z}-sight on egocentric human video and cross-embodiment robot
trajectories, then adapt it across single-arm, bimanual, and humanoid settings
spanning LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023), RoboTwin 2.0 (Chen et al., 2026),
SIMPLE (Wei et al., 2026b), and six physical Unitree G1 tasks. 𝒵\mathcal{Z}-sight achieves strong humanoid loco-manipulation performance, reaching 81.9% success
on SIMPLE and 73.3% on the real robot (+9.6 and +20.0 points over the
strongest baselines) at 110 ms per action chunk, while remaining competitive
on tabletop manipulation benchmarks. Our contributions are
threefold:

We introduce 𝒵\mathcal{Z}-sight, a unified VLA and latent world model that
jointly denoises future spatial visual tokens and continuous actions within
the VLM’s co-evolving visual representation space.

We introduce 𝒵\mathcal{Z}-sight, a unified VLA and latent world model that
jointly denoises future spatial visual tokens and continuous actions within
the VLM’s co-evolving visual representation space.

Through matched architectural controls and test-time interventions,
we demonstrate the advantages of co-evolving native targets and joint
denoising over implicit feature alignment and frozen external targets.

𝒵\mathcal{Z}-sight achieves strong humanoid loco-manipulation results on SIMPLE and six real-world
Unitree G1 tasks at 110 ms per chunk, while
remaining competitive on tabletop manipulation benchmarks.

1. We introduce 𝒵\mathcal{Z}-sight, a unified VLA and latent world model that
jointly denoises future spatial visual tokens and continuous actions within
the VLM’s co-evolving visual representation space.

2. Through matched architectural controls and test-time interventions,
we demonstrate the advantages of co-evolving native targets and joint
denoising over implicit feature alignment and frozen external targets.

3. 𝒵\mathcal{Z}-sight achieves strong humanoid loco-manipulation results on SIMPLE and six real-world
Unitree G1 tasks at 110 ms per chunk, while
remaining competitive on tabletop manipulation benchmarks.

title: Phoenix: Learning Scene Structure Representations for Generalizable World-Action Models
authors: Yupeng Zheng,Chaoyue Li,Linbo Wang,Xiang Li,Yuhang Zheng,Xiaotong Su,Songen Gu,Yichen Zhang,Zebin Xing,Shuai Tian,Jingxiang Guo,Jing Li,Zhiyong Zhao,Zhongpu Xia,Qichao Zhang,Haoran Li,Shuicheng Yan,Dongbin Zhao
abstract:
World-action models jointly predict future observations and actions, yet reconstruction-oriented visual representations do not explicitly emphasize the spatial relationships and object-state changes needed for manipulation.
We introduce Phoenix, which learns representations of scene structure for world-action modeling.
Specifically, Phoenix Encoder enriches DINOv3’s general visual semantics through dual-teacher distillation of geometric and spatiotemporal semantic knowledge.
Next, CS-VAE causally aggregates and compresses Phoenix Encoder features into generative latents while preserving scene information and spatial layout.
Finally, Phoenix jointly predicts these latents, complementary appearance latents, and robot actions, linking scene evolution with action generation.
To study pretraining data efficiency, we curate approximately 39,000 hours of egocentric and robot manipulation data for representation learning and use the robot demonstration subset for WAM pretraining.
Following benchmark-specific post-training, Phoenix achieves state-of-the-art performance across simulation and real-robot benchmarks spanning single-arm, bimanual, and dexterous manipulation.
It demonstrates strong robustness to perturbations, achieving success rates of 94.8% on LIBERO-Plus and 72.4% on RoboTwin 2.0 C2R, alongside strong cross-embodiment transfer and real-world manipulation performance on Bench2Dex and RoboDojo-RealWorld, respectively.
Pretraining-scale analysis shows larger performance gains from data scaling than a video-VAE-only baseline, indicating stronger scaling benefits and more effective data utilization.
Moreover, Phoenix maintains high success rates when adapted with limited downstream demonstrations, demonstrating strong few-shot adaptation.
Our code, pretraining data, and models are available on the project page to help the community reproduce our results.
introduction:
World–action models (WAMs) jointly predict future observations and robot actions,
linking environment modeling with control [27, 64, 56].
They learn from large-scale visual experience to develop manipulation skills that
generalize across scenes, object configurations, and execution
conditions [13, 29, 34].
This requires visual representations that support both environment prediction and policy learning.

In WAMs, visual representations determine how observations are encoded and what the model predicts. Manipulation-centered representations of scene structure should capture spatial organization, visual appearance, and motion. Latents learned for video reconstruction preserve rich visual information, but reconstruction fidelity alone does not ensure that they capture manipulation-relevant structure and its relationship to actions [4, 48, 73]. Recent work on representation alignment and generation with visual foundation model features shows that visual understanding complements generative modeling [68, 77, 45]. We therefore investigate how geometric and spatiotemporal semantic knowledge from these models [44, 49, 39] can be used to build scene representations for joint prediction of future states and actions.

We introduce Phoenix, a WAM that learns generative representations of scene structure. Phoenix Encoder builds on DINOv3’s general visual semantics and learns per-frame scene features through dual-teacher distillation of geometric and spatiotemporal semantic knowledge. CS-VAE aggregates Phoenix Encoder features over causal temporal windows and compresses them into generative latents, preserving scene information and spatial layout. Phoenix jointly predicts these scene latents, complementary appearance latents, and robot actions, learning how actions relate to scene changes. To study pretraining data efficiency, we curate approximately 39,000 hours of egocentric and robot manipulation data for representation learning and use the robot demonstration subset for WAM pretraining.

As shown in Figure 1, after benchmark-specific post-training, Phoenix achieves state-of-the-art performance across six benchmarks: LIBERO-Plus [10], LIBERO-Pro [80], RoboTwin 2.0 C2R [6], RoboCasa-GR1 [40], Bench2Dex [62], and RoboDojo-RealWorld [5]. These benchmarks assess manipulation generalization under environmental perturbations and across robot embodiments, spanning simulation and real-world settings.

We further study how representations of scene structure affect manipulation performance and data efficiency across WAM pretraining and downstream adaptation.
Ablations show that learning these representations and compressing them into generative latents both improve manipulation performance,
accompanied by more faithful predictions of interaction dynamics.
Scaling WAM pretraining data yields larger gains in success rate for Phoenix than for a video-VAE-only baseline, indicating improved pretraining data efficiency. These benefits extend to downstream adaptation, where pretrained Phoenix maintains high success rates with limited task-specific demonstrations, showing effective knowledge transfer in few-shot settings.

Our main contributions are as follows:

Representations of scene structure for world–action modeling. Phoenix Encoder builds on general visual semantics to learn features of scene structure through dual-teacher distillation of geometric and spatiotemporal semantic knowledge. CS-VAE causally aggregates and compresses them into generative latents, preserving spatial layout. Phoenix jointly predicts these latents, complementary appearance latents, and robot actions.

Improved WAM pretraining data efficiency. We compare visual representations across WAM pretraining scales using robot demonstrations and show that our representation yields larger performance gains from scaling data than a video-VAE-only baseline.

State-of-the-art performance across six simulation and real-world benchmarks. Phoenix achieves SOTA results in perturbation robustness, cross-embodiment adaptation, and dexterous and real-world manipulation. Further experiments demonstrate strong few-shot adaptation with limited task-specific demonstrations.

1. Representations of scene structure for world–action modeling. Phoenix Encoder builds on general visual semantics to learn features of scene structure through dual-teacher distillation of geometric and spatiotemporal semantic knowledge. CS-VAE causally aggregates and compresses them into generative latents, preserving spatial layout. Phoenix jointly predicts these latents, complementary appearance latents, and robot actions.

2. Improved WAM pretraining data efficiency. We compare visual representations across WAM pretraining scales using robot demonstrations and show that our representation yields larger performance gains from scaling data than a video-VAE-only baseline.

3. State-of-the-art performance across six simulation and real-world benchmarks. Phoenix achieves SOTA results in perturbation robustness, cross-embodiment adaptation, and dexterous and real-world manipulation. Further experiments demonstrate strong few-shot adaptation with limited task-specific demonstrations.

title: Grana: Compositional Reward Modeling for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation
authors: Zi-ang Cao,Kaiyuan Zheng,Yinzhen Xu,Haonan Duan,Jiasheng Gu,Fengyuan Hu,Nan Zhu,Kun Lei,Kevin Lin,Ruijie Zheng,Shenyuan Gao,Fangqi Zhu,Zhe Zhang,Radha Poovendran,Linxi Fan,Guanzhi Wang,Yuke Zhu
comment: Project website:this https URL
abstract:
Robot reward modeling faces two challenges: generalizing across tasks and accurately tracking progress in long-horizon manipulation.
General-purpose reward models demonstrate broad task transfer, but transfer from short-task pretraining to long-horizon tasks remains underexplored.
Long-horizon progress models often rely on task-specific subtask classifiers or fixed action vocabularies, limiting the reuse of learned progress knowledge when adapting to new tasks.
To address these challenges, we introduce Grana, a vision-language robot reward model that learns to identify unfinished subtasks and estimate their continuous progress using open-vocabulary subtask descriptions.
We train a language-conditioned model to estimate progress in short-horizon tasks and individual subtasks of long-horizon tasks. For long-horizon tasks, we combine the selected subtask’s predicted progress with credit for preceding completed subtasks to estimate whole-task progress.
General progress prediction requires training the model across diverse tasks with progress supervision that accounts for imperfect execution. Elapsed-time proxies can misrepresent progress when relative subtask durations vary, or failures reverse local progress. We therefore introduce an annotation protocol that converts sparse subtask boundaries and action-quality annotations into dense progress targets, without requiring annotators to assign numerical progress scores.
Pretraining with this supervision on 200 diverse, mostly short-horizon manipulation tasks enables zero-shot reward prediction on unseen tasks and improves progress prediction after adaptation to multi-minute, long-horizon tasks.
Experiments demonstrate (i) generalizable reward prediction, including adaptation to five long-horizon tasks, (ii) benefits from pretraining and composing subtask progress estimates, and (iii) improved downstream policy performance.
introduction:
Progress-based reward models estimate how much of a task has been completed, providing learning signals for robot policies [1, 2].
For long-horizon manipulation, these models should reuse progress knowledge learned from shorter tasks while tracking failed attempts and recovery.

Consider assembling a model airplane by placing a wing, inserting a screw, and tightening it with a drill. Completing wing placement should receive the same progress credit across executions, even when the time spent on each subtask varies. During insertion, repeated misalignment should slow progress, while dropping the screw should reset insertion progress without erasing credit for the placed wing. Furthermore, reaching for the drill should not advance progress while insertion remains unfinished. These distinctions motivate us to compose whole-task progress from subtask progress, and to combine subtask boundaries with action-quality annotations to capture setbacks and recovery.

General-purpose reward models learn from diverse robot videos [3, 4, 2] or use pretrained vision-language models directly [5] to provide reward signals across diverse tasks.
We ask whether learning progress at the subtask level improves whole-task progress tracking and supports transfer from short tasks to long-horizon tasks.
Some long-horizon progress models use task-specific subtask classifiers [1] or a fixed action vocabulary shared across tasks [6].
These choices limit reuse of learned progress knowledge when subtasks change in a new long-horizon task.
We seek a model that learns subtask selection and progress prediction through language descriptions, so that knowledge from short tasks can be reused in longer compositions.

Progress supervision poses a second challenge.
Subtask completion keyframes alone do not reflect failed attempts or recovery.
Local execution judgments can describe setbacks [7, 6], but a progress curve must also show how much work is lost.
A brief failure may undo the current attempt without undoing earlier subtasks.

We introduce Grana, a vision-language robot reward model that learns to select the unfinished subtask and predict its local progress from open-vocabulary descriptions (Fig. 1).
We combine this prediction with credit for preceding completed subtasks to estimate whole-task progress.
Incorrect subtask choices can distort this whole-task estimate, so training considers subtask order to define a local-progress target for each selected subtask.
The same language interface lets us reuse the pretrained model on new tasks and longer compositions without replacing model components.

To train this predictor, we combine subtask boundaries with action-quality annotations to construct a dense progress curve without direct numerical scoring.
Subtask boundaries mark when subtasks are completed, while action-quality annotations describe nominal, suboptimal, and regressed execution within each subtask.
The constructed progress curve advances more slowly during suboptimal execution and drops when regressed execution loses local progress.
It rises again during recovery while preserving credit for earlier completed subtasks.
Using this supervision, we pretrain Grana on 200 mostly short manipulation tasks.

We evaluate how these design choices affect progress prediction on new tasks and a different embodiment, as well as downstream policy learning.
We also show that structured supervision improves progress predictions from a prior vision-language model (VLM)- based reward model.
We further show Grana ’s generalization capabilities, achieving 20.7% lower progress RMSE than the strongest evaluated baseline without target-task reward labels or fine-tuning on 50 held-out tasks.
Across five long-horizon tasks with up to 18 subtasks, Grana adapted with 15 labeled trajectories per task achieves the lowest progress RMSE among the evaluated models.
On the two 3–5-minute airplane and red car assembly tasks, it also outperforms baselines adapted with 100 trajectories; matched comparisons show that pretraining improves prediction on both tasks at both adaptation budgets.
The reward model’s zero-shot progress prediction also improves offline reinforcement learning (RL) on held-out tasks.
During iterative policy learning on airplane and red car assembly, progress-weighted behavior cloning improves success over unweighted behavior cloning with the same parent policy and data.

Our contributions are threefold:

Compositional progress prediction. We train the model to select subtasks and predict local progress, then compose their outputs into whole-task progress. During adaptation, task order defines progress targets for the model’s own subtask choices.

Structured progress supervision. We combine subtask boundaries and action-quality annotations to construct dense progress curves, with explicit rules for failure and recovery.

Evidence for reward model generalization and policy improvement. We show that short-task pretraining improves long-task adaptation and that predicted progress supports downstream policy learning.

1. Compositional progress prediction. We train the model to select subtasks and predict local progress, then compose their outputs into whole-task progress. During adaptation, task order defines progress targets for the model’s own subtask choices.

2. Structured progress supervision. We combine subtask boundaries and action-quality annotations to construct dense progress curves, with explicit rules for failure and recovery.

3. Evidence for reward model generalization and policy improvement. We show that short-task pretraining improves long-task adaptation and that predicted progress supports downstream policy learning.

title: Render the Robot, Generate the World: One Video World Model Across Embodiments
authors: Yash Jangir,Karan Mirakhor,Renos Zabounidis,Muhammad Zubair Irshad,Sergey Zakharov,Yonatan Bisk,Homanga Bharadhwaj
comment: Project page:this https URL
abstract:
Predicting the consequences of an agent’s actions requires modeling both the embodiment’s motion and the environment’s response. Most video world models attempt to learn both jointly using only numerical action vectors, even though robot geometry and kinematics already provide information needed to specify the intended robot motion. A general-purpose world model should capture these dynamics across multiple embodiments within a single model. Our key idea is to render the robot along a proposed joint-space trajectory and condition the video model directly on these future robot configurations. To this end, we introduce Doppel, an embodiment-agnostic video world model for learning a dynamics model shared across embodiments. Doppel jointly conditions on camera-aligned robot renderings and numerical action trajectories. Using forward kinematics and differentiable rendering, we explicitly provide the model with the robot’s intended motion. This allows the shared model to focus its capacity on object motion and interaction-driven changes in the environment. Representing robot motion in image space also provides a common conditioning interface across embodiments with different geometries and action spaces. To enable this approach at scale, we recover missing camera extrinsics from offline robot datasets and align the resulting renderings with recorded observations. Using these aligned renderings, we train a single shared video backbone and conditioning adapter jointly on DROID, RoboMIND, Bridge, ABC, T-Rex, GigaHands, OakInk2, and Ego-Exo4D, spanning Franka, UR5e, WidowX, and bimanual YAM arms, an egocentric humanoid with dexterous hands, and human hands, upper bodies, and full bodies, from about 600 hours of video and without an embodiment label. On the three robot-arm datasets, Doppel improves PSNR over action-only baselines by 1.00 dB on unseen trajectories and 1.20 dB under OOD evaluation while predicting more consistent object motion, and training on all eight embodiments (Doppel-8) improves robot predictions over the three-robot model (Doppel-3) on four of six robot evaluation sets.
Project page: https://doppelwm.github.io/.
introduction:
“Civilization advances by extending the number of important operations
which we can perform without thinking about them.”

When we reach for a cup, we have a sense of where our arm is and can anticipate how it will move. Proprioceptive feedback and internal predictions of movement help us estimate the position of our limbs, even when we cannot see them [60]. Knowing our own motion, however, does not fully determine what happens to the cup: it may slide, tip over, or stay in our grasp, depending on how we make contact. In everyday physical interactions, we intuitively combine knowledge of our own body with predictions of how the surrounding world will respond. We build on this factorization by using known robot kinematics and camera extrinsics to render the intended robot motion, allowing the world model to focus on modeling the environment’s response.

For a robot, its geometry and kinematics provide an explicit description of its body. We study how to incorporate this knowledge in video world models, which predict future observations from an initial image and a proposed action trajectory. Recent methods adapt pretrained video generators to this task by conditioning them on numerical action vectors (for example robot joint poses) [3]. The model must then learn both how the actions move the robot in the image and how that motion affects the environment. However, much of the first mapping can already be computed from the robot’s geometry, joint configurations, and camera parameters.

Our key idea is to render the robot along the proposed action trajectory and condition the video model on these future frames. We use forward kinematics to compute link poses from joint configurations and the robot URDF, and a learned differentiable rendering model to generate camera-aligned robot renderings from the observed camera viewpoint. The resulting frames show where the arm and gripper would be if the robot followed the provided action trajectory. In the spirit of Whitehead’s observation, we use this known structure to simplify what must be learned. With the intended robot motion provided explicitly through visual renderings, the video model can focus on predicting its consequences in the environment: whether a grasp would remain stable, how far would a pushed object move, and which way would a cup rotate.

We introduce Doppel, an embodiment-agnostic video world model that uses this conditioning. Doppel combines future robot renderings with the numerical action trajectory. Like a doppelgänger, the rendered robot is a faithful double of the real one; Doppel lets this double show where the robot will move, so the model can focus on how the world responds. Renderings describe the robot’s geometry and motion in the image, while the numerical inputs retain information that may be visually ambiguous. Expressing actions this way also enables learning across robots with different joint structures and control spaces. Although Franka, UR5e, and WidowX move differently, their renderings describe the intended motion in a common image space. We therefore train a shared conditioning adapter and video backbone across these embodiments, using robot-specific geometry and normalization only to construct the inputs. This yields a single set of model weights that can represent multiple robot embodiments, avoiding the need to train and maintain a separate world model for each robot.

Realizing this representation across large-scale robot datasets requires accurate alignment between the rendered robot and the observation camera. This alignment depends on the camera pose relative to the robot base, which is often missing from manipulation datasets. We recover these missing extrinsics by optimizing the differentiable renderer to align rendered robot motion with the observations. This allows us to construct camera-aligned conditioning videos across datasets with different robots and camera setups.

Finally, because our formulation explicitly separates the robot’s intended motion from its effects on the environment, we evaluate these components separately. We measure prediction quality over robot and moving-object regions, allowing us to distinguish accurate generation of the robot’s motion from accurate prediction of the resulting environment dynamics. We train Doppel jointly on Droid (Franka), RoboMind (UR5e), and Bridge (WidowX), a model we call Doppel-3, and evaluate generalization to unseen trajectories and environments. title: Learning to Interact in Multi-Agent Self-Play for Controllable Autonomous Driving Scenario Generation
authors: Beyazit Yalcinkaya,Ethan Pronovost,Maximilian Naumann,Marcell Vazquez-Chanlatte
comment: Preprint
abstract: Large-scale, multi-agent self-play trains robust driving policies effectively in simulation, but controlling these models to generate specific, safety-critical edge cases remains a key challenge. Existing goal-conditioned self-play frameworks rely primarily on static map-location goals and fail to reliably produce complex agent interactions such as aggressive tailgating or adversarial cut-offs. These agent interactions are necessary for rigorous autonomous vehicle (AV) testing. To address this, we present an extended multi-agent self-play framework that introduces agent-relative dynamic goals. By conditioning policies on this extended goal representation, our framework enables targeted, controllable scenario synthesis. We demonstrate that our approach successfully generates interactive driving behaviors that static-goal baselines cannot simulate, providing a flexible tool for long-tail scenario generation in AV testing.
introduction:
Rigorous autonomous vehicle (AV) testing depends on being able to simulate long-tail driving scenarios with agents that react to the vehicle under test rather than ignore it.
Recent advances have shown that large-scale, multi-agent self-play can be used to train such agents [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6].
In contrast, the common alternatives for simulation agents (log replay, hand-scripted actors, and rule-based car-following models [7]) fail to produce realistic interactive behavior.

Gigaflow [1] is the clearest demonstration of this, where copies of one policy control every traffic participant.
This policy is trained against copies of itself in large-scale simulation to optimize a parameterized reward function, with each agent receiving different parameters sampled during training.
Agents observe a local view of the map, goal locations, their own state, nearby agents, and their reward parameters.
From this setup, and without any human driving data, the policy learns generalist, robust, and human-like driving.
Conditioning on the reward parameters allows the agent’s behavior to be controlled at inference time (e.g. to create harder simulations by making agents more aggressive).

Simulation agents are used to test an AV system.
During validation, challenging agent interactions such as cut-offs, tailgating, and brake checks are of particular interest; nominal driving behavior is simply not very useful for testing advanced AV systems.
What we want is an agent that can reliably produce these interactions in simulations with the AV driving system.
The standard self-play recipe, however, cannot achieve this.
As demonstrated below, the reward parameters and static goals used to condition these agents are insufficient to get the agent to perform these key interactions with another agent.
This begs the question: how can we modify the multi-agent self-play training recipe to add support for agent interactions while preserving all the positive attributes of this recipe?

In this work, we improve the multi-agent self-play recipe of Gigaflow by adding support for agent-relative goals through an extended goal interface.
These agent-relative goals are defined with respect to another reference agent and therefore move along with that reference agent.
These new goals allow us to simulate specific agent interactions that otherwise cannot be expressed with the previous static goals.
For example, we can command a red agent to cut-off the blue agent by placing the red agent’s goal in front of the blue agent (Figure 1).
Because the goal is agent-relative, it moves with the blue agent.
The only way for the red agent to reach its goal is to get in front of the blue agent.

We implement this extension with the smallest change possible: an updated goal sampling mechanism during training and a single bit added to the agent observation.
We find that this is sufficient to achieve the desired interactive behaviors.

Specifically, our contributions are:

we introduce agent-relative goals as a novel extension to the multi-agent self-play paradigm

we show a set of scenario demonstrations enabled by agent-relative goals

we demonstrate that adding agent-relative goals preserves the original baseline behavior

title: Communications-free Collective Intelligence Via Allocentric Belief
authors: Cameron Mehlman,Arjun Mulchandani,Hovik Grigoryan,Anurag Koyyada,Gregory Falco
abstract: A team of skilled card players share no information amongst each other, and yet still are able to coordinate their play by watching the same players and reading the same tells. Autonomous systems have failed to exploit this logic, relying instead on explicit communication 7; 2; 42; 37 or complex state estimation schemes 18; 37; 51; 13; 26 that can fail when it matters most. Without it, decentralized agents diverge in their world beliefs, and coordination collapses. Here we show that anchoring all agents to a single shared external actor, a common witness whose reactions encode team state, produces spontaneous, communication-free coordination. An allocentric belief network trained on witness behavior allows each agent to independently reconstruct full team state, keeping group beliefs consistent with no inter-agent exchange. Across five competitive environments allocentric belief alignment outperforms egocentric approaches 8; 19; 21 in collective performance, and even scales to sixty-agent teams where standard methods fail. These results establish a new principle for collective intelligence: in the absence of communication, a shared gaze replaces a shared channel.
introduction:
Teams of robots that cannot talk to one another such as drones beyond radio range, or swarms in remote, and undeveloped regions seem limited to what each member can see. Yet hunters coordinate around prey without speaking, because the prey’s reaction tells each hunter what the others know. This is not dissimilar to poker – a popular application in early game theory works 30; 47 – where a skilled player can learn to read another’s tells.
And, although these works did not assume inferential observation they laid the foundation for multi-agent game theory which has since taken root in numerous fields across science and engineering including decentralized
coordination for collective behavior 10; 52; 44; 23; 50; 41; 46; 28. We study a largely unsolved problem arising from this line of research: how can decentralized agents coordinate without communication and with limited sensing? We investigate whether decentralized agents can estimate task-relevant team state by observing a single external actor whose behavior responds to the team. We refer to this actor as a witness. Common witness equilibrium examines how team response policies shape an opponent’s incentives to reveal or conceal information12. Here, we develop learned state estimators and evaluate decentralized control with fixed witness policies across robotic and economic environments.

Decentralized collaborative control in communications-denied environments poses many challenges, but perhaps the greatest obstacle to coordination is severely limited sensing – often modeled as a single field-of-view (FOV) constraint 9; 8; 29; 40 – in which each agent can observe only one environment entity at a time, and complicates group coordination. Furthermore, a common witness outside the team can compound environment complexity by introducing dynamics that can make teammates’ movements incredibly difficult to predict. In order to achieve stable decentralized team behavior in these highly dynamic and complex systems we develop a decentralized Reinforcement Learning (RL) training framework that leverages a centralized expert to learn a decentralized policy. This provides us with a baseline behavior to expect from the multi-agent system, however, the decentralized policies still react from global state. The problem at hand then becomes one of state estimation: how can agents that each observe only a small part of the environment at any timestep maintain consistent and accurate estimates of the global state? Our approach trains each agent to estimate task-relevant team state from a history of observations of the same external actor.

Traditionally, decentralized cooperative teams in partially observable environments attempt to fill the gaps in unobserved environment through state estimation, however, often suffer from the same failure mode: divergence in believed state among agents degrades coordination. Explicit state estimation methods for group coordination such as communications based data-fusion 7; 2; 3157096.3157348, and model-based estimation of unobserved environment variables 18; 37; 51; 13; 26 are plagued by this due to the asynchronicity of individual team members observations. Other methods that support implicitly estimating hidden environment variables from limited observation such as inference learning
43; 25; 3; 15; 36; 48, and stigmergy
39; 49; 6; 20 are often employed to predict more general environment phases or interpret simple passive team messages, and cannot provide rich, full state estimates. As a result, no existing approach reliably provides decentralized cooperative agents with consistent, complete estimates of the global state.

We address these limitations with an allocentric belief network, a mechanism that infers team state from the behavior of a witness which acts as an external reference shared by all agents. Allocentric observation is a popular method in both computer vision and robotics that entails representing observation from a centralized reference point 16; 53; 45; 38. In this work, each agent applies the belief network to observations of the same external actor, providing a common reference for state estimation. This is in contrast to egocentric methods where each agent observes different environment variables as needed – representing the state of the art discussed in the previous passage. The difference between the two is illustrated in Figure 1. Inferring full state from allocentric observation offers two major improvements to the current state of the art: both divergence between agent estimates and complexity of mapping partial-observation to global state is reduced by inferring state from the same information. Our work will highlight that the proposed approach not only produces more agreeable state estimates among decentralized agents, but can more accurately predict general team state than methods that allow for observation of other team members, thereby enabling better coordination. We then leverage the lessons learned on smaller scale collaborative teams to demonstrate allocentric belief’s ability to scale to team sizes where precise coordination is generally believed infeasible.

title: DiWALI: Diffusion Policy Learning in World Models via Latent Action Inference from Human and Robot Play
authors: Akshay L Chandra,Iman Nematollahi,Lingyue Zhao,Daria Kulikova,Angela P. Schoellig,Fabien Despinoy,Abhinav Valada
abstract:
Learning robot manipulation is constrained by the availability of action-labeled robot data,
for both imitation and world models. Humans can demonstrate
skills in seconds, but their demonstrations lack the required robot actions. We introduce DiWALI, a framework that learns and improves diffusion policies within a
world model trained on human and robot play. DiWALI infers latent
actions from consecutive frames using an inverse dynamics model, enabling
world model training without action labels, and grounds them in robot
commands through a decoder trained separately on robot play. Skill policies
are trained over latent actions from action-free human demonstrations and
improved with reinforcement learning in imagination. On the CALVIN
benchmark, DiWALI policies trained solely from human demonstrations substantially
outperform baselines trained with robot demonstrations. Incorporating human play into
the world model training also yields stronger policies after fine-tuning than using the same
amount of robot play alone. Experiments on a physical robot show that skills
learned primarily from human demonstrations are further improved in
imagination with a world model trained on human and robot play. Together, these results demonstrate that human experience can support both manipulation skill acquisition and subsequent policy improvement, reducing reliance on action-labeled robot data. Videos, dataset and code are available at https://diwali.cs.uni-freiburg.de.
introduction:
Robot manipulation data is fundamentally constrained by robot time.
Demonstrations are typically collected through teleoperation, with a single
operator controlling a single robot in real time. As a result, every hour of
recorded data requires roughly one hour of both human and robot
time [1], leaving even the largest robot
datasets small by the standards of vision and language. World models [2, 3]
learned from play can stretch this limited data budget. A single play dataset
collected in a scene can support a simulator in which policies are trained
and refined through imagined
rollouts [4, 5]. However, both the play
data and the demonstrations must still include robot actions, since the
learned dynamics are conditioned on those actions.

Human demonstrations are not subject to the same robot-time bottleneck. A
person can demonstrate a skill in seconds, yielding an order of magnitude
more demonstrations per hour than teleoperation. This
makes human interaction a far more scalable source of behavioral data, and
policies pre-trained on tens of thousands of hours of human data have
required only a few hours of robot data for
adaptation [6].
However, these results rely on sensorized humans using tracked
hands [7],
gloves [6], or handheld and wearable
grippers [8] to convert human motion into action
labels. Plain video of a person acting in the
robot’s workspace provides no such action signal and, moreover, depicts a
different embodiment.

We seek a single model that learns from such video and subsequently serves
as a simulator in which a robot policy can be improved. Two lines of work
each address one half of this challenge. Latent action
models [9, 10, 11] infer
transformations between consecutive frames of action-free video and use them
to pre-train policies, but the learned dynamics serve only as a training
signal rather than as a simulator. Action-conditioned world models provide
such a simulator [12, 13, 14, 15], but require action-labeled data. To our knowledge, no existing method combines both capabilities in a
single learned model that is used to improve a robot policy.

We close this gap with DiWALI, which conditions the world model
on a latent action inferred from two consecutive observations rather
than on a robot command (Fig. 1). An inverse dynamics model
infers this latent action, which the forward dynamics of a recurrent
state-space model use to predict the next latent state. Both are trained
end-to-end without action supervision, so the latent action captures whatever
aspects of a transition are needed to predict the next observation, with the
same representation used for human hands and robot grippers. A single model
can therefore learn scene dynamics from both human and robot play. A small
decoder, trained only on robot play and conditioned on the latent state,
grounds latent actions in executable robot commands, while a diffusion policy
is trained and fine-tuned entirely in the latent action space. The world
model thus serves both as the bridge between embodiments and as the simulator
in which the policy improves.

As imitation takes place in the latent action space, demonstrations no
longer require action labels. A skill shown by a human is encoded as latent
actions, imitated by the diffusion policy and decoded into
executable robot commands. On the CALVIN benchmark [16], a
DiWALI policy trained solely from human demonstrations outperforms
policies trained with a few robot demonstrations, whether based on a world
model conditioned on ground-truth robot actions or a latent action model
with a jointly trained decoder. Human play further broadens the world
model’s training distribution, enabling imagination-based fine-tuning to
produce stronger policies than with the same amount of robot play alone.
Finally, on a real robot, policies learned primarily from
human demonstrations improve further through imagination, without
additional real-world interaction.

In summary, our contributions are:

A latent-action world model for human and robot play: a
recurrent state-space model driven by an inverse dynamics model and trained
end-to-end without action supervision, together with an action decoder
trained separately on robot play and conditioned on the latent state.
The ablations show that both design choices are critical for making the latent
actions decodable.

Skill policies from action-free human demonstrations: diffusion
policies over latent actions that, when trained solely from human
demonstrations, outperform baselines trained with robot demonstrations.

Human play for policy improvement in imagination: action-free
human play is incorporated into the latent-action world model that serves
as the simulator, allowing human experience to shape the imagined rollouts
used for policy improvement rather than only policy pre-training. Policies
fine-tuned in this simulator outperform those fine-tuned with the same
robot play alone.

Real-world validation: the full pipeline, from
play data to a fine-tuned skill policy, deployed on a physical robot.

We make the code publicly available at https://diwali.cs.uni-freiburg.de.

title: RoboMorpher: Scaling Robot Morphology Representations for Cross-Embodiment Action Prediction
authors: Wenwei Lin,Yan Qin,Weiliang Deng,Zixuan Li,Kaixuan Wang,Zanxin Chen,Yue Chen,Tianshuo Yang,Junting Chen,Zhixuan Liang,Yao Mu,Ximin Lyu,Renjing Xu,Ping Luo,Tianxing Chen
comment: Website:this https URL
abstract: Learning shared action representations is central to cross-embodiment manipulation. However, identical joint values can produce different spatial configurations across robots, limiting representations learned from joint values alone. We introduce RoboMorpher, a morphology-conditioned action tokenizer that jointly reconstructs joint angles and link poses to associate control coordinates with their kinematic effects. MorphGen supplies scalable kinematic supervision by generating serial-arm descriptions from survey-derived geometric priors. We pretrain RoboMorpher on 40 million morphology–state pairs and integrate the frozen tokenizer into a vision–language–action policy for discrete prediction and continuous refinement. We also introduce EmbodiBench, a ten-task benchmark with 30 generated URDFs per task. With downstream URDFs excluded from tokenizer pretraining, the policy achieves 56.40% success on RoboTwin 2.0 and 23.27% on EmbodiBench, exceeding continuous joint-space control by 9.73 and 15.34 percentage points. Removing link-pose supervision reduces EmbodiBench success by 17.94 percentage points, supporting morphology-aware geometric supervision for joint-action representation learning.
introduction:
Generalist robot policies learn from demonstrations across platforms [14, 13, 11], but the kinematic meaning of joint-space actions depends on robot morphology. Identical joint values can produce different link poses as link lengths and joint arrangements vary; padding actions to a common dimension does not resolve this ambiguity. End-effector (EE) control provides Cartesian targets but requires robot-specific inverse kinematics and does not uniquely specify the full joint configuration. A shared joint-action representation should therefore preserve control coordinates while accounting for their morphology-dependent spatial effects.

To learn this relationship without collecting manipulation demonstrations for every morphology, we use robot kinematics as supervision. We introduce MorphGen, a procedural generator informed by a survey of 33 URDF/MJCF descriptions. MorphGen normalizes serial-arm kinematics into a common local-ZZ convention, samples six- and seven-joint manipulators from empirical link-length priors, and selects feasible home poses through collision-aware inverse kinematics. Forward kinematics provides link-pose targets for 40 million morphology–state pairs.

We present RoboMorpher, a morphology-conditioned action tokenizer pretrained on these data. Morphology conditions its encoder and decoder, while kinematic-chain attention biases encode relative joint positions along the chain. Joint-angle reconstruction preserves control coordinates, and link-pose reconstruction supervises their kinematic effects. The pretrained tokenizer is then frozen and integrated into a vision–language–action (VLA) policy. Following Discrete Forcing [21], a discrete branch predicts action codes, which are decoded into coarse trajectories and refined by a continuous flow-matching branch. Pretrained morphology features condition both branches.

We evaluate on 15 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks across five embodiments [3] and introduce EmbodiBench, comprising ten tabletop tasks with 30 generated URDFs each. Downstream URDFs are excluded from tokenizer pretraining; policies learn from task demonstrations. RoboMorpher achieves 56.40% and 23.27% success, exceeding continuous joint-space control by 9.73 and 15.34 percentage points. Removing link-pose supervision reduces EmbodiBench success to 5.33%, supporting its contribution to downstream performance.

Our contributions are as follows.

title: Planner-Controller Interaction for Ackermann Navigation: A Matched Simulation and Hardware Benchmark
authors: Moaiz Saeed,Marah Saleh,Mounis Shawgi,Mohamed Al Musleh

abstract: Global planners and path-tracking controllers are often evaluated independently, although their interaction determines how a vehicle follows a planned path. Whether simulation accurately predicts the performance of specific planner–controller combinations on Ackermann-steered hardware remains uncertain. This study evaluated three geometric controllers (Regulated Pure Pursuit, Stanley, and Vector Pursuit) paired with two global planners (Hybrid A* and NavFn) on a 1/10-scale Quanser QCar and in a matched Gazebo simulation. Both environments used shared custom planning and control algorithms, matched route geometry and goals, ground-truth pose references, and a common evaluation pipeline. Five runs per configuration and environment yielded 60 benchmark runs. Controller rankings for tracking accuracy and command smoothness transferred consistently between environments, with Spearman correlations of 0.77–0.94. However, planner-dependent effects showed substantially weaker agreement. In simulation, planner selection changed the root-mean-square (RMS) angular acceleration of the commanded velocities by no more than 0.030 rad/s20.030\text{\,}\mathrm{rad}\text{/}{\mathrm{s}}^{2}, whereas Hybrid A* increased it by 0.141–0.843 rad/s20.1410.843\text{\,}\mathrm{rad}\text{/}{\mathrm{s}}^{2} on hardware, depending on the controller. These differences coincided with planner-dependent achieved speeds that the simulation’s idealised longitudinal response did not reproduce. Mean controller computation times remained below 0.5 ms0.5\text{\,}\mathrm{ms} on the Jetson TX2. The findings demonstrate that agreement in controller rankings does not guarantee accurate prediction of planner-dependent performance for specific controller pairings on hardware, highlighting the importance of physical validation.
introduction:
Autonomous navigation systems separate global planning, which determines a path to the goal, from local control, which generates commands to track that path. The Nav2 framework of the Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2) provides a modular architecture in which planners and controllers can be selected independently Macenski et al. (2020). However, their interaction is particularly important for Ackermann-steered vehicles, which cannot turn in place and are constrained by a minimum turning radius. Grid-based planners may generate paths containing curvature that the vehicle cannot follow Macenski et al. (2026), whereas kinematically constrained planners such as Hybrid A* account for vehicle turning limits during planning Dolgov et al. (2008); Dolgov et al. (2010). Consequently, the global planner determines not only the route but also the tracking demands imposed on the controller.

Geometric path-tracking controllers, including pure pursuit and Stanley, remain widely used because of their low computational requirements and relatively simple formulations Rokonuzzaman et al. (2021). However, their responses to planned path geometry differ. Lookahead-based controllers attenuate local path variations, while controllers incorporating direct cross-track and heading-error feedback respond more closely to the local path geometry. Planner selection may therefore influence each controller differently. The Nav2 maintainers have also recognised this coupling, recommending that path smoothing and controller selection be considered together Macenski et al. (2023a). Despite this, the influence of global planner selection on geometric controller performance, particularly under physical Ackermann steering constraints, remains insufficiently characterised.

Previous evaluations have predominantly compared controllers using fixed paths Patnaik et al. (2020); Dominguez et al. (2016); Kong et al. (2024) or global planners using a fixed controller Borse et al. (2025). Filotheou et al. Filotheou et al. (2020) evaluated combinations of global and local planners on a differential-drive platform, but the physical environment was not matched to the simulated environment. Although small-scale vehicles provide a practical intermediate platform between simulation and full-scale deployment Caleffi et al. (2024), simulation does not necessarily preserve controller performance rankings on hardware Kadian et al. (2020); Kong et al. (2024). Existing comparisons therefore leave two related questions unresolved: whether the effect of global planner selection depends on the controller and whether these planner–controller interactions transfer from simulation to hardware. Addressing both requires matched experiments that control the planning and control implementations, route geometry, localisation reference, and evaluation procedure.

This study investigates these questions through a full-factorial benchmark of three geometric controllers (Regulated Pure Pursuit, Stanley, and Vector Pursuit) paired with two global planners (Hybrid A* and NavFn). Experiments were conducted on a 1/10-scale Quanser QCar equipped with an NVIDIA Jetson TX2 De La Trinidad-Rendon et al. (2025) and in a matched Gazebo simulation. The hardware and simulation environments used ROS 2 Dashing and Jazzy, respectively, while sharing the custom planning and control algorithms, parameters, route geometry, and key performance indicator (KPI) evaluation pipeline. Both environments employed ground-truth pose references to minimise the influence of localisation uncertainty. Five runs were conducted for each planner–controller combination in both environments, yielding 60 benchmark runs. Tracking accuracy, command smoothness, mission efficiency, and embedded computational performance were evaluated.

The study addresses three research questions:

How does global planner selection influence tracking accuracy and command smoothness, and to what extent does this influence depend on the controller?

How does global planner selection influence tracking accuracy and command smoothness, and to what extent does this influence depend on the controller?

Which controller rankings and planner–controller effects transfer from simulation to hardware across the evaluated KPIs?

What computational resources do the planning and control algorithms require on the embedded platform?

The principal contributions are:

A matched simulation–hardware benchmark of six planner–controller configurations on an Ackermann-steered vehicle, using shared custom algorithms and evaluation procedures with documented differences between environments.

A matched simulation–hardware benchmark of six planner–controller configurations on an Ackermann-steered vehicle, using shared custom algorithms and evaluation procedures with documented differences between environments.

A quantitative analysis of planner effects, controller effects, and their interactions, supported by bootstrap confidence intervals, demonstrating substantially larger planner-dependent command variations on hardware than in simulation.

An evaluation of simulation–hardware performance transfer using controller rankings, Spearman correlations, and planner-effect directions, showing that consistent controller rankings do not guarantee reliable prediction of individual planner–controller interactions.

An assessment of computational performance on the Jetson TX2, accompanied by publicly available navigation software, simulation resources, analysis scripts, and processed KPI results.

2. Which controller rankings and planner–controller effects transfer from simulation to hardware across the evaluated KPIs?

3. What computational resources do the planning and control algorithms require on the embedded platform?

title: HINT-WAM: Hindsight-Informed Training for World Action Models
authors: Phuong Tuan Dat,Qi Li,Xinchao Wang
abstract: World action models (WAMs) have shown promising generalization and data efficiency in robot manipulation by coupling action generation with predictions of future visual dynamics. Translating these capabilities into reliable task execution, however, remains a challenge for existing post-training methods. Offline supervised fine-tuning provides dense supervision on expert trajectories, but its flow-matching action expert is trained only on noised demonstration actions and never on the intermediate states produced by its own sampler; task-specific adaptation can also compromise pretrained capabilities. On-policy reinforcement learning trains on the policy’s own behavior, yet sparse task rewards make exploration and credit assignment difficult, while dense reward shaping still provides scalar evaluations rather than direct action targets. We introduce HINT-WAM, the first on-policy self-distillation framework that supervises the action expert on its own sampling trajectories using hindsight, the future video of the demonstration, as privileged information available to the WAM itself. For each demonstration observation, the student generates its action through its own denoising trajectory, and at the states along this trajectory the same model acts as a teacher conditioned additionally on this hindsight, providing a conditional action distribution as a dense training target, while the student sees only deployment-time inputs and needs no environmental rewards or simulator interaction. To transfer this supervision to a flow-matching action expert, HINT-WAM distills the teacher into the student with an energy score, a distribution-level objective that matches the teacher’s action distribution from the student’s own samples rather than regressing its velocity field. The project web is available in this link.
introduction:
World action models (WAMs) have demonstrated promising generalization and data efficiency for robot manipulation by coupling action generation with future visual prediction [17, 49, 21]. Recent models generate continuous action chunks through flow matching, providing an expressive interface between visual predictions and robot motion [21, 2]. Despite this progress, reliable execution on downstream tasks [24, 23] still requires adaptation to task-specific demands and to the deviations that arise during closed-loop interaction.

Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) offers a straightforward adaptation strategy by providing dense action targets from expert demonstrations. However, SFT supervises the model only on demonstration data. During training, the action expert sees only noised versions of the ground-truth actions and never the intermediate states produced by its own sampler, a form of exposure bias [33] and the sampler-level counterpart of the compounding errors at deployment [38], whose environment-level gap requires closed-loop interaction. Moreover, given only the current observation, a demonstrated action chunk is one of several plausible continuations, and the SFT target does not reveal which one the demonstrator followed. Finally, adapting a pretrained model to a narrow task distribution can degrade previously acquired capabilities [40].

On-policy reinforcement learning (RL) addresses the state-distribution mismatch by optimizing the policy on its own rollouts, motivating its use in VLA and WAM post-training [20, 32, 36]. However, many manipulation tasks offer only sparse success rewards, making exploration and credit assignment costly when successful trajectories are rarely sampled. Even with denser, reconstruction-based rewards [36], reward-based optimization only evaluates sampled behavior through scalar feedback, leaving the policy to infer how its actions should change. This motivates supplying structured action supervision directly on the states produced by the policy’s own action sampler.

Our key insight is that the future frames of a demonstration, which we call hindsight, carry privileged information about the intended task progression, connecting learning with privileged information [43, 8] to on-policy distillation [1]. We build on this insight in HINT-WAM: the same model serves as a teacher that additionally reads the hindsight, whereas the student observes only the inputs available at deployment and is supervised on the states produced by its own action sampler. Throughout this paper, on-policy refers to the generation of actions: as in on-policy distillation for language models [1], where prompts are drawn from a dataset and the student generates the response, observations are drawn from demonstrations and the student generates the denoising trajectory of its action chunk. We do not collect new environment states.

Transferring this supervision to a flow-matching action expert introduces a further challenge. Such experts generate continuous actions by integrating a velocity field, so the token-level probability matching used in autoregressive distillation does not apply directly. Regressing the teacher’s velocity field would drive the student toward the teacher’s conditional mean, which averages over modes that the student cannot distinguish without hindsight. We therefore distill the teacher with the energy score [14], a strictly proper scoring rule that matches the teacher’s action distribution from the student’s own samples and one teacher sample.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We introduce HINT-WAM, a self-distillation framework for world action models in which the policy acts as its own teacher given hindsight, requiring neither a separately trained teacher nor environmental rewards or simulator interaction.

We propose a distribution-level distillation objective for flow-matching action experts based on the energy score, which avoids the mode averaging of velocity regression and requires no action-likelihood evaluation. The framework adapts the action expert while keeping the world-modeling backbone frozen.

Comprehensive experiments on LIBERO-90 and RoboTwin 2.0 demonstrate that HINT-WAM consistently improves post-training performance over SFT and matched baselines, while mitigating the catastrophic forgetting of pretrained skills.

1. We introduce HINT-WAM, a self-distillation framework for world action models in which the policy acts as its own teacher given hindsight, requiring neither a separately trained teacher nor environmental rewards or simulator interaction.

2. We propose a distribution-level distillation objective for flow-matching action experts based on the energy score, which avoids the mode averaging of velocity regression and requires no action-likelihood evaluation. The framework adapts the action expert while keeping the world-modeling backbone frozen.

3. Comprehensive experiments on LIBERO-90 and RoboTwin 2.0 demonstrate that HINT-WAM consistently improves post-training performance over SFT and matched baselines, while mitigating the catastrophic forgetting of pretrained skills.

title: Hierarchical Admittance-Impedance Control for Mobile Manipulator Load Transfer
authors: Minghao Xu,Thushara Sandakalum,Christina Dao Wen Lee,Marcelo H. Ang Jr
comment: Accepted at the International Symposium on Robotics Research (ISRR 2026); 5 figures
abstract: This paper presents a hierarchical admittance–impedance controller that combines an inner Cartesian impedance controller, an outer 6D admittance supervisor, and workspace-aware mobile-base assistance for guided load transfer. The method is motivated by assistive tasks such as airport baggage handling, where a robot should support a payload while a human worker guides its motion through small physical forces. Following an interaction-role interpretation of admittance and impedance, the torque-controlled Franka Research 3 manipulator behaves as a Cartesian impedance at the robot–object interface, providing compliant load support around a commanded equilibrium pose. At the human-facing interaction level, the outer admittance supervisor converts measured human wrench input into smooth Cartesian reference motion. The workspace-aware assistance layer shares the admittance-generated translational motion between the manipulator and a velocity-controlled base when larger motion is required, while front-side load alignment keeps the carried object near the robot’s frontal region for safer and more intuitive guidance. The system was implemented in ROS and validated through a suitcase transfer experiment, showing that the robot can support the load while allowing the human to guide the transfer with relatively little effort.
introduction:
Physical human-robot collaboration requires robots to respond safely and intuitively to human-applied forces while maintaining task performance [8, 9]. One motivating application is airport baggage handling, where workers repeatedly lift, pull, reposition, and transfer baggage between carts, conveyors, and aircraft-side equipment. These operations are physically demanding and often involve heavy and/or irregularly shaped objects. A mobile manipulator can assist by supporting most of the payload weight while allowing a human worker to guide the baggage through small corrective forces.

In this setting, the robot should not simply execute a fully autonomous trajectory. Instead, the robot should behave as a compliant partner that reduces human effort while preserving the worker’s authority over the robot motion. The human should be able to push, pull and correct the object’s pose through direct physical interaction, while the robot provides load support and whole-body motion assistance. This requires a control architecture that presents admittance-like behavior to the human while maintaining stable impedance behavior at the manipulator.

The motivation of this work follows the interaction-theoretic view of impedance and admittance introduced by Hogan [1, 2, 3]. Rather than treating impedance and admittance as two alternative controller choices, this work assigns them to different interaction roles. At the robot-object interface, the manipulator behaves as an impedance, regulating the relation between displacement, velocity, and interaction wrench. At the human-robot/object interface, the combined robot-object system behaves as an admittance, where measured human force generates motion. This role assignment motivates a hierarchical architecture in which an inner impedance-controlled manipulator is guided by an outer admittance supervisor.

Prior work has established impedance control for compliant manipulation, admittance control for force-guided motion, and whole-body compliance for mobile manipulators. However, less attention has been given to a simple and implementable hierarchy that combines these ideas for human-guided load transfer, while also extending workspace through the mobile base and maintaining a favorable carrying pose.

This paper presents an implemented hierarchical admittance-impedance controller for a mobile manipulator. The platform consists of a torque-controlled Franka Research 3 (FR3) manipulator mounted on mobile base. The manipulator is governed by an inner Cartesian impedance controller, while an outer admittance supervisor converts measured interaction wrench into desired compliant end-effector motion. A workspace-aware base assistance layer then determines how much of the translational motion should be realized by the mobile base and how much should remain as a Cartesian reference update for the manipulator.

For guided load transfer, safety depends not only on compliant interaction but also on maintaining a favorable loaded configuration. Excessive manipulator extension can move the manipulator toward its workspace boundary, while lateral payload drift can create side loading and an unfavorable load distribution. The proposed supervisor, therefore, includes workspace-aware base assistance to limit manipulator reach and frontal load alignment to keep the payload near the robot’s frontal support region during carrying.

This paper makes the following contributions:

A hierarchical admittance-impedance control framework for human-guided load transfer with a mobile manipulator.

A torque-level Cartesian impedance controller for the FR3 manipulator, that provides local compliant load support around a moving equilibrium pose.

A 6D outer admittance supervisor that converts measured human interaction wrench into smooth Cartesian reference motion.

A workspace-aware mobile-base assistance strategy that shares translational motion between the manipulator and the base, with frontal load alignment to keep the payload in front of the robot.

An experimental suitcase-transfer validation showing that the robot can support the payload while the human provides only small guidance forces.

title: Conceptual full-vehicle modeling of a modular all-wheel-drive robotic ADS test platform as a foundation for a digital twin architecture
authors: Felix Florian Schwald,Martin Meiners,Michael Viehof,Erik Hultman,Edwin Kamau
comment: . Supplementary project files are available atthis https URL
abstract:
This paper presents the development of an initial full-vehicle simulation model of the PixKit modular electric test platform in IPG CarMaker. The objective is to create a physics-based and extendable model structure that can serve as a low-level foundation for future digital twin applications. The reference vehicle is a skateboard chassis combining unconventional vehicle characteristics such as four independent wheel-hub motors and rear axle steering capable of high steering angles. Since complete measurement data of the vehicle is not yet available, the model parameterization is based on a combination of manufacturer documentation, derived values and engineering assumptions. The modeling approach focuses on the system-level integration of the main vehicle subsystems rather than on a fully validated representation.
The resulting model was assessed through basic driving scenarios with different steering inputs and configurations. The simulations showed stable model behavior and physically plausible interaction between the subsystems. The all-wheel-drive configuration produced symmetric wheel responses in longitudinal driving, while counter-phase rear axle steering increased the yaw response and reduced the simulated turning circle diameter compared with front axle steering only. The circular driving scenario further indicated bounded roll and slip behavior. Overall, the implemented CarMaker model provides a traceable and functional simulation basis for the PixKit vehicle. It can support future model refinement, calibration with real vehicle data and development with the goal of creating a validated digital twin architecture.
introduction:
Modular electric vehicle platforms with distributed drives and steer-by-wire functionality provide additional degrees of freedom for vehicle dynamics, control development and automated driving research [1]. Their simulation requires a consistent representation of interacting subsystems such as powertrain, suspension, tires, steering and vehicle body.
The PixKit platform utilized in this work is a modular electric skateboard chassis with all-wheel drive, four wheel-hub motors and selectable steering modes including rear axle steering [2]. These features make the vehicle suitable for future investigations of steering strategies, vehicle dynamics and digital-twin-oriented development. The absence of a parameterized full-vehicle model of the platform available in simulation environments like IPG CarMaker was therefore the reason for this project.
This paper presents the development of a first functional and extendable vehicle model of the PixKit platform in IPG CarMaker. The model is not intended as a fully validated high-fidelity representation of the real vehicle. Instead, it is designed as a physically plausible model that integrates all relevant subsystems in a traceable structure. Due to the incomplete data basis, the parameterization combines documented vehicle data, derived values and assumptions.
The resulting model is evaluated through basic simulation scenarios, including straight-line acceleration, minimum turning circle comparison and steady-state circular driving. These tests are used to assess simulation stability, subsystem interaction and qualitative plausibility of the vehicle response. The main contribution of this work is the structured transfer of the PixKit vehicle architecture into an executable CarMaker model that can serve as a low-level basis for future refinement.
The paper addresses the question of how the PixKit platform can be represented in IPG CarMaker as a functional and extendable full-vehicle model based on incomplete parameter data.
