title: SearchDiffusion: Information-Guided Diffusion Planning for Object Search
authors: Sausar Karaf,Dmitrii Plotnikov,Alexey Kotcov,Dzmitry Tsetserukou
abstract: Object search in unknown environments requires robots to gather useful observations while avoiding obstacles and accounting for limited sensor visibility. We present SearchDiffusion, a diffusion-based planner that generates position and heading trajectories using a learned dense utility map. The map represents geometric accessibility, useful visibility, and semantic progress. It conditions trajectory generation and provides an objective for sampling guidance. Sampled map hypotheses provide additional geometric context, while geometric and heading guidance, validity checks, and analytical selection support execution. Across 90 simulated tasks on 24 map layouts, SearchDiffusion achieved 95.6% target detection at greater computational cost. Ablations show complementary benefits from utility and guidance, with limited additional detection benefit from runtime map hypotheses. In ten physical quadruped trials using OneMap relevance maps, eight were successful under operator assessment, without fine-tuning on real-robot data. These results support combining learned spatial utility with guided trajectory generation for object search under partial observability.
introduction:
Autonomous object search requires robots to gather useful observations while avoiding obstacles. Observation quality depends on the camera’s field of view, range, and viewing direction. Informative path planning therefore considers expected observation value alongside motion and safety constraints.

Diffusion planners learn trajectory distributions and generate candidates through iterative denoising [1, 2]. Object search requires adaptation to new geometric and semantic evidence. Semantic relevance alone does not indicate accessibility or routes that provide useful views, motivating a spatial utility map that relates available evidence to search progress.

We propose SearchDiffusion, a trajectory planner that learns dense utility from geometric accessibility, useful visibility, and semantic relevance. The predicted map conditions trajectory denoising and provides a differentiable objective for sampling guidance.

Counterfactual map hypotheses provide context about unobserved geometry while preserving observed free and occupied cells. Utility, geometric, and heading guidance refine candidates before validity checks and analytical ranking. The robot executes an initial portion of the selected trajectory, updates observations, and replans.

We compare detection, trajectory efficiency, and planning time under matched simulated conditions. Ablations disable inference components with network weights fixed. Physical robot experiments use OneMap [3] relevance maps to demonstrate compatibility with perception-derived inputs.

The main contributions are:

Utility-conditioned trajectory generation.
A learned dense utility map encodes geometric accessibility, useful visibility, and semantic progress to condition trajectory diffusion.

Guidance, validation, and selection.
Utility, geometric, and heading objectives refine candidates during sampling. Validity checks and analytical scoring select a trajectory for partial execution.

Evaluation of component interactions.
Across 90 simulated tasks in 24 map clusters, SearchDiffusion improves detection over the tested baselines. Ablations support combining utility and guidance, with limited additional detection benefit from runtime hypotheses.

A learned dense utility map encodes geometric accessibility, useful visibility, and semantic progress to condition trajectory diffusion.

2. Guidance, validation, and selection.
Utility, geometric, and heading objectives refine candidates during sampling. Validity checks and analytical scoring select a trajectory for partial execution.

3. Evaluation of component interactions.
Across 90 simulated tasks in 24 map clusters, SearchDiffusion improves detection over the tested baselines. Ablations support combining utility and guidance, with limited additional detection benefit from runtime hypotheses.

title: Towards Pose-Robust Few-Shot Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Wenhao Li,Zhongyi Han,Yuhao Wei,Liang Han,Yilong Yin,Liqiang Nie
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: (including supplementary material). Project page:this https URL
abstract:
Fine-tuning a vision-language-action (VLA) model on a few dozen demonstrations is the standard way to put a manipulation policy on a robot, yet the resulting policy silently assumes that the camera and the robot base stay exactly where they were during data collection: a bumped tripod or a base re-docked a few centimetres away makes it reach for the wrong place.
We show that both failures are one phenomenon, a change of the camera-to-base extrinsic that the policy has memorised, and that the robot carries everything needed to undo it.
We introduce WACO, a world-anchored canonicalization framework for VLA models: the arm, placed by forward kinematics at the measured joint angles, serves as a metric calibration target, and the static scene serves as the world anchor that tells a moved camera from a moved robot.
From a single RGB-D frame, WACO estimates both shifts without ground-truth extrinsics or extra data, canonicalises the image to the calibration viewpoint and the state, action and start pose to the calibration base frame, and fine-tunes the unmodified policy under the artefacts of its own estimator.
We also introduce LIBERO-PoseShift, the first benchmark for RGB VLAs with graded camera, base and compound shifts.
Across LIBERO-PoseShift, the LIBERO-Plus camera track and four real-world tasks on a UR5e robot, WACO consistently outperforms the standard few-shot recipe and prior viewpoint-robust methods, raising shifted success by 13.2 points in simulation and by 36.7 points on the real robot, recovering 90% of the simulation gap to a ground-truth oracle and 87% of the real-robot gap, and establishing a new state of the art among methods that use no perturbed training data, with no test-time calibration.
Project page: https://peacelwh.github.io/WACO/.
introduction:
Recent vision-language-action (VLA) models [1, 2, 3, 4] have made few-shot fine-tuning the standard route to a deployed manipulation policy: mount a camera, dock the robot at a table, teleoperate 50–100 episodes, fine-tune a pre-trained model and deploy.
In distribution the recipe works remarkably well; the public LIBERO release of π0.5\pi_{0.5} succeeds in 97%97\% of episodes [5, 6].

However, the demonstrations are collected from a single camera pose and a single robot-base pose, and the policy silently bakes both into its weights.
In practice the tripod gets bumped, the camera is re-mounted after maintenance, or the mobile base re-docks a few centimetres off; each of these is a rigid pose shift of a few centimetres and degrees, and each makes the policy reach for the wrong place (Fig. 1).
A 5∘5^{\circ} camera yaw moves the target by 21 pixels in a 2562256^{2} image; a 5 cm base offset moves it by 5 cm in the frame in which the policy commands its end effector, while the third-person image barely changes.
LIBERO-Plus [7] has quantified the camera half of this problem, with π0\pi_{0} dropping from 94%94\% to 16%16\% under camera perturbations, but the base half has neither a benchmark nor a method for RGB VLAs.
This raises two questions: (1) Can a policy trained at a single camera and base pose be made robust to pose shifts without data from other poses? (2) Can the shifts be recovered at deployment without a calibration object, ground-truth extrinsics or new data?

Existing remedies answer the first question with data or with geometry.
Data-side methods synthesise thousands of viewpoints [8, 9, 10, 7] or regularise the policy across simulator-rendered views [11]; they need perturbed data at a scale that few-shot fine-tuning cannot afford, and they have no counterpart for a moved base, whose action labels change as well as its images.
Geometry-side methods condition the policy on camera rays [12, 13, 14] or re-synthesise the training view [15], but they need the true extrinsics at test time, which a bumped camera no longer has; the one calibration-free VLA we know of [16] regresses the hand-eye transform with an error of 9∘9^{\circ} at a 15∘15^{\circ} shift.
None of them addresses a moved robot base.

We answer both questions with world-anchored canonicalization: instead of asking the policy to learn to generalise across poses from data, we recover the shifts from what the robot already knows and map the observation back to the pose it was trained at.
Three observations make this possible.
First, both shifts are one quantity: each changes the camera-to-base extrinsic 𝐓b​c\mathbf{T}_{bc}, and a base shift also moves the objects in the base frame.
Second, the arm is its own calibration target: forward kinematics at the measured joint angles places every link in the base frame, so the visible arm pins down 𝐓b​c\mathbf{T}_{bc} from a single RGB-D frame, without a checkerboard and without training [17, 18].
Third, the arm alone is not enough: every camera and base shift with the same 𝐓b​c\mathbf{T}_{bc} renders the arm identically yet demands different actions, the classical A​X=Y​BAX{=}YB ambiguity [19], and the static scene provides the missing world anchor for free.
WACO (Fig. 2) turns these observations into a training-free estimator with a ground-truth-free consistency gate, a canonicaliser that warps the image with the camera shift only and re-expresses state, action and start pose with the base shift only, and an error-aware fine-tuning that trains the policy on the canonicaliser’s own artefacts.
The policy architecture is untouched, and a base shift is reduced to “the object is elsewhere on the table”, a variation the demonstrations already cover.

Our contributions are as follows:

We formulate camera and base shifts of a VLA as one extrinsic change, expose the gauge ambiguity of arm-based self-calibration, and show that LIBERO’s world-frame convention silently absorbs base shifts.

We propose WACO, a calibration-free two-anchor estimator, a channel-separated canonicaliser and an estimator-matched augmentation that make an unmodified π0.5\pi_{0.5} robust to camera, base and compound shifts.

We introduce LIBERO-PoseShift, the first RGB-VLA benchmark with graded base and compound shifts and a base-frame protocol that is isomorphic to a real robot.

On LIBERO-PoseShift, the LIBERO-Plus camera track and four real-world tasks on a UR5e robot, WACO outperforms the standard few-shot recipe and prior viewpoint-robust methods, recovers most of the gap to a ground-truth oracle, and gains the most where demonstrations are scarcest.

1. We formulate camera and base shifts of a VLA as one extrinsic change, expose the gauge ambiguity of arm-based self-calibration, and show that LIBERO’s world-frame convention silently absorbs base shifts.

2. We propose WACO, a calibration-free two-anchor estimator, a channel-separated canonicaliser and an estimator-matched augmentation that make an unmodified π0.5\pi_{0.5} robust to camera, base and compound shifts.

3. We introduce LIBERO-PoseShift, the first RGB-VLA benchmark with graded base and compound shifts and a base-frame protocol that is isomorphic to a real robot.

4. On LIBERO-PoseShift, the LIBERO-Plus camera track and four real-world tasks on a UR5e robot, WACO outperforms the standard few-shot recipe and prior viewpoint-robust methods, recovers most of the gap to a ground-truth oracle, and gains the most where demonstrations are scarcest.

title: Proprioceptive Simultaneous Base and Terrain Elevation Estimation for Legged Robot Locomotion
authors: Michael Maravgakis,Stylianos Piperakis,Panos Trahanias
abstract:
Legged robots in visually degraded environments must rely exclusively on
proprioceptive sensing, under which global position and yaw are
unobservable. Vertical drift is particularly detrimental, as it corrupts
the height reference required by swing-leg trajectories and can
destabilize the robot. We treat the terrain itself as a persistent
proprioceptive landmark: every footstep provides a height measurement
that anchors the vertical axis. We propose Simultaneous Base and
Elevation Estimation (SBEE), a real-time open-source framework
in which a Left-Invariant Extended Kalman Filter (LI-EKF) for
floating-base estimation and a grid-based elevation map are coupled in a
bidirectional loop, mirroring SLAM with terrain elevation in place of
landmarks. Stable foot contacts insert uncertainty-aware height samples
into the map, and previously mapped cells are fed back as
uncertainty-weighted vertical pseudo-measurements that act analogously to
loop closures. Unlike contact-aided invariant filters, the LI-EKF consumes
a kinematic velocity measurement instead of augmenting the state with a
contact model per leg, so its state dimension is independent of the
number of legs. We evaluate SBEE in MuJoCo on quadrupedal and bipedal
platforms and on the ANYmal-D GrandTour dataset over 296 m of
locomotion, reducing the absolute trajectory error by 22.1% relative to
the best of three state-of-the-art proprioceptive estimators.
introduction:
Legged
robots have been at the cutting-edge of robotics research for years,
and recently, they have started proving their advanced capabilities in
industrial workplaces. This success is attributed to their ability to
navigate and operate alongside humans in unstructured environments.
By discretizing space through consecutive steps, legged robots can
traverse obstacles, stairs, and other space discontinuities that traditional
wheeled platforms are inherently incapable of navigating.

While discrete foot-ground contacts enable this mobility,
they also pose significant challenges for autonomous operation.
Feedback controllers require continuous, high-rate information to maintain balance; robust locomotion therefore
relies strictly on accurate, high-frequency state estimation.
In visually degraded conditions or
on platforms lacking exteroceptive sensors, estimators must rely entirely
on proprioceptive sensing. As the robot walks over time, relying purely on
this relative proprioception causes the robot’s global pose to
drift arbitrarily from reality, eventually destabilizing the locomotion
controller. This drift is attributed mainly to unmodeled dynamic phenomena,
such as slippage, external forces and collision with obstacles as well as
noisy sensor measurements and additive IMU biases that build up over time.
The obvious solution is an external reference to correct such errors, but by assumption,
there is none available in the very conditions that make proprioceptive estimation
necessary.

Available information to reduce this drift is already present, but it is usually
discarded. Every footstep provides a height measurement expressed in the robot’s base frame.
Once these measurements are retained, the already contacted terrain can serve as a reference point.
Similarly, when lacking external optical references, humans construct an internal
mental map of their surroundings using strictly proprioceptive and tactile
feedback. Each step yields a noisy height measurement, which is subconsciously
fused to calibrate a vertical state estimate. Upon revisiting the same location,
the familiar terrain functions as an absolute spatial anchor. Any uncertainty
in the internal sense of elevation is immediately bounded and corrected by the
mismatch between the anticipated floor height and the physical contact.

This paper formalizes that intuition for legged robots
with either flat or point feet. We propose a real-time proprioceptive state estimation
framework that jointly estimates the robot’s base state and a terrain elevation map using
inertial, force, and kinematic measurements. By acting as the robotic equivalent of
walking in the dark, this framework effectively anchors the unobservable vertical drift, as graphically illustrated
in Fig. 1,
facilitating real-time feedback controllers with continuous, smooth, and globally consistent
state estimates.

title: Remote Teleoperation of Endovascular Robots: A Network Emulation Framework for Systematic Performance Evaluation
authors: Xingyu Chen,Nikola Fischer,Harry Robertshaw,Weiyuan Deng,Christos Bergeles,Thomas Booth
abstract: Remote endovascular teleoperation requires network performance to be evaluated in relation to physical navigation and operator experience, while the effects of network degradation on the usability of remote endovascular systems remain insufficiently characterized from the perspective of clinical users. We developed a network emulation and benchmarking framework that combines an endovascular robot with data streaming. We conducted a user study involving eight clinicians from interventional neuroradiology and general interventional radiology and eight engineering students, who performed 480 navigation attempts across 15 network conditions. Communication performance and received video quality were assessed alongside navigation outcomes, confidence, workload and clinician rated acceptability. Under the most impaired combined condition, success was 78.1%, compared with 93.8% under the reference condition, and mean attempt time increased from 63.5 to 94.3 s. At 5% configured packet loss, 87.5% of attempts succeeded, although all eight clinicians rated the condition unacceptable. Perceived video quality was associated with clinician confidence and acceptability, with mean within participant Spearman correlations of 0.72 and 0.78, respectively. Framework integration on a second robotic platform additionally supported successful remote navigation over a real network. Our framework provides a reusable basis that can help identify communication bottlenecks and assess their effects on navigation and clinician acceptance for endovascular intervention telesurgery tasks.
introduction:
Endovascular interventions use guidewires and catheters to diagnose and treat diseases affecting the blood vessels through minimally invasive access with improved precision and reduced patient morbidity [1]. Robotic manipulation can support controlled device navigation and separate the operator from the radiation environment, while providing a basis for remote intervention [2].

Despite progress in robotic endovascular interventions [3], the process of remote teleoperation remains insufficiently addressed. Remote teleoperated endovascular robots could expand access to urgent procedures by enabling specialists to intervene from geographically distant locations [4]. This is particularly relevant to mechanical thrombectomy (MT) for acute ischemic stroke, an effective treatment [5] whose functional benefit declines with each hour of delay [6, 7]. However, access to MT remains unequitable, constrained by specialist availability and the geographical distribution of MT capable centers [8]. In the United Kingdom, only 4.4% of stroke patients receive MT despite approximately 15% being eligible [9]. Comparable disparities exist internationally: 8.4% of ischemic stroke patients receive MT in Germany [10], 5.6% across the United States [11], and 1.45% in China [12].

Patients presenting to local hospitals with imaging facilities but no MT capability often require transfer to comprehensive stroke centers, adding treatment delays [13]. Remote robotic intervention could allow a distant specialist to perform MT at a suitably equipped presenting hospital, potentially reducing transfer delays, mitigating local specialist shortages and improving resource allocation in time critical care [14].

Fig. 1 illustrates a telerobotic configuration, in which the patient-side robot operates in the operating room (OR) while the clinician manipulates the system in real time from a geographically separated control console via a telecommunication network. In systems that manipulate endovascular intervention instruments, the operator’s inputs drive proximal translation and rotation, whereas navigation decisions depend on the distal tip’s position and orientation within the vasculature. Instrument compliance and friction within the guidewire–catheter–vessel assembly complicate the relationship between proximal inputs and distal motion [15]. Operators use returned images to interpret motion and adjust subsequent commands [16]. Command transmission and visual feedback together close this human-in-the-loop process. Delayed commands affect motion timing, while delayed or degraded images alter the information available for correction. Network performance must therefore be evaluated in relation to the robot, its communication paths and the navigation task [17].

Clinical and preclinical studies have established several remote endovascular capabilities. Patel et al. demonstrated clinical remote percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with on-site support [2]. Cao et al. developed a remote vascular robotic control system using Web Real-Time Communication (WebRTC) and fifth generation of cellular network technology (5G) [18]. Madder et al. performed transatlantic robotic coronary angiography in a phantom and compared on-site and remote catheter engagement across different Internet access modes [19]. In another study, long distance teleoperation has been reported as feasible at transcontinental scales, including separations up to 9000 km9000\text{\,}\mathrm{km} [20]. For neurovascular applications, Duckwiler et al. demonstrated integrated remote control with fluoroscopy and fluid management in a silicone phantom [16]. Olson et al. extended magnetic navigation to intercontinental phantom experiments and demonstrated clot aspiration in selected trials [4].

Controlled impairment studies have begun to quantify how network conditions affect operation. Madder et al. introduced 0–1000 ms of additional signal latency during coronary guidewire navigation in ex vivo and in vivo models, finding that completion time did not differ significantly across the tested range, whereas added delays of at least 400 ms were reported as perceptible [21]. Zhang et al.’s NetFI study combined a physical surgeon console with a Davinc robotic simulation kits to evaluate delay, packet loss and communication interruptions while the returned video was not subjected to the injected impairments [22]. Heemeyer et al. evaluated physical electromagnetic neurovascular navigation under combined latency, jitter, packet loss and bandwidth constraints with eight robotic engineers [23].

However, translating existing evidence into reproducible, system specific communication requirements for remote endovascular intervention remains challenging. A recent discussion paper from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) highlights degraded real-time imaging and asynchronous motion control and audio visual feedback as potential risks of remote teleoperation for endovascular stroke treatment [24]. Inconsistent reporting of network conditions and measurement endpoints limits comparison and replication across studies [17]. Recent multi-parameter investigations have advanced the evaluation of physical endovascular navigation under controlled network impairments [23], but did not include clinician assessments across the tested network conditions. Nevertheless, configured network conditions alone do not describe the command and video performance experienced by the operator, while aggregate latency measures obscure differences between these channels. A remaining need is therefore to connect controlled network conditions, separately measured command and video transmission, and received visual quality with physical navigation outcomes and assessments by clinical users. Such an integrated evaluation is needed to establish how communication degradation affects task performance and operational acceptability, and to inform the design of networks, middleware and video pipelines for remote endovascular intervention. Such evaluation can guide system design and support the progression from demonstrations of remote feasibility towards reliable telesurgery.

In this work, we present a modular benchmarking framework that connects physical endovascular robots and their command and video traffic to configurable ns-3 network emulation [25], with a dedicated GStreamer pipeline for video feedback [26]. The main contributions of this study are summarized as follows: (i) a modular framework for systematically evaluating network conditions through separately measured command and video transmission and received visual quality. (ii) a user study of guidewire navigation in a vascular phantom involving 16 participants, comprising eight clinicians and eight engineering students, who completed 480 navigation attempts across 15 network conditions, combining representative network settings with targeted parameter sweeps. and (iii) implementations across distinct control architectures, including a Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2)-based system [27], and supplementary physical remote navigation over an actual network connection, further demonstrating the framework’s applicability. To our knowledge, this is the first study to integrate systematic network performance evaluation of physical endovascular remote teleoperation with clinician informed assessments. The evaluation jointly characterizes command and video transmission, received visual quality, navigation outcomes and operator experience, providing a basis for interpreting technical degradation in the context of physical operation. The framework provides a common workflow for measuring communication performance alongside navigation outcomes and clinician assessments across robot implementations to identify system bottlenecks and inform communication requirements for future clinical application.

title: QDD-MM: A Simple and Compact Open-Source Muscle Module with Quasi-Direct-Drive Motor for Tendon-driven Robots
authors: Kento Kawaharazuka,Yoshimoto Ribayashi,Takahiro Hattori,Shunnosuke Yoshimura,Kei Okada
comment: Accepted to IEEE-RAS Humanoids 2026, website -this https URL, youtube -this https URL
abstract:
Tendon-driven robots, which actuate like biological muscles by using motors to wind wires, offer advantages such as variable stiffness and redundant actuation.
Despite these advantages, musculoskeletal structures inherently involve a large number of diverse muscles, making it desirable to compactly modularize each muscle unit and flexibly accommodate diverse muscle arrangements.
While various small muscle modules have been proposed to date, existing designs tend to be complex, difficult to maintain, and suffer from low backdrivability and limited actuation speed due to their high gear ratios.
In this work, we propose QDD-MM, a muscle module that leverages recent advances in quasi-direct-drive motors to achieve a simpler and more compact structure with higher backdrivability and faster actuation than previous modules.
By utilizing quasi-direct-drive motors, the module eliminates the need for dedicated force-sensing mechanisms, significantly simplifying the overall design, while also supporting flexible wire routing in multiple directions, various module-to-module connections, and even the use of the module body itself as a structural component.
QDD-MM integrates these capabilities into a reusable muscle module, and its design is openly available at github.com/haraduka/qddmm.
We developed tendon-driven robots with one joint and either two or three muscles, as well as a partial musculoskeletal humanoid, using the proposed QDD-MM and verified their effectiveness.
We expect that this muscle module will democratize tendon-driven robotics and further accelerate progress in the field.
introduction:
A variety of tendon-driven humanoids that closely mimic human anatomical structures have been developed to date [1, 2, 3, 4].
Beyond purely biological imitation, many tendon-driven robots have been created to leverage the advantages of wire-driven actuation [5, 6, 7, 8, 9].
These robots offer numerous benefits, such as enabling variable stiffness control through nonlinear elastic elements [10, 11], maintaining functional operation even after muscle failure due to redundancy [12], allowing flexible changes in body morphology by reconfiguring wire routing [9], and reducing the weight of distal body segments by proximally locating actuators [7, 8].

However, musculoskeletal structures tend to become complex because they involve a large number of diverse muscles.
Thus, it becomes crucial to compactly modularize each muscle and to ensure that the muscle module can accommodate a wide variety of possible muscle arrangements.
If the same muscle module can be used across different body parts, the design and fabrication of tendon-driven robots become significantly easier, and maintainability is improved.

Motivated by these challenges, several small muscle modules have been proposed in previous work [13, 2, 14, 15].
These modules commonly have adopted a slender cylindrical form factor and integrate a BLDC motor, a custom motor driver, a pulley for wire winding, and a tension sensor.
Although relatively compact and capable of supporting diverse wiring configurations, these modules employ small motors paired with high gear-ratio transmissions for miniaturization.
As a result, they suffer from low backdrivability and limited actuation speed.
Furthermore, the high gear ratio makes it difficult to estimate muscle tension from motor current alone, necessitating dedicated force sensors.
This increases structural complexity and reduces maintainability.
QDD actuation has also been applied to cable-driven robots.
Mi et al. developed a modular tensegrity robot with QDD cable actuators, enabling force estimation and variable stiffness control without external force sensors [16].
Sawaguchi et al. developed Vlimb, a wire-driven wearable robot using AK60-6 actuators and reconfigurable wire routing to balance lifting capability and reachability [17].
These studies establish the applicability of QDD actuation to cable-driven systems.
Our focus is an open-source, reusable muscle module with configurable wire outlets and module connections, together with a direct experimental comparison against a conventional high-gear-ratio muscle module.

In this work, we propose Quasi-Direct-Drive Muscle Module (QDD-MM), a muscle module that leverages quasi-direct-drive motors [18] to achieve a simpler and more compact design, while providing high backdrivability and fast actuation that exceed those of previous muscle modules.
Recent advances in quasi-direct-drive motors have significantly improved torque density and efficiency, making it possible to generate sufficient muscle force even with low gear ratios.
Consequently, by reducing the gear ratio, backdrivability can be improved and dedicated force-sensing mechanisms can be removed, which greatly simplifies the structure of the muscle module.
In addition, QDD-MM retains the capabilities of previous modules, such as flexible wire routing in multiple directions and support for various module-to-module connections.
It also introduces a mechanism that allows the module itself to serve as a structural component of the robot body.
The contribution of QDD-MM lies in integrating configurable wire routing, parallel and series module connections, and structural use of the module body into a compact, open-source design available through the Supplementary Materials.
The high torque density and backdrivability originate primarily from the commercial QDD actuator; our module design makes these properties usable across different tendon-driven structures through common mechanical interfaces.
Fig. 1 illustrates the concept of constructing diverse tendon-driven robots from a common muscle module, with the full humanoid on the right representing a future application.
Using QDD-MM, we constructed tendon-driven robots with one joint and either two or three muscles, as well as a partial musculoskeletal humanoid, and we verified their effectiveness experimentally.
We show that a simple one-joint–two-muscle tendon-driven robot can be extended by using an additional muscle through modular connections, and that a compact tendon-driven robot can be realized by using the muscle module itself as a skeletal structure.
These results suggest that tendon-driven robots, which have long been considered difficult to work with, may become increasingly accessible and continue to advance through the use of the proposed module.

title: Old Experience, New Lessons: Relabeling Autonomous Robot Rollouts in Interactive Imitation Learning
authors: Zhaoting Li,Cosimo Della Santina,Jens Kober
abstract:
Interactive imitation learning enables robots to learn from human
interventions during deployment. These interactions naturally produce sparse
human corrections and abundant autonomous robot experience without human
action labels. Yet existing methods either leave this experience unused for
action supervision or imitate historical robot actions, which can reinforce
suboptimal behavior. To address this limitation, we propose
Set-valued Relabeling of Autonomous experience (SeRA), a framework that learns from
autonomous robot experience through set-valued supervision of policy
relabels. Later policy checkpoints relabel this experience, and agreement
across checkpoints filters the relabels. Since agreement does not guarantee
correctness, SeRA constructs desired action sets around accepted relabels.
Following Set-Supervised Diffusion Policy (SDP), it trains an action-chunking
diffusion policy to increase the probability of actions within these sets.
A step-masked denoising loss combines accepted relabels with
available human corrections in partially supervised chunks. Experiments
across five simulated manipulation tasks in online and offline settings show
that SeRA improves policy performance over SDP and outperforms baselines that imitate
historical robot actions or exact relabels. On a real-robot tomato-picking
task, SeRA achieves 80% success, compared with 40% for SDP, using the
same human feedback and training budget. These results demonstrate that
relabeled autonomous robot experience can complement human corrections to
improve policy performance.
introduction:
Learned manipulation policies remain vulnerable to failures around contacts,
task bottlenecks, and states outside the demonstration distribution.
Interactive imitation learning (IIL) addresses these failures by allowing a human
teacher to intervene during deployment and provide
corrections [1, 2]. These interactions
naturally produce two streams of data: sparse human corrections and abundant
autonomous robot experience without human action labels. Learning only from
the corrections leaves this experience unused for action supervision. We
instead treat it as unlabeled data and seek to learn from it alongside human
corrections.

Prior work has sought to exploit autonomous robot experience by retaining
historical robot actions as imitation targets. IWR imitates these actions
alongside human corrections [3]; CEILing uses additional evaluative
feedback to select useful behavior [4]; and
Sirius downweights pre-intervention actions using intervention
context [5]. However, autonomous actions need not be optimal,
even when they do not trigger an intervention or occur in a successful
trajectory. Retaining them as targets can therefore reinforce suboptimal
behavior. This raises a central question: how can autonomous robot experience
support policy learning without imitating imperfect historical robot actions?

Our key insight is that later policies incorporate additional human
corrections and may generalize these corrections to observations collected
earlier. We use the latest policy to relabel autonomous robot experience
and accept these relabels based on agreement across later policy checkpoints.
Yet agreement alone does not
guarantee correctness: multiple checkpoints can share the same error.
Directly imitating even these accepted relabels can reinforce prediction
errors through confirmation bias [6]. Learning
from this experience therefore requires supervision that tolerates imperfect
relabels.

In this work, we introduce Set-valued Relabeling of Autonomous experience
(SeRA),33
3
            
            
          Webpage: https://sera-webpage.github.io/ a
framework that combines policy relabeling with set-valued supervision for
action-chunking diffusion policies. Building on Set-Supervised Diffusion
Policy (SDP) [7], we supervise each accepted relabel with a
desired action set: a region of action space centered at the relabel, whose
radius is scaled by its distance from the historical robot action. Rather
than requiring the relabel itself to be optimal, we assume that the desired
set contains an optimal action. Following SDP, we train the policy
to increase the probability of actions within the desired sets. A further
challenge arises because intervention boundaries and relabel filtering leave
action chunks only partially supervised. Discarding these chunks would
waste usable feedback. We therefore introduce a step-masked denoising loss that
combines retained human corrections and accepted relabels within a chunk,
learning from supported steps while excluding unsupported steps.

We evaluate SeRA in online and offline learning across five simulated
manipulation tasks and in a real-robot tomato-picking task. Comparisons with
methods that imitate historical robot actions and with exact relabel
imitation examine how autonomous robot experience contributes to policy learning,
while ablations assess each component of SeRA. Across these
experiments, SeRA consistently outperforms the baselines.

In summary, this work makes the following contributions:

Set-valued supervision of policy relabels to learn from autonomous
robot experience, using checkpoint agreement to accept relabels and
desired action sets to relax exact matching of these imperfect relabels.

A step-masked denoising loss that learns from partially supervised action
chunks by combining retained human corrections and accepted relabels.

An evaluation in online and offline simulation and on a real robot,
with baseline comparisons and component ablations.

1. Set-valued supervision of policy relabels to learn from autonomous

desired action sets to relax exact matching of these imperfect relabels.

2. A step-masked denoising loss that learns from partially supervised action

3. An evaluation in online and offline simulation and on a real robot,
with baseline comparisons and component ablations.

title: CommDreamer: Radio-Geometric World Models for Mapless Cellular-Connected UAV Trajectory Planning
authors: Yuqi Ping,Tianhao Liang,Tingting Zhang
abstract: Reliable cellular connectivity and collision-free flight are essential for unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) operations in low-altitude urban canyons, where dense 3D buildings obstruct flight clearance, shadow serving base stations, and create strong co-channel interference at street intersections. Existing planners either require prior 3D city meshes and channel knowledge maps unavailable onboard, or rely on model-free reinforcement learning with low sample efficiency and poor cross-city generalization. We propose CommDreamer, a mapless radio-geometric world model that fuses raw onboard 3D LiDAR scans, multicell cellular reports, and shift-invariant relative kinematics to jointly infer local obstacle clearance and directional signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) dynamics. Using a categorical recurrent state-space model, CommDreamer compresses multimodal measurement histories into a coordinate-invariant latent belief, enabling the UAV to foresee deep shadow zones and train a lightweight online policy purely via multi-step latent imagination without prior maps or antenna patterns. Zero-shot evaluations across unseen urban morphologies in our open-source ray-tracing simulator, AeroCity-RT, show that CommDreamer converges within 150150 episodes where model-free reinforcement learning fails to complete flights, achieving 100.0%100.0\% mission success with zero collisions while lifting median route SINR to 8.02​dB8.02\,\mathrm{dB} and cutting effective SINR outage by over 50%50\% relative to radio-blind world-model and reactive LiDAR baselines.
introduction:
Rapid growth of the low-altitude economy has accelerated urban deployments of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) for parcel delivery, infrastructure inspection, and emergency rescue [1, 2]. Safe execution of such missions requires reliable command, control, and payload links between the UAV and ground cellular base stations (BSs) [3]. Unlike flights at high altitude with dominant line-of-sight (LoS) propagation, urban airspace below rooftop height experiences coupled collision risks and abrupt coverage degradation: dense 3D buildings obstruct flight clearance, cast deep non-LoS (NLoS) shadow fading on serving BSs, and expose UAVs at street intersections to strong LoS co-channel interference from neighboring sectors, causing severe signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) outages [4, 5]. Safe and connectivity-aware trajectory planning in unfamiliar urban canyons is therefore essential.

Early trajectory planning relied on mathematical optimization under statistical path loss or probabilistic LoS models [6, 4], which average out local building geometry and miss sharp shadowing transitions. Subsequent studies adopted channel knowledge maps (CKMs) [7] and ray tracing simulators such as Sionna RT [8] for site specific channel modeling, yet both offline trajectory optimization [9] and CKM aided planning depend on prior information unavailable onboard during flight, including global 3D city meshes, full area radio maps, and exact BS antenna patterns. Although deep reinforcement learning (DRL) relaxes explicit channel priors in communication-aware trajectory planning [10, 11], existing DRL planners still suffer from poor generalization across cities and low sample efficiency: policies conditioned on global coordinates over a fixed BS layout memorize a city specific SINR lookup map that fails in unseen cities [10], whereas model-free value and actor-critic planners [11] map instantaneous observations directly to actions without a predictive model of blockage and interference evolution, requiring extensive interactions and failing to foresee abrupt corner outages [12].

To address these challenges, we propose CommDreamer, a radio-geometric world model for mapless cellular-connected UAV trajectory planning in unfamiliar urban canyons. Our core physical insight is that the omnidirectional 3D building facades captured by raw onboard LiDAR point clouds are the exact scatterers governing directional LoS blockage and intercell interference shielding, inherently coupling visible street geometry with multicell radio propagation. Inspired by DreamerV3 [13], which decouples dynamics modeling from policy learning via imagined rollouts, CommDreamer compresses local LiDAR and cellular measurement histories into a compact latent belief invariant to global coordinates, eliminating explicit 3D maps and global CKMs. Predicting future trajectories in latent space enables the UAV to foresee upcoming shadow zones and interference surges, bypassing obstacle traps and coverage holes with a lightweight online policy. Our main contributions are threefold:

We formulate mapless cellular-connected UAV trajectory planning as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) invariant to coordinate shifts, driven solely by raw onboard 3D LiDAR point clouds, multicell RSRP and SINR reports, and relative BS and goal kinematics without prior 3D maps or BS antenna patterns.

We develop a multimodal radio-geometric world model fusing spherical LiDAR projections with symlog encoded cellular and kinematic features inside a categorical recurrent state space model (RSSM), jointly inferring local obstacle clearance, directional LoS/NLoS shadowing, and multicell interference dynamics for multi-horizon latent trajectory optimization.

We build an open-source 3D urban wireless simulator, AeroCity-RT11
1
https://github.com/ppppyq/AeroCity-RT, coupling procedural city generation and 3GPP multicell deployments with Sionna RT ray tracing [8]. Zero-shot evaluations across unseen urban morphologies show that CommDreamer converges within 150150 episodes where model-free DRL fails to complete flights, achieves 100.0%100.0\% mission success with zero collisions, boosts mean route SINR by 1.59​–​1.78​dB1.59\text{--}1.78\,\mathrm{dB} to 7.69​dB7.69\,\mathrm{dB} and median SINR by 3.31​–​3.64​dB3.31\text{--}3.64\,\mathrm{dB} to 8.02​dB8.02\,\mathrm{dB}, and cuts effective link outage by 50.1​–​51.5%50.1\text{--}51.5\% down to 12.0%12.0\% over radio-blind world-model and reactive LiDAR baselines.

title: ProbeShare: Probing a Few, Sharing Across Many for Fast World-Model Planning
authors: Zejian Kang,Xiantao Lin,Zekai Chen,Boyang Shen,Mingyu Ma,Shengwen Zheng,Chengtai Guo,Xiangru Huang
abstract: Visual planning with a frozen joint-embedding world model supports robotic reaching and object manipulation by evaluating candidate action sequences against an image goal before execution. Standard cross-entropy method (CEM) planners roll out every candidate independently through a billion-parameter predictor, even when nearby actions induce similar scene changes. This redundant computation grows with population size and search rounds, slowing closed-loop replanning. We observe that candidates within a planning step share an observation history and thus a common action-to-feature map. Based on this insight, we propose ProbeShare, which measures local responses with a few representative probes and reconstructs each candidate’s feature grid through scene-conditioned, geometry-aware weighting. When promising candidates move beyond existing probe coverage, ProbeShare evaluates a new probe to rescore nearby candidates. Across four RoboCasa tasks, ProbeShare accelerates episode planning by 43.843.8–128.9×128.9\times over dense RoboJEPA and at least 14.2×14.2\times over competitive baselines, with greater mean goal progress in a matched-time comparison.
introduction:
A robot reaching a target evaluates candidate motions with different directions and step sizes. A joint-embedding world model predicts the visual features at the end of each proposed action sequence [1, 30]. The cross-entropy method (CEM) [23] ranks candidate sequences by their feature distance to the goal image and samples new sequences around the lowest-cost candidates. Selecting spatial features or compressing the latent state reduces the cost of each rollout [26, 27, 11]. As CEM narrows its search, many candidates differ only slightly in their commanded motion. Dense CEM still evaluates each through a separate rollout.

These candidates share an observation history and hence an action-to-feature map. If the predicted features vary approximately linearly with small changes in the commands, a few rollouts can describe that variation across nearby candidates. ProbeShare measures these local responses using selected action sequences, termed probes. It weights nearby probes using action geometry and a scene-conditioned similarity learned offline from the frozen model’s predictions. When the weighted probe motion differs from a candidate’s motion along a probed direction, shifting weight between opposite probes corrects the difference. The planner applies the adjusted weights to the full probe grids and compares the reconstructed features with the goal.

In later rounds, CEM may favor motions beyond the coverage of the initial probes. ProbeShare groups these promising sequences by their commanded motion. It evaluates a representative when its distance to the nearest probe is large relative to the spread of motions in its group. This single rollout supplies a feature grid that is reused to rescore nearby candidates in the current and subsequent rounds. After the robot executes the first command, the planner builds a fresh probe bank from the new observation.

This reuse enables a larger search under the same time budget. On RoboCasa’s obstacle-reaching task with a five-step horizon, ProbeShare scores 40 times as many candidate sequences per episode as dense CEM at a target budget of 569 s per episode. Across four paired starts, the end effector moves an average of 26.0 cm closer to its goal over eighteen actions with ProbeShare and 17.0 cm with dense CEM (Figure 3). Our contributions are as follows:

Feature sharing across action candidates. We reconstruct each candidate’s full feature grid from a few probe rollouts using action geometry, scene-conditioned similarity and a correction along the probed directions.

Search-guided probe selection. We use provisional goal scores and distances to existing probes to select representative actions whose predictions can be reused across nearby candidates and search rounds.

Efficient closed-loop planning. Across 16 paired starts on four RoboCasa tasks, ProbeShare accelerates episode planning by 43.843.8–128.9×128.9\times over dense CEM at the same search size (Table 1). At comparable planning times, mean terminal reward on obstacle reaching rises from 0.361 with dense CEM to 0.532 with ProbeShare.

1. Feature sharing across action candidates. We reconstruct each candidate’s full feature grid from a few probe rollouts using action geometry, scene-conditioned similarity and a correction along the probed directions.

2. Search-guided probe selection. We use provisional goal scores and distances to existing probes to select representative actions whose predictions can be reused across nearby candidates and search rounds.

3. Efficient closed-loop planning. Across 16 paired starts on four RoboCasa tasks, ProbeShare accelerates episode planning by 43.843.8–128.9×128.9\times over dense CEM at the same search size (Table 1). At comparable planning times, mean terminal reward on obstacle reaching rises from 0.361 with dense CEM to 0.532 with ProbeShare.

title: Neural Network-Based In-Contact Task Segmentation of Demonstrated Robot Motions via Hand Guiding
authors: Johannes Hartwig,Marcello Kögler,Dominik Henrich
comment: Extended abstract, accepted and presented at the 1st German Robotics Conference (GRC 2025), Nuremberg, 13-15 March 2025; no official proceedings, not peer-reviewed; see alsothis https URL
abstract:
Intuitive robot programming approaches, such as Programming by Demonstration, enable non-experts to teach robots tasks through hand-guided demonstrations.
However, for in-contact tasks requiring force control for parts of the motion, automated segmentation of motion types is crucial for improving usability.
Considering the related work, this work proposes a neural network-based segmentation method categorizing motion into three fundamental types using input data of cartesian twists and wrenches at the end effector.
We collect demonstration data using a 7-axis robot with a wrist-mounted force torque sensor and generate ground truth labeling by hand.
While still in development, our research direction aims to enable non-experts to program in-contact tasks more intuitively.
introduction:
The shortage of skilled workers significantly affects the economy, making automation a key strategy to enhance work efficiency [1].
As more affordable robot models enter the market [2], cobots are also becoming accessible to small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).
Nevertheless, hiring a robot expert to program such systems is often not affordable for SMEs.
Intuitive robot programming approaches focus on simplifying robotic systems and minimizing this problem by enabling non-experts to program them [3].

Programming by Demonstration (PbD) provides an intuitive solution by allowing users, for example, to move the robot along the desired path via hand guiding [4, 5].
However, the robot’s trajectory alone is sometimes not sufficient to achieve all the goals intended by the user.
For some tasks, the interaction force with the environment is also required (e.g., during surface treatment or assembly).
Therefore, these so-called in-contact or contact-rich tasks require a specification of position and force over time.
To enable non-experts to program such tasks, we extend an existing intuitive programming framework [6, 7] for pick-and-place tasks to in-contact tasks.
For this, we developed an intuitive visualization and force input method via a touch GUI in our previous work [8, 9].
To further extend our approach, measuring the interaction forces with the environment directly during the user’s demonstration would be beneficial.
Often, a wrist-mounted force torque sensor [10, 11] or a sensor attached to the environment [12] is utilized.

The user typically demonstrates a task of different motion segments during the programming process.
For example, when wiping a whiteboard with an already gripped sponge, the segments are approaching, wiping, and departing the whiteboard (see Fig. 1).
Segmenting and labeling the recorded path data is a lengthy and complex task that exceeds non-experts’ capabilities.
Therefore, automating this procedure is necessary for an intuitive workflow.
The advantages of such segmentation are, for example, extraction of the end condition of the segment, optimization of the movement (acceleration, adaption through machine learning models), or visualization in the programming system.

While previous literature has proposed various labeling approaches (see Sect. II), we aim for a method segmenting a robot motion into universally applicable motion types related to the fundamentals of force-controlled actions [13, 14].
To achieve this, we categorize motion segments into three distinct types:
(a) Guarded motion, which terminates upon reaching a predefined force/torque condition (Fig. 1(a));
(b) Compliant motion, where interaction with the environment continues until a specified trajectory is completed (Fig. 1(b));
(c) Free space motion, where the robot moves without external contact (Fig. 1(c)).
A key advantage of such a segmentation approach is its generality, as these three motion types allow for a complete and assumption-free decomposition of any demonstrated task.

Early segmentation methods relied on rule- and threshold-based techniques [15, 16], which limit adaptability across various tasks, application areas, and robotic systems.
To overcome these limitations, we propose a research direction exploring machine learning-driven segmentation.
By training a model to classify motion segments, we aim to eliminate the need for predefined thresholds, creating a more adaptive and parameter-free method.
Our goal is to enable non-expert users to intuitively program general in-contact tasks, enhancing the accessibility of robot programming.
We start by reviewing related work with a focus on machine learning approaches (Sec. II), followed by our proposed method (Sec. III), and conclude the extended abstract in Sec. IV.

title: TapTacTouch: Shape Completion from Sparse Tactile Contacts with Geometric Priors
authors: Yoobin Shin,Jaeyoung Lee,Jieun Kang,Hyun Song,Woojin Kim,Andrew Jaeyong Choi
abstract: 3D object reconstruction is essential for robotic perception and manipulation, yet conventional approaches predominantly rely on visual observations that can be limited by occlusion or unavailable in visually constrained environments. In this work, we propose a vision-free, training-free, and category-agnostic framework for reconstructing 3D object meshes from sparse tactile contacts without relying on pretrained shape models. A 6-DoF robotic arm equipped with a 20-DoF multi-finger robotic hand collects tactile observations using 3 × 3 pressure sensor arrays mounted on the finger pads. The acquired tactile measurements are transformed into 3D contact constraints through robot kinematics and integrated into a multi-scale Gaussian Process Implicit Surface (GPIS). To address sparse and incomplete surface observations, the proposed method incorporates contact-confidence weighting, weak pseudo-surface constraints, and an observation-driven geometric prior to preserve local surface geometry and provide structural guidance in unobserved regions. Real-world experiments on six objects achieve a Chamfer Distance (CD) of 1.610, an Earth Mover’s Distance (EMD) of 7.738, and an F-Score of 95.00, with reconstruction completed in an average of 49.99 s per object. These results demonstrate that sparse tactile sensing can provide sufficient geometric information for continuous 3D object reconstruction without visual or semantic information.
introduction:
3D object reconstruction is an important component of robotic perception and manipulation, enabling robots to understand object geometry for downstream tasks such as grasping, interaction, and shape-aware manipulation [1, 2]. Many existing 3D reconstruction approaches rely primarily on visual observations, including RGB and depth images, to recover object geometry [1]. Although vision provides rich global information, its effectiveness can be limited in real-world manipulation scenarios. In particular, parts of an object may be occluded by the robotic hand, surrounding objects, or the object itself, making it difficult to obtain complete geometric information from visual observations alone [3, 4]. This limitation becomes more pronounced in cluttered environments, where multiple objects may further restrict camera visibility [3].

Tactile sensing provides an alternative means of perceiving object geometry through direct physical interaction. Unlike vision, tactile sensing does not rely on line-of-sight visibility and can acquire local contact information from regions that are difficult to observe from external viewpoints [1, 2, 5]. These characteristics make tactile sensing particularly suitable for robotic manipulation scenarios in which visual information is limited or unavailable [4, 6].

In this work, we investigate whether a robot can reconstruct the 3D geometry of an object using tactile data alone, without relying on external cameras or explicit object class labels. We propose a vision-free 3D mesh reconstruction framework using a 6-DoF robotic arm equipped with a 20-DoF right robotic hand. During interaction with an object, tactile data are collected from sensors mounted on the finger pads of the robotic hand and used to infer the object geometry. We employ Gaussian Process Implicit Surfaces (GPIS) [7, 6] to reconstruct a continuous object surface from the acquired tactile contacts and extract its 3D mesh. Since GPIS does not require data-driven model training, the proposed framework can reconstruct previously unseen objects directly from tactile measurements without a separate training stage or explicit object category information. Fig. 1 illustrates the overall pipeline from tactile data acquisition and point-cloud construction to GPIS-based 3D mesh reconstruction.

We evaluate the proposed approach on a physical robotic system using tactile data collected through direct interactions with real objects. The proposed framework reconstructs 3D object meshes from sparse tactile contacts without requiring visual input, prior knowledge of the object class, or model training. Once the tactile contacts are acquired, the GPIS-based reconstruction generates a 3D mesh in approximately 20 s, demonstrating that object geometry can be recovered efficiently without a separate training stage. Our real-world experiments demonstrate the feasibility of training-free, tactile-only 3D reconstruction and highlight the potential of tactile sensing for object reconstruction in scenarios where visual sensing is limited or unavailable.

The main contributions of this work are as follows:

We propose a vision-free 3D object reconstruction framework that reconstructs object meshes using tactile data alone.

We develop a tactile data acquisition pipeline using a 6-DoF robotic arm and a 20-DoF robotic hand equipped with finger-pad tactile sensors.

We validate the proposed framework on a physical robotic platform using real objects, demonstrating the feasibility of tactile-only 3D mesh reconstruction in real-world settings.

1. We propose a vision-free 3D object reconstruction framework that reconstructs object meshes using tactile data alone.

2. We develop a tactile data acquisition pipeline using a 6-DoF robotic arm and a 20-DoF robotic hand equipped with finger-pad tactile sensors.

3. We validate the proposed framework on a physical robotic platform using real objects, demonstrating the feasibility of tactile-only 3D mesh reconstruction in real-world settings.

title: High-Precision Docking of Differential-Drive Mobile Robots Through LiDAR and Vision Collaboration
authors: Zaide Zhang,Zheyuan Zhang
abstract: Precise docking requires a differential-drive robot to correct lateral offset through coupled rotation and translation within a short approach distance. We combine global navigation with terminal control using complementary LiDAR and visual observations. A line fitted to the cabinet front gives normal distance and heading. An AprilTag identifies the workstation; intersecting its center ray with the LiDAR plane determines tangential position. Taught observations define the docking reference and can cancel repeatable fixed biases under unchanged mounting and geometry. Lateral pre-alignment and continuous visual servoing coordinate the approach, with predictive stopping to account for low-speed actuation lag. Across two sessions using the same navigation and docking code at five workstations on Robot 2, all 111 tasks completed, including 101 on the first attempt. Relative to the taught observations, onboard longitudinal, lateral and heading residual root-mean-square values were 1.51 mm, 5.93 mm and 0.238∘0.238^{\circ}, respectively. Joint acceptance within ±10\pm 10 mm per position axis and ±1∘\pm 1^{\circ} heading was 96.4% (107/111), or 95.5% (106/111) with a ±0.5∘\pm 0.5^{\circ} heading limit.
introduction:
A differential-drive robot cannot translate sideways. Millimeter-scale lateral alignment at a workstation must therefore be achieved through coupled rotation and translation, while the remaining distance for correction shrinks near the endpoint. Turning in place can introduce additional lateral slip. For food-service robots retrieving ingredients or operating equipment at cabinet fronts, the controller must align position and heading within a confined approach region. Reaching a nearby map goal does not by itself establish the required pose relative to the physical interface.

Simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM)[1], SLAM Toolbox[2], and Navigation2[3] support travel between workstations, with local motion controlled through methods such as model predictive control[4] and regulated pure pursuit (RPP)[5]. Terminal docking also requires observations of the workstation. V-shaped features[6] and reflective markers[7] make LiDAR targets identifiable but require dedicated geometry or reflective material. Fitting a scan line to an ordinary cabinet front yields normal distance and heading. Translation along that surface leaves the line unchanged, so tangential position requires another reference.

AprilTag[8, 9] identifies the workstation and establishes a visual position reference. Perspective-nn-point (PnP) methods, including infinitesimal plane-based pose estimation (IPPE)[10], estimate pose from planar image features; refined tag edges improve feature measurement[11]. As the projected tag shrinks with range, pixel perturbations propagate differently into lateral position and depth. We retain the tag-center bearing and intersect its ray with the LiDAR surface, assigning heading feedback to LiDAR.

We implement this allocation with a taught reference and a terminal controller on Robot 2. Across two sessions with the same navigation and docking code, all 111 tasks completed and 107 met a unified onboard feedback residual criterion of ±10\pm 10 mm per position axis and ±1∘\pm 1^{\circ} in heading. The contributions are:

A local three-degree-of-freedom feedback construction that combines surface normal distance and heading with tag-based tangential position, including a taught zero-residual condition and distance-dependent compensation.

A differential-drive docking controller that combines affine lateral pre-alignment, distance-scheduled steering, and predictive stopping.

A workstation-level evaluation of 111 same-version tasks that distinguishes completion, first-attempt success, and residual acceptance.

title: Worth Another Look:Constrained World-Model Planning for Visual Inspection
authors: Ziyue Kang,Zixi Qi,Yuchen Dai,Nana Lv,Xirong Cheng,Liang Liu,Ying Li,Haoyan Wei,Haiyang Yao
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Multimedia (cs.MM)
abstract: Visual inspection in field robotics and environmental monitoring must localize multiple targets under strict compute and sensing caps. Exhaustive sweeps waste calls on absent classes, while myopic and search-free policies stumble over heterogeneous tariff cliffs or discard viewport edits whose value emerges only after re-querying. We formulate inspection over frozen detectors as neuro-symbolic observation planning under partial observability, decoupling a compact recurrent world model (WM) from exact symbolic feasibility and tariff rules. Receding-horizon beam search with online replanning jointly schedules class queries, crops, enhancements, and termination (stop), paired with slack-aware shadow pricing and legal fallback at larger budgets. Across eight terrestrial, optical, and sonar benchmarks, multi-step lookahead outperforms static schedules and search-free offline RL under tight budgets—gaining up to 28.4 AP percentage points over static priority on RUOD and 15.1 on ARIS—while dynamic pricing lifts large-budget performance on all eight domains at 11 ms planning cost. Ultimately, pairing lightweight learned dynamics with exact symbolic constraints turns frozen detectors into adaptive, budget-aware inspection agents without retraining.

title: Dual-Actuation Emulation of Scaled Relative Orbital Dynamics on a Free-Flyer
authors: Elias Krantz,Pedro Roque,Gunnar Tibert,Huina Mao,Christer Fuglesang
comment: . Presented at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Space Robotics (iSpaRo); to appear in IEEE Xplore
abstract: Ground-based free-flyer testbeds reproduce the planar motion of a free-floating spacecraft using air bearings, but not the relative dynamics of spacecraft in orbit. We present a dual-actuation architecture that physically emulates Clohessy–Wiltshire dynamics on an open-source free-flyer. Two model predictive controllers run in parallel: one drives the solenoid thrusters with an orbital dynamics model, representing the spacecraft under test; the other drives bidirectional propellers that physically apply the orbital accelerations, continuously updating its reference to account for thruster-induced velocity changes. A dynamic similitude maps the orbital scenario onto the limited floor area and actuation rates of the testbed, letting the spacecraft controller run directly at orbital scale. We validate the architecture on hardware and against a high-fidelity orbital simulation, where the orbital accelerations instead arise naturally, both driven by the identical spacecraft controller. Their agreement indicates that the testbed reproduces the relative orbital motion the controller would encounter in flight.
introduction:
Ground-based spacecraft simulators are essential tools for developing and validating guidance, navigation, and control algorithms for on-orbit proximity operations [1, 2]. These testbeds typically employ flat surfaces and air bearings to approximate undamped planar motion, enabling the study of microgravity rendezvous, docking, and formation flying scenarios [3]. While they closely reproduce free-floating rigid-body dynamics, they do not capture the relative dynamics of spacecraft in orbit, commonly described by the linearized Clohessy–Wiltshire equations [4]. Emulating these dynamics requires physically applying Clohessy–Wiltshire-equivalent accelerations to the platform while it executes spacecraft maneuvers.

Physically emulating these accelerations on a free-floating testbed has been attempted in only a few works, which fall into two families. One commands the platform’s own compressed-air thrusters to apply the Clohessy–Wiltshire-equivalent accelerations, with the laboratory-to-orbit mapping derived through Buckingham’s Π\Pi theorem, emulating coasting trajectories with an open-loop model-following controller [5]; the same Π\Pi-theorem similitude has since been applied to emulate other scaled space dynamics on air-bearing platforms [6]. Sharing one actuation system between emulation and spacecraft control has two drawbacks: the on-off, duty-cycle nature of solenoid thrusters limits the resolution of the continuous orbital forces, and a fixed share of the thrust budget must be reserved for the emulation. A second family tilts the support surface so that gravity supplies the in-plane acceleration [7]. Kinematic and hybrid simulators, by contrast, reproduce orbital motion through robotic manipulators or motion tables that constrain the platform [1].

We present a dual-actuation architecture that emulates relative orbital dynamics on a free-flyer while preserving its free-floating motion, demonstrated on the open-source ATMOS platform [8]. ATMOS moves nearly frictionless over a flat, level floor on air bearings, with compressed-air solenoid thrusters providing holonomic three-degrees-of-freedom actuation in the plane (position and yaw). By adding a dedicated, propeller-based actuation modality for the emulation, the architecture separates dynamics emulation from spacecraft control, each driven by its own Model Predictive Controller and tuned independently (see Fig. 2).

Closing the loop on both roles avoids the open-loop error accumulation of model-following emulation and supports active translational and attitude maneuvers concurrently with the applied orbital forces. We map the orbital scenario onto the testbed using the similitude established for Clohessy–Wiltshire emulation on air-bearing testbeds [5], applied so that the spacecraft controller runs directly in the orbital scale and is identical on hardware and in high-fidelity simulation. We openly release the controller stack, the propeller-module documentation, and the supporting PX4 airframe, so the emulation can be reproduced on any ATMOS platform and adapted to similar free-flyers.

The main contributions of this work are:

A dual-actuation architecture that decouples dynamics emulation from spacecraft control, driving each role with its own closed-loop model predictive controller and continuously updating the emulated Clohessy–Wiltshire acceleration reference to account for the spacecraft’s commanded thrust.

A propeller actuation module that applies these accelerations as continuous proportional thrust, removing the duty-cycle quantization of on-off thrusters and adding a second actuation modality to ATMOS.

An experimental and numerical validation comparing hardware emulation on ATMOS against a high-fidelity Basilisk simulation [9], both driven by the same spacecraft controller operating in the orbital scale.

title: Efficient World-Model Planning via Physics-Guided Search Distillation
authors: Hongyu Zhang,Xiaoshuai Hao,Heye Huang,Qingwen Meng,Wenjun Shi,Jianao Xu,Xin Hu,Xuanru Jin,Jingyi Zhang,Baicang Guo
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
World models support autonomous driving by evaluating candidate trajectories through predicted future scene evolution.
However, accurate future prediction does not ensure road-compliant execution; when all candidates violate road boundaries, re-ranking cannot select a feasible trajectory.
We propose Physics-Guided Search Distillation (PGSD), a single-view planning framework that combines future representations and execution feedback for verified beyond-pool repair through three components:
(1) Execution-Aware Selection checks ego-vehicle road compliance under simulated execution and selects the highest-scoring feasible trajectory;
(2) a Clearance-Aware Search Teacher generates beyond-pool corrections and selects demonstrations with larger minimum road-boundary clearance during execution to buffer imitation errors;
and (3) a Future-Conditioned Repair Student predicts one correction from rewarder features and execution feedback for single-rollout verification.
The pretrained planner and rewarder remain frozen; no future scenes are generated online.
On NAVSIM v1, single-view PGSD achieves 90.97 PDMS, exceeding all compared prior single-view planners and retaining 73.2% of the search teacher’s PDMS gain over execution-aware selection.
On NAVSIM v2 navhard, it reaches 38.96 EPDMS, improving on WorldDrive by 11.24 points (40.5%).
The student replaces up to ten search rollouts with a single verification rollout per repair trigger.
HUGSIM Hard examples provide qualitative evidence of zero-shot transfer.
introduction:
End-to-end autonomous driving has attracted increasing attention by learning to map sensor observations to driving trajectories [1, 2, 3]. Driving world models extend this capability by anticipating action-conditioned scene evolution, using predicted visual, structured, or latent representations to inform planning [4, 5, 6]. Such future evidence helps evaluate the consequences of alternative maneuvers, but prediction fidelity alone does not establish the quality of a candidate plan. The vehicle must also execute the chosen motion within road boundaries under its tracking controller and dynamics. Near a road edge, tracking error and vehicle footprint can turn a seemingly acceptable nominal path into an infeasible execution. Planning benchmarks and closed-loop simulators therefore evaluate executed behavior rather than prediction quality alone [7, 8, 9]. This motivates explicit execution checks alongside predictive scene features.

Existing world-model planners generate candidate trajectories and select a plan through future-aware scoring [6, 10], as illustrated in Figure 1(a). A distilled rewarder supplies predictive evidence without generating future scenes online. However, candidate evaluation leaves two execution gaps. First, future-aware selection does not establish road compliance under tracking. Second, re-ranking is bounded by candidate coverage: even a perfect ordering cannot return a feasible trajectory when the retained pool contains none. Our diagnostic on 12,146 NAVSIM v1 scenarios identifies 278 requiring intervention, including 106 (38.1%) without a road-compliant in-pool alternative. These cases require beyond-pool correction. Physical search can find such corrections, but repeated rollouts are costly. Learning to imitate search introduces a further difficulty: a teacher trajectory that barely passes the execution constraints leaves little tolerance for student prediction errors. Low action error alone may then fail to preserve the teacher’s feasibility. This motivates clearance-aware demonstrations and a future-conditioned policy verified with one rollout.

In this paper, we propose Physics-Guided Search Distillation (PGSD), combining execution-aware selection with our search teacher and repair student (Figure 1(b,c)). Execution-Aware Selection (EAS) first checks tracked vehicle footprints and selects a road-compliant in-pool trajectory when available. For triggered cases without a feasible alternative, our offline Clearance-Aware Search Teacher (CAST) searches for lateral corrections and prioritizes larger minimum executed road-boundary clearance. The larger target margin buffers imitation errors under the same verifier. Our Future-Conditioned Repair Student (FCRS) then maps frozen rewarder features and physical execution feedback to one beyond-pool correction. The future features supply candidate-conditioned scene context, while execution feedback describes tracking errors and road clearance. PGSD thus transfers inherited predictive knowledge into corrective action while keeping the planner, rewarder, and pretrained physical branch frozen; only the added future-conditioned branch is learned. Single-Rollout Verification (SRV) checks the predicted correction and retains the EAS reference if verification fails. With single-view visual input and map-based execution geometry, PGSD achieves 90.97 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 38.96 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 navhard. The student retains 73.2% of the search teacher’s incremental gain over EAS while replacing up to ten search rollouts with one verification rollout; HUGSIM provides complementary qualitative zero-shot examples.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

Execution-aware selection and beyond-pool repair. We address both executable candidate selection and the absence of a feasible in-pool plan, mapping inherited future features and physical feedback to a verified correction.

Clearance-aware search distillation. We select teacher corrections by minimum executed road-boundary clearance, providing a geometric buffer against imitation errors and distilling search into one student prediction.

Single-view planning with fixed repair cost. Two NAVSIM benchmarks demonstrate improved planning with one additional verification rollout, while controlled ablations isolate clearance supervision, execution feedback, and future conditioning.

1. Execution-aware selection and beyond-pool repair. We address both executable candidate selection and the absence of a feasible in-pool plan, mapping inherited future features and physical feedback to a verified correction.

2. Clearance-aware search distillation. We select teacher corrections by minimum executed road-boundary clearance, providing a geometric buffer against imitation errors and distilling search into one student prediction.

3. Single-view planning with fixed repair cost. Two NAVSIM benchmarks demonstrate improved planning with one additional verification rollout, while controlled ablations isolate clearance supervision, execution feedback, and future conditioning.
