title: LaST1.0: A Unified Latent World-Action Model with Control-Centric SpatioTemporal Reasoning
authors: Hao Chen,Xuheng Zhang,Zhuangzhe Wu,Jiaming Liu,Shaobo Zhang,Jialin Gao,Zhonghao Yan,Di Wu,Sixiang Chen,Peng Jia,Chi-Wing Fu,Shanghang Zhang,Pheng-Ann Heng
abstract: World-Action Models couple action learning with future prediction, enabling robotic policies to capture environmental dynamics for robust control. However, prevailing methods take a reconstruction-oriented approach to model future videos, allocating substantial capacity to appearance details that are incidental to control. In this work, we reformulate world modeling for manipulation as control-centric future prediction in latent space, and present LaST1.0, a unified latent World-Action Model. Rather than modeling an observation-complete video future, LaST1.0 predicts compact, geometry-aware latent targets derived from future wrist views, focusing the supervision on the evolving robot–object interactions required for fine-grained manipulation. To better support this control-centric paradigm, LaST1.0 revisits the visual input interface and attention mechanism of its unified architecture. It adopts a vision-encoder-free design with a lightweight patch embedder, exposing fine-grained visual cues directly to the backbone, and introduces LaST-Attention for structured spatiotemporal interactions across modalities. Evaluations across two robot embodiments, five challenging manipulation tasks, and three simulation benchmarks—RLBench, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus—demonstrate that LaST1.0 achieves state-of-the-art success rates and generalizes to novel scenarios. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of control-centric latent world modeling for robust manipulation.
introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have become a strong foundation for generalist robot manipulation by directly mapping visual observations and language instructions to actions [1, 2, 3, 4]. Despite their strong visual and semantic capabilities, the imbalance between dense visual inputs and sparse action supervision can lead to shortcut mappings rather than learning underlying physical dynamics [5, 6].
Consequently, these models can struggle with robust control in complex scenarios that require anticipation of future interactions.
World-Action Models (WAMs) address this limitation by coupling action learning with future-state prediction, using future prediction as an auxiliary objective that encourages the shared representation to capture task-relevant changes in the environment [7, 8, 9, 10].

A central question, however, is what a policy model should predict about the future. Many existing WAMs instantiate future-state modeling through video generation [5, 7, 11, 9].
While visually expressive, this paradigm allocates substantial capacity to texture, illumination, background appearance, and other photometric details that have little bearing on the next physical interaction [6].
In contrast, fine-grained control depends more directly on localized object motion, relative geometry, contact configuration, and how the interaction region between robot-object evolves over time.

We therefore propose that world modeling for manipulation should be control-centric rather than observation-complete. For manipulation, the future latent representation should satisfy three properties: (1) preserve the geometric evidence needed for precise action, (2) focus modeling capacity on the region where interaction occurs, and (3) provide predictive supervision during training without becoming mandatory computation at deployment. This perspective changes the role of future prediction: the goal is not to reproduce the world in all observable detail, but to predict the subset of future dynamics that is useful for control.
Guided by this principle, we introduce LaST1.0, a unified latent WAM that jointly optimizes action generation and control-centric future dynamics prediction. Rather than predicting appearance-oriented video latents or visual-semantic image latents, LaST1.0 utilizes a geometry-aware encoder [12] to construct compact targets exclusively from future wrist-camera observations, as described in Fig. 1(a). This concentrates the latent supervision on the interaction region, forcing the policy to capture fine-grained relative motions and robot–object geometric relationships. Crucially, our experiments reveal that formulating latent world modeling as a training-time regularizer not only yields improved performance but also enhances closed-loop control efficiency.

To operationalize this control-centric paradigm, we further redesign the visual interface and attention mechanism for LaST1.0, as shown in Fig. 1(b) and (c). Semantic vision encoders and reconstruction-oriented VAEs can bias visual representations toward high-level semantics or appearance reconstruction, potentially attenuating the localized visual details vital for manipulation [13, 14, 15, 16, 17]. LaST1.0 therefore adopts a vision-encoder-free interface, using a lightweight patch embedder to project raw image patches directly into the unified Transformer backbone, thereby preserving fine-grained visual cues. Within this backbone, rather than relying on conventional attention mechanisms, we introduce LaST-Attention to facilitate the spatiotemporal fusion of multimodal information across 4D subspaces (token sequence, image height, image width, and relative time), effectively supporting our latent world-action modeling paradigm.

For evaluation, we deploy LaST1.0 across two distinct embodiments, utilizing both parallel grippers and dexterous hands across five challenging manipulation tasks. These tasks evaluate the model’s ability to perform fine-grained control, spatial reasoning, and long-horizon manipulation. Empirical results demonstrate that LaST1.0 achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) success rates, exhibiting remarkable generalization to novel object, background, and position settings. Moreover, evaluations on three benchmarks—RLBench, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus—confirm that LaST1.0 outperforms prior SOTA baselines, further validating the efficacy of our latent world-action modeling paradigm, as shown in Fig. 1(d).
The main contributions of this work are as follows:

We reformulate world modeling as the prediction of geometry-aware, control-centric future dynamics in latent space, using latent targets derived from future wrist views to capture evolving robot–object interactions.

We introduce LaST1.0, a latent World-Action Model that natively unifies vision-language understanding, latent world modeling, and action generation. Within this model, we design a vision-encoder-free interface and LaST-Attention to preserve fine-grained spatial cues and facilitate structured spatiotemporal fusion across modalities.

Experiments demonstrate that LaST1.0 achieves state-of-the-art performance across two embodiments, five challenging manipulation tasks, and three simulation benchmarks, together with robust generalization to novel scenarios.

1. We reformulate world modeling as the prediction of geometry-aware, control-centric future dynamics in latent space, using latent targets derived from future wrist views to capture evolving robot–object interactions.

2. We introduce LaST1.0, a latent World-Action Model that natively unifies vision-language understanding, latent world modeling, and action generation. Within this model, we design a vision-encoder-free interface and LaST-Attention to preserve fine-grained spatial cues and facilitate structured spatiotemporal fusion across modalities.

3. Experiments demonstrate that LaST1.0 achieves state-of-the-art performance across two embodiments, five challenging manipulation tasks, and three simulation benchmarks, together with robust generalization to novel scenarios.

title: CoRA-VTLA: Contact-Guided Attention and Queryable Response Memory for Tactile Post-Training
authors: Chengye Song,Rui Song,Shengqi Wang,Jiawei Zhang,Hongzhou Wang,Xueyang Guo,Yang Liu

abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models reuse visual and linguistic knowledge across manipulation tasks [6, 24, 39]. Yet precision manipulation requires corrections after contact: small alignment errors can jam assemblies, while excessive force can deform parts or fixtures [46, 8]. Visual observations guide approach and alignment but cannot reliably distinguish free motion from hidden resistance once parts touch. This makes post-contact adjustment crucial in assembly and delicate handling. In peg insertion, combining visual feedback with wrist force/torque measurements improves policy learning [26]. In Fig. 1(a), a part appears aligned but stops advancing against a fixture. Tactile sensing reveals such interactions and supports corrective action. Tactile data are scarce in VLA pretraining. Task demonstrations with tactile observations offer a practical route to post-training for contact-rich manipulation [48].

Force-aware control uses measured loads to guide motion [30]. Tactile prediction provides supervision for learning contact dynamics [48, 22]. Force histories have also been used to track task progress through repeated contact events [28]. The challenge during recovery is to determine which recent responses matter for the next correction. For example, initial engagement and a sustained jam can produce similar instantaneous loads, yet call for continued insertion or withdrawal and realignment (Fig. 4). Prior work uses executed motion to interpret sensor measurements [4] and predict tactile signals during slip [34]. For recovery, we consider how past contact responded to motion and which responses matter in the current state. How can a pretrained policy retrieve the contact responses most relevant to its next action?

Tactile post-training also challenges visual grounding. Prior work uses the location of touch to relate local readings to the full visual scene [31] and uses tactile geometry to localize grasped parts for insertion [27]. Direct tactile injection can disrupt visual dynamics modeling in world action models [47]. In VLAs, direct tactile fusion can draw action-expert attention away from the target, motivating adaptive tactile injection [29]. On matched MuJoCo observations, direct tactile fusion likewise produces more dispersed main-camera attention for the first action token at layer 17 (Sec. 4.4). Regulating tactile injection leaves a spatial question open: which image regions correspond to the sensed contact? Reliable correction therefore requires both identifying where contact occurs and retrieving how it has evolved in response to motion.

To address these challenges, CoRA-VTLA is proposed as a tactile post-training framework combining response-aware action generation with spatially grounded tactile perception. At the action level, a queryable action–response memory encodes measured contact changes and retrieves responses conditioned on current contact and robot state. At the perception level, contact-guided gaze supervision directs a tactile semantic token’s visual attention toward projected fingertip contact regions. The two mechanisms support different aspects of contact-aware correction within one pretrained VLA. The action expert combines retrieved responses, current feedback, and VLM task context to generate the next action chunk. The main contributions are summarized as follows:

Queryable action–response memory.
CoRA-VTLA introduces state-conditioned retrieval of measured contact responses for corrective action generation, with next-step response prediction on task demonstrations to initialize action-side tactile encoders.

Contact-guided gaze supervision.
Projected fingertip contacts provide spatial supervision for grounding tactile semantic representations in visual contact regions during VLA post-training.

Simulation and real-robot evaluation.
CoRA-VTLA achieves 73.33% mean success across three custom MuJoCo tasks, compared with 50% for direct tactile fusion with matched inputs. The memory design reaches 67% on a public UniVTAC optical-tactile task [8]. The full framework averages 66.7% across three real-robot tasks.

title: 3DTouch: A Tactile-aware VLA Model with 3D Geometric Relations for Dexterous Manipulation
authors: Xin Zhang,Shiqi Zhang,Siyuan Cao,Juncheng Cai,Yedong Shen,Yuxuan Gao,Dianlong Wen,Kaixue Long,Lu Zhang,Yao Li,Jiajun Deng,Yanyong Zhang
abstract: In contact-rich dexterous manipulation, occlusion by the fingers and interacting objects obscures local geometry, preventing visual observations from fully capturing contact locations. Visually similar scenes may also differ subtly in the relative positions of interacting objects, leading to different contact states. We propose 3DTouch, a tactile-geometric conditioning approach for vision-language-action (VLA) models. 3DTouch constructs a shared 3D visuo-tactile representation by expressing RGB-D scene points and dense five-finger tactile measurements in the robot-base frame, preserving each taxel’s spatial location and force vector. Hand–object and object–object relations derived from hand landmarks and pose-aligned reconstructed surfaces explicitly describe the relative arrangement of interacting entities. Together, these representations condition the VLA action expert on spatially localized contact forces and relative surface geometry, providing explicit cues for contact adjustment and object alignment. We evaluate 3DTouch on five real-world contact-rich dexterous manipulation tasks using a UR7e robot arm equipped with an XHand dexterous hand. 3DTouch improves the average success rate by 42 percentage points over the corresponding VLA baseline and by 20 percentage points over the strongest evaluated alternative. Ablation studies reveal the complementary benefits of scene geometry and spatial tactile feedback, with further gains from shared spatial grounding and explicit geometric relations.
introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated promising capabilities in general robotic manipulation through large-scale pretraining on robot manipulation data  [16, 2, 1].
However, contact-rich dexterous manipulation remains challenging, as small deviations in object alignment or contact conditions can lead to task failure. Similar visual observations may correspond to different physical interaction states, requiring the model to refine actions according to additional contact information. Moreover, visual observations alone usually lack critical local manipulation geometry, especially under occlusion which commonly occurs in dexterous manipulation. These limitations show the necessity for fusing complementary geometric and tactile information into VLA models to support precise action control.

Recent studies have explored incorporating 3D spatial information and tactile feedback into robot policies.
3D-aware VLA methods mainly adopt two schemes to integrate spatial information, using 3D positional encoding to fuse depth with visual features
 [24],
or conditioning the action expert with separately encoded geometric features extracted from 3D reconstruction
 [36]
or observed point clouds
 [4].
Additionally, tactile-aware VLA methods incorporate tactile feedback into action generation by encoding tactile data as additional input tokens alongside visual-language tokens [12, 32].
3D visuo-tactile methods further represent visual observations and gripper tactile measurements as 3D points for visuo-tactile fusion, preserving their spatial relationships [11].

Despite these advances, two key limitations remain for contact-rich dexterous manipulation. First, although 3D visuo-tactile methods have explored unified visual-tactile 3D representations for policy learning, how to effectively encode spatially grounded multi-finger tactile feedback for pretrained VLA models remains underexplored.
In particular, without explicitly associating multi-finger taxel force measurements with their corresponding 3D locations in scenes, the model may struggle to relate local contact conditions of the hand to surrounding objects.
Second, downsampled scene point clouds are often too coarse and heavily occluded during five-finger grasping to capture small interaction clearances. Even when complete object surfaces are tracked, implicitly inferring fine-grained hand–object and object–object alignment without explicit relational descriptors remains challenging.
These limitations motivate jointly modeling spatially grounded tactile feedback and explicit interaction relations to support precise dexterous manipulation.

To address these challenges, we propose 3DTouch, a 3D conditioning approach to enhance pretrained VLAs with spatially encoded tactile representations and explicit interaction relations for contact-rich dexterous manipulation. As shown in Fig. 1, 3DTouch consists of two complementary modules. 3D Tactile Grounding (3DTG) represents RGB-D scene point clouds and dense five-finger tactile measurements in a shared robot-base coordinate system. By encoding each taxel’s 3D position alongside force vectors, 3DTG provides tactile tokens spatially aligned with scene tokens.
Geometric Relation Modeling (GRM) further leverages kinematic hand landmarks and tracked 3D object surface points in the robot base frame to construct hand–object and object–object relation tokens, explicitly encoding relative displacements and distances between interacting entities. Together, spatially grounded tactile feedback supports
contact-aware motion refinement under visual ambiguity,
while explicit interaction geometry facilitates more precise
hand–object positioning and object–object alignment.
The resulting scene, tactile, and relation tokens jointly enhance VLA models for dexterous action generation.

We evaluate 3DTouch on five real-world contact-rich dexterous manipulation tasks using a UR7e robot arm equipped with an XHand dexterous hand. 3DTouch improves the average success rate by 42 percentage points over the corresponding VLA baseline and 20 percentage points over the strongest tactile-aware VLA. Ablation studies demonstrate the complementary benefits of scene geometry and spatial tactile feedback, with shared spatial grounding improving the average success rate by 11 percentage points over hand-local tactile encoding. Explicit interaction geometry further improves the average success rate by 12 percentage points, showing improvements in target localization and grasp stability during dexterous manipulation.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We propose 3D Tactile Grounding (3DTG), which encodes dense five-finger tactile measurements and RGB-D scene geometry in a shared 3D coordinate system, providing spatially localized tactile feedback.

We propose 3D Tactile Grounding (3DTG), which encodes dense five-finger tactile measurements and RGB-D scene geometry in a shared 3D coordinate system, providing spatially localized tactile feedback.

We introduce Geometric Relation Modeling (GRM), which constructs structured hand–object and object–object representations from hand landmarks and 3D object geometry, explicitly encoding task-relevant relative displacements and distances for dexterous action control.

Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of 3DTouch on real-world dexterous manipulation tasks, with ablations validating the benefits of multimodal spatial grounding and explicit geometric relations, particularly with stronger target localization and grasp stability.

1. We propose 3D Tactile Grounding (3DTG), which encodes dense five-finger tactile measurements and RGB-D scene geometry in a shared 3D coordinate system, providing spatially localized tactile feedback.

2. We introduce Geometric Relation Modeling (GRM), which constructs structured hand–object and object–object representations from hand landmarks and 3D object geometry, explicitly encoding task-relevant relative displacements and distances for dexterous action control.

3. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of 3DTouch on real-world dexterous manipulation tasks, with ablations validating the benefits of multimodal spatial grounding and explicit geometric relations, particularly with stronger target localization and grasp stability.

title: Effects of Locomotion and Viewpoint Control on Immersive Robot Telepresence for Navigation and Inspection
authors: Ammaar Zaman,Neven ElSayed,Oliver Prentner,Mohamed Ellethy,Mostafa M. Lotfy,Maram Selsabila Mahmoudi,Eduardo Veas
abstract: In many robot telepresence interfaces, movement and viewing are managed through handheld inputs. This can divide attention between steering, looking, and inspection. We compared joystick versus omnidirectional treadmill locomotion and joystick-based versus head-guided camera control in a within-subject 2×22\times 2 study in which 17 participants used a virtual reality headset to guide a quadruped robot through a physical maze while locating marked wall symbols and capturing them as visual evidence. Mixed-effects analyses showed that head-guided camera control was associated with faster completion, lower wall-contact cost, lower workload, and more favorable presence, usability, technology acceptance, and flow than joystick-based camera control. The strongest overall objective performance was observed in the joystick locomotion plus head-guided camera condition, whereas the omnidirectional treadmill plus head-guided camera condition emerged as the strongest experiential compromise. Exploratory camera analyses showed that head-guided camera control reduced switching, increased reliance on the pan-tilt view, and supported a more stable viewing strategy across the maze. These strategy differences were consistent with part of the performance advantage, especially for wall-contact duration. Targets captured remained near ceiling and simulator sickness remained low across all conditions. Overall, the results indicate that viewpoint control was the stronger differentiator in this combined navigation and inspection task, while locomotion still shaped the objective and experiential tradeoff.
introduction:
Mobile robot telepresence is increasingly relevant in scenarios where people must act in spaces that are distant, hazardous, or difficult to access directly. In these settings, the operator must do more than drive a remote platform from one point to another. The operator must also inspect the environment, notice relevant details, and make decisions through mediated perception. Telepresence has developed from simple mobile video access toward richer robotic systems that support navigation, inspection, collaboration, and remote action across domains such as industry, healthcare, and hazardous field work [1, 2]. In parallel, immersive interfaces have become more prominent in robot operation, with recent reviews showing growing interest in VR based control, visualization, and interaction [3, 4]. This shift matters because immersive telepresence involves concurrent driving, inspection, and viewpoint management.

In many practical situations, operators must keep making progress while searching for cues, checking objects or structures, and documenting what is found. This creates a dual task burden in which navigation competes with visual inspection for attention and control. Work on multiple resource use and task switching suggests that performance can suffer when perceptual and control demands compete for overlapping resources [5, 6]. In telepresence, this burden is often expressed through viewpoint management. The operator must decide when to keep moving, when to reorient attention, and how to coordinate robot motion with the currently available view. Prior teleoperation research shows that camera and viewpoint control can directly shape workload, visual attention, usability, and operational performance [7, 8, 9].

These challenges drive a shift from telepresence as remote control toward telepresence as body coupled interaction at a distance. Conventional telepresence interfaces control robot motion and viewpoint through handheld input. They can be convenient and familiar, but they divide attention across multiple control loops. A body coupled interface translates body motion to robot control and head motion to viewpoint, linking movement and looking to bodily action. Prior telepresence work connects agency, self-location, and perceptual transparency to how naturally the operator can act through the remote system [10, 11]. Head-based viewpoint control has shown promise in teleoperated tasks, but the joint role of body coupled locomotion and camera control in immersive robot telepresence is underexplored [12, 13, 9].

We study this question in a robot navigation and inspection task. Participants wear a VR headset and teleoperate a quadruped robot through a physical foam-wall maze, while searching and capturing wall symbols as visual evidence. The study compares conventional joystick control for locomotion and viewpoint with omnidirectional walking and head tracking respectively in a within-subject 2×22\times 2 design. Hereby, whole-body locomotion on an active omnidirectional treadmill is paired with head tracking for loco-viewpoint control of a quadruped robot. Since the robot has no human-like body, the study focuses on the relation between user action, camera control, robot response, and remote visual feedback [3, 14].

Across the mixed-model analyses, head-guided viewpoint control was associated with faster completion, lower workload, and more favorable presence, usability, technology acceptance, and flow than joystick-based viewpoint control. Joystick locomotion with head-guided viewpoint showed the strongest objective performance, while body coupled locomotion with head-guided viewpoint offered the strongest experiential compromise. Target capture was near ceiling and simulator sickness remained low across all conditions. Overall, the results suggest that, in telepresence tasks combining movement and inspection, body coupled locomotion is most useful when the viewpoint control keeps visual inspection easy to maintain.

title: Facet-SLAM: Real-Time Triangle Splatting SLAM
authors: Edward Beng Wai Tan,Siew-Kei Lam
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Dense SLAM systems based on 3D Gaussian splatting build maps that render photorealistically, but their surface geometry is poor, and obtaining a mesh requires extraction or fusion stages. Triangle splatting avoids this with surface primitives whose vertices can be triangulated directly into a connected mesh, yet SLAM with this representation has so far relied on photometric tracking, which is too slow for localization at sensor rate. We present Facet-SLAM, the first real-time triangle splatting SLAM system for RGB-D cameras. Fast geometric registration is the natural alternative, but it is not sufficient alone, since the mapper’s optimization displaces triangles from the observed surface and makes them unreliable registration targets. We therefore separate the two roles: the tracker sets each triangle’s centroid from fused depth and registers frames to these centroids by GICP, while the mapper is restricted to non-translating updates via a change of variables. Our system achieves competitive tracking accuracy at around 100 FPS on a desktop GPU and runs at sensor rate on a Jetson AGX Orin. Compared with the photometric approach, it is over 20 times faster, matches rendering quality, and improves surface accuracy, reducing the chamfer distance of the Delaunay mesh on Replica from 1.55 to 0.86 cm. We will release the implementation at https://github.com/edward62740/Facet-SLAM.
introduction:
Recent SLAM systems use differentiable representations such as 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) [1] to build maps that render photorealistically. This is useful for applications such as visual navigation and embodied AI training, but many of these also need geometrically accurate maps. 3DGS maps often have poor surface geometry, and obtaining a good mesh requires post-hoc extraction [2], an intermediate representation [3, 4], or 2DGS [5] primitives requiring fusion. In contrast, the primitives of a differentiable triangle soup [6] are themselves surface elements, so a connected mesh can be obtained by triangulating their existing vertices, without an intermediate representation or a separate fusion stage.

More recently, Triangle Splatting SLAM [7] (TS-SLAM) introduced the first dense SLAM method based on triangle primitives, demonstrating the above-mentioned geometric properties, in addition to the ability to generate a photorealistic map. However, TS-SLAM lacks real-time performance, limiting deployment flexibility and its use for on-device localization while constructing the map.

We present, to the best of our knowledge, the first real-time triangle splatting SLAM method. It runs in real-time on both desktop GPU and Jetson AGX Orin, with pose accuracy competitive with photometric methods, rendering quality on par with TS-SLAM, and more accurate map geometry than prior triangle splatting and 3DGS SLAM methods.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We introduce a real-time triangle splatting SLAM system that runs at sensor rate on a Jetson AGX Orin, and from which a connected mesh can be extracted directly.

We propose a tracking-and-mapping strategy that makes triangles reliable GICP registration targets, by fixing their centroids to fused depth and restricting the mapper to non-translating updates.

We improve surface accuracy over both prior triangle splatting and 3DGS SLAM methods while maintaining visual quality relative to triangle splatting methods.

1. We introduce a real-time triangle splatting SLAM system that runs at sensor rate on a Jetson AGX Orin, and from which a connected mesh can be extracted directly.

2. We propose a tracking-and-mapping strategy that makes triangles reliable GICP registration targets, by fixing their centroids to fused depth and restricting the mapper to non-translating updates.

3. We improve surface accuracy over both prior triangle splatting and 3DGS SLAM methods while maintaining visual quality relative to triangle splatting methods.

title: Emo-H2A: Driving a Facial Robot Directly from LLM Hidden States at Token Rate
authors: Yige Liu,Jingcheng Huang,Hao Sun,Min Li,Zhouping Yin
abstract: Diverse, semantically synchronized, and low-latency facial expressions are essential for human-robot interaction. While large language models (LLMs) have endowed anthropomorphic robots with fluent speech, facial expression still struggles to follow the conversation. Motivated by this gap, we present Emo-H2A (hidden-to-actuation), a paradigm that drives a facial robot directly from LLM hidden states during autoregressive decoding. Without a separate emotion label, expression stays continuous and context-sensitive, and the face moves with the unfolding reply. We instantiate this paradigm as EmoManifold, a training-free method that extracts a valence–arousal–dominance (VAD) coordinate from each hidden state, projects it, and drives the face at token granularity. The readout is checked on six language models, and the same projection drives our 29-degree-of-freedom (DoF) facial robot. When driven by this projection, the face shifts its expression in the matching direction on 87.5%87.5\% of within-reply valence transitions—whereas holding a single label for the whole reply leaves directional tracking near the 50%50\% chance level—and first moves in 0.960.96 s rather than waiting 1010–2626 s for the reply to finish and a turn-level label to return.
introduction:
In face-to-face communication, humans perceive spoken words and facial expressions as an inseparable composite. To reproduce this natural affinity in embodied systems, anthropomorphic platforms with high-DoF physical actuation are actively being developed [3, 4], while modern LLMs provide the linguistic engine for fluent dialogue. Yet, despite these advances, modern conversational robots remain fundamentally desynchronized: the facial robot falls out of step with the affective nuance of its own speech.

This desynchronization stems from treating emotion as an extrinsic label rather than an endogenous signal. In existing pipelines, an utterance opening with sympathy and closing with encouragement is assigned a single categorical tag, appearing only after the full reply has been generated [1, 5]. Recent prompt-engineering and multi-stage scheduling approaches attempt to develop intra-utterance trajectories by matching generated segments to expression presets [2]. However, this strategy introduces complex prompt designs and additional parsing passes that substantially increase inference latency. As a result, conventional frameworks struggle to balance response latency against affective granularity, highlighting the need to move beyond label-mediated emotion generation.

Affective diversity presents another major hurdle. Traditional discrete emotion categories correspond to only a handful of static motor templates, which fail to match the rich and nuanced expressive capabilities of modern language models. Consequently, an urgent need exists for a continuous affective space capable of modeling fine-grained emotional transitions. Recent interpretability studies find a low-dimensional affective manifold in LLM hidden states, with directions resembling valence, dominance, and arousal [6]. The emergence of this VAD-like geometry suggests that LLMs can provide the representational foundation for continuous facial affect modeling.

To address these challenges, we introduce Emo-H2A, a paradigm that couples the LLM’s autoregressive hidden states at each generated token directly to facial actuator commands. We instantiate this paradigm as EmoManifold, an online framework that projects token-level hidden representations onto a continuous VAD subspace derived from the model’s unembedding vectors and maps the resulting affective coordinates to physical motor commands. Physical deployment on our 29-DoF facial robot demonstrates that EmoManifold follows within-utterance affective shifts with low initial response latency, achieving an 83.5%83.5\% preference rate from human observers over both a static expression held for the entire utterance and a temporally shuffled control.

To foster further research, we will open-source our codebase and evaluation benchmarks. In summary, our main contributions are:

Emo-H2A: a paradigm that maps the hidden state at each decoding step to facial motor commands, without a separate emotion label.

EmoManifold: a training-free method that builds a VAD subspace, projects each token’s hidden state onto it, and drives the face from that coordinate.

Physical evaluation: On our 29-DoF facial robot, token-level actuation tracks within-reply transitions above chance, where turn-level baselines stay near chance, and observers prefer the token-level motion over a static expression.

1. Emo-H2A: a paradigm that maps the hidden state at each decoding step to facial motor commands, without a separate emotion label.

2. EmoManifold: a training-free method that builds a VAD subspace, projects each token’s hidden state onto it, and drives the face from that coordinate.

3. Physical evaluation: On our 29-DoF facial robot, token-level actuation tracks within-reply transitions above chance, where turn-level baselines stay near chance, and observers prefer the token-level motion over a static expression.

title: A Hierarchical Onboard Vision-Language-Navigation Framework for Aerial Robots in Complex Environments
authors: Yuze Wu,Mo Zhu,Xingxing Li,Yuheng Du,Zhaoqi Wang,Yuxin Fan,Wenjun Li,Kenghou Hoi,Zhichao Han,Xin Zhou,Fei Gao
abstract:
Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are expected to achieve semantic reasoning, intelligent decision-making, and long-horizon navigation under strict onboard constraints. While recent foundation-model-driven approaches have shown promising progress toward this goal, existing methods remain limited by challenges in 3D data availability, trajectory feasibility, long-horizon reasoning, and computational efficiency in complex environments.
To bridge these gaps, we propose VLN-AR, a hierarchical vision-language-navigation (VLN) framework for aerial robots. VLN-AR decouples multimodal reasoning and low-level control, enabling structured prediction of 3D pose commands and navigation intentions that are translated into dynamically feasible actions. To mitigate data scarcity and domain gaps, we introduce a fully automated 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)-based pipeline to generate scalable photorealistic UAV navigation data. A progressive three-stage training strategy further enhances grounding, scene reasoning, and complex navigation. In addition, a lightweight cognitive agent improves long-horizon reasoning via memory-aware task decomposition. Finally, we design onboard optimization techniques, including token sparsification and model lightweighting, achieving 7.1×–9.4× speedup while maintaining high navigation performance on resource-limited UAV platforms. Experiments show great improvements over existing methods in both simulation and real-world UAV navigation. Project website: https://wyz000.github.io/VLN-AR/.
introduction:
Autonomous unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) have been widely deployed in diverse applications including infrastructure inspection, search and rescue, environmental monitoring, and logistics delivery. In such scenarios, UAVs are often required to operate in unstructured and partially observable environments. Beyond reliable low-level flight control, these settings demand high-level intelligence, including the ability to comprehend natural-language instructions, reason about spatial semantics, and generate safe and dynamically feasible actions under strict onboard computational constraints. Enabling such capabilities is critical to advancing UAV systems from task-specific navigation toward general embodied autonomy. While Vision-Language-Navigation (VLN) [1] and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) [2, 3] paradigms have shown considerable potential for autonomous robots, such methods remain underexplored for agile, resource-constrained UAVs.

Most existing UAV navigation methods follow modular perception–planning–control pipelines [4, 5, 6], relying on predefined algorithms, hand-crafted policies, or explicit mapping strategies. While effective in well-defined tasks, they lack general task understanding and reasoning capabilities, particularly the ability to interpret open-vocabulary language instructions.
Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) [7, 8, 9, 10] have enabled VLN and VLA systems for ground robots, allowing natural language to be grounded in visual observations and translated into executable commands within a unified framework. However, adapting these methods to agile aerial robots is non-trivial due to fundamental differences in system dynamics, action spaces, data distributions, safety constraints, and deployment requirements. In particular, several critical challenges are as follows:

Scarcity of 3D navigation data and domain shift. Most navigation foundation models are pretrained on large-scale ground-view 2D navigation datasets, which differ drastically from UAV-centric views that exhibit large variations in pose and scale. Existing UAV navigation datasets are often limited to outdoor environments with coarse visual features and insufficient fine-grained structural details, resulting in sim-to-real domain gaps.

Scarcity of 3D navigation data and domain shift. Most navigation foundation models are pretrained on large-scale ground-view 2D navigation datasets, which differ drastically from UAV-centric views that exhibit large variations in pose and scale. Existing UAV navigation datasets are often limited to outdoor environments with coarse visual features and insufficient fine-grained structural details, resulting in sim-to-real domain gaps.

Mismatch between 3D action representation and safety-aware control. UAV navigation requires safe and reliable control. End-to-end continuous commands derived from foundation models often fail to guarantee safety or satisfy dynamical constraints, while semantically discrete action representations offer limited maneuverability. Balancing 3D maneuverability, control stability, and collision avoidance remains a core challenge.

Insufficient reasoning for long-horizon embodied navigation. Existing VLN/VLA methods typically rely on single-frame or short-term reasoning, making it difficult to integrate historical observations in complex indoor environments. Long-horizon aerial navigation requires spatial grounding, conditional inference, and sequential task decomposition, which cannot be sufficiently supported by single-step prediction schemes.

Prohibitive onboard computational constraints. State-of-the-art foundation models are computationally intensive, making real-time deployment on small UAVs with strict size, weight, and power (SWaP) constraints challenging [11]. Practical onboard deployment therefore requires preserving strong inference capability while significantly reducing computational and memory overhead.

To address these challenges, we propose VLN-AR, a hierarchical Vision Language Navigation framework for Aerial Robots in complex environments. The proposed system integrates data generation, multimodal learning, and onboard deployment into a unified closed-loop framework (Fig. -1). At its core, VLN-AR decomposes the navigation problem into two tightly coupled components: a navigation-oriented vision language model (VLM) that performs multimodal reasoning and predicts structured navigation intentions, and a lightweight action expert that translates these intentions into dynamically feasible control commands. Instead of directly generating low-level actions, the model generates diverse navigation representations tailored to different task requirements. Specifically, it outputs a structured representation comprising 3D pose commands, 2D bounding-box guidance, and chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, establishing an effective interface between high-level cognition and low-level control. The proposed model achieves a maximum success rate of 98.1% on single navigation tasks and an overall aerial navigation success rate of 92.7%, while attaining success rates of 78.15% and 76.88% on the AerialVLN and OpenFly datasets, respectively.

To mitigate flight data scarcity and sim-to-real domain gaps in UAV navigation, we develop a high-fidelity data generation pipeline based on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [12], enabling photorealistic and temporally consistent UAV-centric observations. Combined with an automated data collection and annotation pipeline, it produces a large-scale 3D aerial navigation dataset with approximately 4 million samples, covering navigation data, general visual question answering (VQA), grounding data, reasoning data, spatial VQA, and more.

Building upon this data foundation, we introduce a progressive three-stage training strategy that sequentially enhances multimodal grounding, navigation-specific motion prediction, and reasoning-aware navigation, as shown in Fig. -1(II). The first two stages perform supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on large-scale mixed datasets to improve scene understanding and spatial reasoning for navigation, while the third stage applies reinforcement learning in closed-loop simulation to further improve reasoning-aware navigation [13].

To support long-horizon and ambiguity-aware navigation, we incorporate a lightweight cognitive-driven agent that aggregates historical observations, task states, and action states into a unified temporal memory, enabling structured reasoning, task decomposition, intelligent exploration, and failure recovery in partially observable environments. For efficient onboard deployment, we further combine instruction-guided visual token sparsification with operator-level acceleration and low-precision computation, achieving a 7.1×–9.4× speedup on resource-limited UAV platforms.

This work substantially extends the previous work [14], which introduces preliminary components of the 3DGS-based data pipeline, hierarchical navigation architecture, training framework, and onboard deployment stack. The present study further introduces a cognitive navigation agent, instruction-guided token sparsification, and richer structured model outputs for planning and replanning. Additionally, the training and robustness evaluation have been significantly expanded, and a wider range of scenarios have been tested, thereby constructing a more complete onboard aerial VLN framework. The main contributions are summarized as follows:

We propose VLN-AR, a hierarchical onboard VLN framework that integrates high-level task reasoning with diverse action representations to enable efficient, closed-loop semantic aerial navigation in complex 3D environments.

We present a cognitive navigation agent with dynamic memory fusion and heuristic task decomposition to enhance long-horizon reasoning, resolve ambiguous instructions, and improve resilience under partial observability in unknown environments.

We develop systematic onboard optimization techniques, including instruction-guided visual token sparsification and model lightweighting, achieving a 7.1×–9.4× inference speedup while maintaining high navigation performance on resource-limited UAV platforms.

We conduct comprehensive evaluations in both simulation and real-world environments, demonstrating that the proposed VLN-AR achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of success rate, accuracy, robustness, and computational efficiency.

1. Scarcity of 3D navigation data and domain shift. Most navigation foundation models are pretrained on large-scale ground-view 2D navigation datasets, which differ drastically from UAV-centric views that exhibit large variations in pose and scale. Existing UAV navigation datasets are often limited to outdoor environments with coarse visual features and insufficient fine-grained structural details, resulting in sim-to-real domain gaps.

2. Mismatch between 3D action representation and safety-aware control. UAV navigation requires safe and reliable control. End-to-end continuous commands derived from foundation models often fail to guarantee safety or satisfy dynamical constraints, while semantically discrete action representations offer limited maneuverability. Balancing 3D maneuverability, control stability, and collision avoidance remains a core challenge.

3. Insufficient reasoning for long-horizon embodied navigation. Existing VLN/VLA methods typically rely on single-frame or short-term reasoning, making it difficult to integrate historical observations in complex indoor environments. Long-horizon aerial navigation requires spatial grounding, conditional inference, and sequential task decomposition, which cannot be sufficiently supported by single-step prediction schemes.

4. Prohibitive onboard computational constraints. State-of-the-art foundation models are computationally intensive, making real-time deployment on small UAVs with strict size, weight, and power (SWaP) constraints challenging [11]. Practical onboard deployment therefore requires preserving strong inference capability while significantly reducing computational and memory overhead.

1. We propose VLN-AR, a hierarchical onboard VLN framework that integrates high-level task reasoning with diverse action representations to enable efficient, closed-loop semantic aerial navigation in complex 3D environments.

2. We present a cognitive navigation agent with dynamic memory fusion and heuristic task decomposition to enhance long-horizon reasoning, resolve ambiguous instructions, and improve resilience under partial observability in unknown environments.

3. We develop systematic onboard optimization techniques, including instruction-guided visual token sparsification and model lightweighting, achieving a 7.1×–9.4× inference speedup while maintaining high navigation performance on resource-limited UAV platforms.

4. We conduct comprehensive evaluations in both simulation and real-world environments, demonstrating that the proposed VLN-AR achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of success rate, accuracy, robustness, and computational efficiency.

title: GTI: Grounding Task Intent Throughout Long-Horizon VLA Manipulation
authors: Tianqi Gong,Haochen Niu,Yusheng Zhao,Lantao Zhang,Haoyu Liu,Rendong Ying,Peilin Liu
abstract: Vision–language–action (VLA) models generate local actions from visual observations, language, and robot state, but long-horizon manipulation requires the global task intent to remain grounded in the currently executable context. We propose GTI (Grounding Task Intent), which uses the current observation and execution history to localize the active subtask and its execution phase. For the same local subtask, GTI generates two phase-dependent visual targets: an interaction/contact state and a local completion state. The local language instruction and the corresponding phase-specific visual target jointly condition the VLA, specifying both what to do now and what state should be reached at the current phase. During execution, anomaly monitoring and local recovery re-establish an intent-consistent execution context through rollback, re-observation, and phase re-evaluation after persistent deviation. We evaluate GTI on RoboCasa365, VLA-Arena Horizon-Long, and real-world PiPER tasks. Relative to matched Global-FT baselines, GR00T success on seen composite RoboCasa365 tasks increases from 14.6%/12.1% to 31.8%/20.4% under ID/OOD evaluation. On VLA-Arena, GTI+π0.5\pi_{0.5} reaches 47.6% overall success versus 45.2% for an adapted ForeAct baseline, with gains of 5.2/6.0 percentage points on the harder L1/L2 tasks. In the three real-robot task experiments, mean full-task success increases from 21.7% to 59.2%. The results indicate that persistent semantic intent localization and phase-conditioned visual grounding improve multi-stage execution, while failure-triggered local recovery provides additional deployment-time support.
introduction:
Vision–language–action (VLA) models such as π0.5\pi_{0.5} [1] and GR00T N1.5 [2] map visual observations, language, and robot state to actions, enabling multi-task manipulation. However, a global instruction remains unchanged while the robot encounters different subtasks and interaction states. Successful long-horizon execution therefore requires identifying not only which subtask is currently active, but also which interaction phase should be executed. Without this distinction, the policy may skip or repeat subtasks, switch phases prematurely, or continue executing after a failure.

Hierarchical methods narrow the gap between complex instructions and low-level actions. Hi Robot [3] translates high-level reasoning into local language instructions, while ForeAct [4], VISTA [5], and H-WM [6] use predicted future states as execution references. Language specifies what to do but leaves contact geometry to the executor, and a single completion state cannot represent the distinct interaction and completion relations within one subtask. For grasping or placing, establishing contact and reaching local completion require different visual targets within the same subtask. Phase therefore determines how intent should be concretized visually.

We therefore view long-horizon manipulation as a continuous task-intent-grounding problem with three coupled questions: which part of the global intent should be executed now; what visual target should represent that local intent in the current phase; and how an executable context consistent with that intent should be restored after persistent anomalies. GTI addresses these questions through history-based intent localization, phase-conditioned visual grounding, and failure-triggered local recovery.

GTI’s planner localizes the active subtask and phase from current observations and execution history. A phase-conditioned visual predictor grounds the local instruction into an interaction/contact (K1) or completion (K2) target using the current observation, instruction, and phase. The target and instruction jointly condition the VLA. When an internal-feature monitor detects persistent anomalies, local rollback and re-observation are followed by phase re-evaluation to restore alignment with the current subtask and visual milestone.

The key contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

We introduce GTI, a continuous task-intent-grounding framework for long-horizon VLA manipulation that localizes the active subtask and phase from current observations and execution history, and re-establishes an intent-consistent context after persistent anomalies.

We propose a high-level mechanism combining a structured planner with phase-conditioned visual grounding: the planner localizes local task intent, while the visual model generates a K1 interaction/contact target or K2 completion target according to phase; both language and phase-specific visual targets condition the VLA.

We evaluate GTI on RoboCasa365, VLA-Arena Horizon-Long, and real PiPER tasks using complete-system comparisons, matched visual-grounding ablations, and deployment-sensitivity tests.

1. We introduce GTI, a continuous task-intent-grounding framework for long-horizon VLA manipulation that localizes the active subtask and phase from current observations and execution history, and re-establishes an intent-consistent context after persistent anomalies.

2. We propose a high-level mechanism combining a structured planner with phase-conditioned visual grounding: the planner localizes local task intent, while the visual model generates a K1 interaction/contact target or K2 completion target according to phase; both language and phase-specific visual targets condition the VLA.

3. We evaluate GTI on RoboCasa365, VLA-Arena Horizon-Long, and real PiPER tasks using complete-system comparisons, matched visual-grounding ablations, and deployment-sensitivity tests.

title: ReLoco: Unified Humanoid Locomotion and Fall Recovery via Behavior-Conditioned Motion Priors
authors: Lequn Fu,Yufeng Hu,Yijun Zhong,Jie Zhang,Xiao Li,Lingxiang Ji,Zhiyuan Xu,Jian Tang,Shiqi Li
abstract:
Humanoid robots must recover from falls and resume commanded motion to sustain locomotion. Learning these behaviors in one policy requires supervision that accommodates both upright movement and ground-contact recovery. We present ReLoco, a framework that uses behavior-conditioned adversarial motion priors to learn locomotion, get-up from arbitrary fallen postures, and command resumption within one proprioceptive policy. During training, robot posture selects the expert pool and conditions a shared discriminator with two behavior-specific outputs. Task rewards and shared regularization support command tracking and recovery, while temporary assistance facilitates exploration. A simulation-based refinement stage supplies robot-executed motion references for this supervision. Ablations examine conditional supervision, output separation, and reference quality under matched settings. At a common training iteration, the full policy achieves 96.80%96.80\% independent get-up success and 96.96%96.96\% push-recovery success, including command resumption. Its torso planar velocity root-mean-square error is 0.12660.1266 m/s, 14.7%14.7\% lower than the conditional single-output variant, with similar joint-angle discrepancy measured by dynamic time warping. Deployment on the 64.5-kg Tiangong 3.0 humanoid demonstrates walking, running, get-up, and locomotion resumption after falls using one proprioceptive actor, without controller switching or on-robot policy fine-tuning.
Project page: https://lequn-f.github.io/ReLoco
introduction:
A humanoid robot that falls during locomotion must regain support, stand up, and continue its task. These abilities require coordinated motion across markedly different postures and contacts. Walking emphasizes command following and upright support, whereas recovery can involve rolling, arm support, and substantial torso rotation. A velocity command specifies the motion to be resumed, but does not describe how to establish support from a fallen posture. A single policy must therefore learn recovery actions that restore support before returning to velocity tracking.

Legged control has advanced through model-based planning [1], combined planning and learned tracking [2], and reinforcement learning (RL) in parallel simulation [3, 4]. Learned controllers have achieved adaptive bipedal locomotion [5], real-world humanoid walking [6], versatile dynamic gaits [7], and compliant sim-to-real control [8]. Recent approaches further address difficult terrain, policy smoothness, and sparse footholds [9, 10, 11]. Sustained mobility additionally requires recovery when disturbances take the robot outside its nominal locomotion states.

Human motion provides useful structure for whole-body coordination. Reference-tracking methods learn physically simulated skills from prescribed trajectories [12, 13, 14]. Adversarial motion priors (AMP) learn a motion reward from examples [15], while skill embeddings and conditional models support diverse behaviors [16, 17, 18]. Human-reference and generative-prior approaches extend motion supervision to humanoid locomotion [19, 20, 21]. Related systems demonstrate expressive and agile whole-body control [22, 23, 24, 25], human-to-humanoid teleoperation [26, 27, 28], and contextual skills learned from video [29]. Retargeting addresses embodiment differences in human-to-robot transfer [30] and semantic consistency across characters [31]; recent frameworks further support humanoid retargeting and motion imitation [32, 33].

Recovery has also become a learned robot capability. HoST addresses standing-up exploration, optimization, and deployable motion through a force curriculum, multiple critics, and motion constraints [34]. Other learning-based recovery methods include HumanUP, HiFAR, and FRASA [35, 36, 37]. AHC consolidates behavior-specific policies through distillation and RL fine-tuning [38], while X-Loco trains a vision-based generalist through specialist supervision [39]. These studies motivate learning recovery together with the motion that the robot must resume.

After a disturbance, the robot’s configuration depends on the preceding gait, disturbance direction, and sequence of contacts, and need not coincide with a reference frame. Recovery must also begin from the velocity and support conditions produced by the fall, which can differ from those in a demonstration. AMP guides locally observed motion without prescribing frame-by-frame reference alignment [15], allowing the feedback policy to respond from the state actually reached.

We present ReLoco (Recovery and Locomotion), a framework for unified locomotion and fall recovery through behavior-conditioned motion supervision. A posture-derived supervision route selects the locomotion or get-up reference pool. The discriminator scores motion histories together with their recorded conditions, using a shared feature network and two behavior-specific outputs. Posture-appropriate task rewards support command following or getting up, while shared penalties regulate actuation and joint motion across both routes. This formulation accommodates recovery-specific contacts and postures while retaining the velocity command that the robot must eventually track.

To provide suitable references for this supervision, we refine retargeted human motions in simulation. Kinematic retargeting preserves human coordination but can introduce contact and joint-limit errors on the robot. An offline tracking policy refines locomotion and get-up motions under the contact and actuator models used for final policy training. The resulting robot-executed examples supply the expert data used to train the final controller through adversarial motion supervision.

Recovery training covers configurations that need not align with individual reference frames. Reference-state initialization exposes the policy to fallen and transitional postures, while velocity perturbations generate falls during motion. Temporary assistance supports early recovery learning and is removed as training progresses. These settings provide experience for learning the transition back to commanded locomotion. Deployment uses a proprioceptive actor with velocity commands, without the reference tracker, recovery assistance, or an externally supplied behavior label.

We evaluate the resulting policy through torso planar velocity tracking, motion similarity, independent get-up, and command resumption after disturbances. AMP ablations compare pooled and conditioned supervision; a conditional single-output comparison holds expert sampling and task objectives fixed to assess output separation. Reference-refinement experiments examine the effect of expert-motion quality. Independent get-up trials use settled fallen states, whereas disturbances during locomotion test recovery from moving states. Hardware tests on the 64.5-kg Tiangong 3.0 humanoid demonstrate walking, running, get-up from arbitrary fallen postures, and locomotion resumption after falls. The main contributions are:

A behavior-conditioned motion-prior scheme that selects reference pools using robot posture and scores motion histories with their conditions, supporting command tracking, fall recovery, and resumption of commanded motion within the same actor.

A simulation-based refinement procedure that converts retargeted locomotion and get-up motions into robot-executed references, reducing contact and joint-limit violations in the expert data used for adversarial supervision.

Demonstration of locomotion, autonomous get-up from arbitrary fallen postures, and resumption of the commanded motion after falls on a full-size humanoid using the same deployed proprioceptive policy.

title: Scalable Iterative Multi-Agent Path Finding under Turn Constraints
authors: Zheyu Tao,Chunlong Yu,Yicheng Hu
abstract: Large-scale multi-mobile-robot systems require fast and reliable path planning under realistic motion constraints. Multi-Agent Path Finding with turn actions (MAPFT) explicitly models orientation changes and turn-induced delays, but these constraints increase the computational burden of search-based methods. Priority-inheritance-based planning offers a highly scalable alternative, yet directly extending it to MAPFT is nontrivial because turn actions break the immediate node-vacation assumption underlying conventional priority inheritance. To address this challenge, this paper proposes PIBTT*{}^{\text{*}}_{\text{T}}, an efficient iterative solver for MAPFT. PIBTT*{}^{\text{*}}_{\text{T}} advances scalable multi-agent coordination by preserving the lightweight single-timestep planning mechanism of Priority Inheritance with Backtracking (PIBT), while introducing dedicated mechanisms to handle turn-induced dependencies, local deadlocks, livelock, and inefficient repeated pushing. Experiments on standard MAPF benchmarks show that PIBTT*{}^{\text{*}}_{\text{T}} achieves high success rates and strong scalability, solving instances with up to 1,000 agents within seconds. For realistic engineering environments, Action Dependency Graph (ADG)-based execution simulation and a flexible manufacturing system case study show that turn-aware planning better reflects robot execution and reduces actual makespan compared with classical MAPF planning. Experiments with TurtleBot4 robots further validate the practical feasibility of the proposed method.
introduction:
Multi-mobile-robot systems (MMRSs) are increasingly deployed in automated warehouses, flexible manufacturing systems, intelligent transportation, and other large-scale autonomous systems (Liu et al., 2023). Their effectiveness depends critically on the ability to coordinate large robot fleets safely and efficiently, particularly in confined environments where robot interactions are frequent and replanning must be performed online. This creates a practical demand for path-planning methods that are not only computationally scalable, but also sufficiently consistent with the motion capabilities of physical robots.

Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) provides a widely used discrete framework for coordinating multiple robots (Stern et al., 2019). Recent developments, including bounded-suboptimal conflict-based search (Li et al., 2021c), large-neighborhood-search methods (Li et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2025), and LaCAM-style search (Okumura, 2023b; Idgar et al., 2026), have enabled increasingly large MAPF instances to be solved efficiently. However, classical MAPF typically assumes that an agent can move to any neighboring vertex within one timestep, regardless of its current orientation. This abstraction ignores an important characteristic of many warehouse and logistics robots: a robot must first rotate toward its desired direction before moving forward (Yan and Li, 2025). Consequently, a path that is short under the classical MAPF metric may still incur substantial execution delay when it contains frequent direction changes.

This discrepancy is illustrated in Fig. 1. A classical MAPF planner may favor staircase-like paths because movements in different directions are assigned identical unit costs. When executed by a mobile robot, however, each direction change introduces additional rotational, acceleration/deceleration, and synchronization delays. Explicitly modeling turn actions at the planning level can therefore produce paths that better reflect physical execution. This motivates Multi-Agent Path Finding with turn actions (MAPFT), in which orientation is included in the agent state and in-place rotations are represented explicitly. MAPFT improves motion fidelity, but the enlarged state space and additional temporal dependencies make large-scale coordination substantially more difficult.

Existing high-level MAPFT methods are predominantly search-based. Orientation-augmented ECBS formulations incorporate turning costs into bounded-suboptimal planning (Varambally et al., 2022; Hönig et al., 2019), while CBST explicitly models turn actions within conflict-based search and provides optimal solutions (Zhang et al., 2023). These methods demonstrate the benefit of incorporating realistic actions during high-level planning, but their computational burden increases as the number of agents and conflicts grows. This limitation is important in logistics and manufacturing applications, where hundreds or even thousands of robots may need to be coordinated within highly structured environments.

Priority Inheritance with Backtracking (PIBT) (Okumura et al., 2022) provides an attractive alternative because it generates only the next joint configuration through lightweight priority inheritance and recursive backtracking, enabling real-time coordination of very large agent populations. Extending this mechanism to MAPFT, however, is nontrivial. Conventional PIBT implicitly couples an accepted request to a neighboring vertex with the release of the agent’s current vertex. Under turn constraints, these two events become temporally decoupled: an agent may successfully request a neighboring vertex but first rotate in place, leaving its current vertex occupied at the next timestep. This delayed vertex release disrupts the node-based dependency reasoning underlying priority inheritance and may create cyclic or persistent local interactions that cannot be handled effectively by conventional PIBT (Jiang et al., 2024).

The preliminary conference work, PIBTT, was the first, to the best of our knowledge, to extend priority-inheritance-based iterative planning to MAPFT, demonstrating that explicit turn actions can be incorporated while retaining lightweight single-timestep planning (Tao and Yu, 2025). Nevertheless, the resulting local coordination remains vulnerable to several failure modes. Mutual blocking can prevent agents from making progress, repeated displacement of goal-reaching agents can delay or prevent simultaneous termination, and repeated pushing can introduce substantial detours and degrade solution quality. These limitations become increasingly important in dense interactions and restrictive map structures.

Building on this foundation, this paper develops PIBT∗T{}^{*}_{\textsubscript{T}}, a more robust priority-inheritance-based framework for large-scale MAPFT. The proposed method preserves the computationally efficient single-timestep planning paradigm of PIBT, while strengthening its local coordination mechanisms to address deadlock, livelock, and inefficient repeated pushing. The resulting framework is evaluated not only in terms of planning performance and scalability, but also with respect to realistic robot execution through ADG-based simulation, a flexible manufacturing system case study, and physical TurtleBot4 experiments.

The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

We develop PIBT∗T{}^{*}_{\textsubscript{T}}, a robust and scalable priority-inheritance-based solver for MAPFT. The proposed framework preserves lightweight single-timestep planning while improving coordination under turn-induced temporal dependencies.

We develop PIBT∗T{}^{*}_{\textsubscript{T}}, a robust and scalable priority-inheritance-based solver for MAPFT. The proposed framework preserves lightweight single-timestep planning while improving coordination under turn-induced temporal dependencies.

We introduce two complementary coordination mechanisms to address characteristic failure modes in turn-aware priority-inheritance planning. The swap pattern detector (SPD) identifies local blocking configurations and enables cooperative yielding to resolve deadlock, while the kk-Push Escape Trigger (PET) exploits interaction history to mitigate livelock and inefficient repeated pushing. Their individual and combined effects are systematically examined through ablation experiments.

We provide a comprehensive evaluation of both algorithmic and execution-level performance. Standard MAPF benchmarks and large-scale stress tests demonstrate high success rates and scalability for up to 1,000 agents with limited computational overhead. ADG-based execution simulation and a flexible manufacturing system case study quantify the gap between discrete planning cost and realistic execution cost, while experiments with TurtleBot4 robots further validate the practical applicability of the proposed approach.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work. Section 3 defines the MAPFT problem. Section 4 presents the proposed PIBT∗T{}^{*}_{\textsubscript{T}} framework. Section 5 reports the computational experiments and execution-oriented validation. Section 6 presents the real-robot demonstration, and Section 7 concludes the paper.

title: Navigating Robots from Unknown and Uncalibrated Exocentric Cameras via Map Estimation
authors: Raul Steinmetz,Raphael Druon,Yusuke Yoshiyasu,Akihisa Ohya,Ayanori Yorozu
abstract: Exocentric cameras, mounted on walls or ceilings in indoor environments, offer wider vantage points and are less easily occluded than robot-mounted cameras, making them an appealing alternative for perception in robot navigation algorithms. Previous methods that use such cameras, however, require their pose and intrinsics to be known before deployment, demanding calibration that is time-consuming, requires specialized personnel, and must be repeated whenever a camera moves or a new room is navigated. We propose Robot-centric Obstacle Maps from Unknown and uncalibrated eXocentric cameras (ROMUX), an agent that navigates a robot toward point goals while avoiding obstacles using exocentric cameras that are both uncalibrated, meaning the system does not require their pose or intrinsic information as input, and unknown, meaning it is not fit to a specific camera during training and does not require pre-deployment fine-tuning. We train a cross-view transformer on large-scale simulation data to predict metric robot-centric obstacle maps from exocentric images, without conditioning image tokens on camera information. A small policy trained with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) then navigates on the predicted maps toward a goal coordinate relative to the robot. We benchmark our agent in simulation with cameras randomized per episode, and it matches the success rates of a PPO policy that navigates from a robot-mounted camera. Further, ROMUX works with one camera or multiple cameras with partial views and has been transferred zero-shot to a real robot using a camera at varying positions and orientations across various room layouts.
introduction:
Navigating towards a goal while avoiding collisions with obstacles is an essential capability for many autonomous service robots. Recent trends in robotics research have explored alternatives to classical mapping and planning algorithms, towards agents that learn to navigate from experience and perceive their environment using raw images. Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has emerged as a central methodology for learning such navigation policies. Given enough interactions with a simulated environment, DRL produces neural network policies capable of navigating unknown environments with state-of-the-art success rates [1].

However, most navigation policies in this context use cameras mounted on the robot frame for perception, while few works have explored the usage of exocentric cameras. Exocentric cameras, such as monitoring cameras mounted on walls and ceilings in indoor environments, offer several advantages for indoor navigation, such as: wider coverage of the environment in a single observation and less risk of heavy occlusion than robot-mounted sensors; no drain on robot battery or payload; and availability in many of the environments where service robots already operate, enabling their use at little extra cost.

Previous work on navigation from exocentric cameras requires cameras to be known in advance, either through classical calibration that recovers camera pose and intrinsics [2, 3] or through pre-deployment learning stages that fit perception models to each camera view [4, 5]. Both assumptions are limiting, as classical calibration demands specialized personnel and time and must be repeated whenever a camera moves or a new room is navigated, and fitting models to specific views likewise requires retraining for every new room and camera placement.

We propose the problem of navigating robots toward a point-goal while avoiding collisions with obstacles, using images from exocentric cameras that are both uncalibrated, meaning their pose and intrinsics are not provided to the system, and unknown, meaning the agent is not fitted to any specific camera during training. To enforce these constraints, we randomize camera pose and intrinsics at every evaluation episode. We show that Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) [6], which achieves near-perfect point-goal navigation from robot-mounted camera images [1], fails to learn obstacle avoidance from exocentric cameras in our setup, even when a fixed camera is used throughout training and evaluation. We hypothesize that this occurs because obstacle avoidance requires mapping obstacles from the exocentric image into the robot frame, and PPO does not recover this transformation within our setup and training budget.

To navigate robots under this setup, we propose Robot-centric Obstacle Maps from Unknown and uncalibrated eXocentric cameras (ROMUX), an agent architecture that decouples the aforementioned perspective transformation from the reinforcement learning objective and formulates it as a supervised learning problem. We collect diverse pairs of exocentric camera images and obstacle maps at scale in simulation, randomizing camera pose and intrinsics, and environment layout per data point, and train a cross-view transformer-like neural network [7] on top of image features from a fine-tuned DINOv2 [8] to learn the mapping between the two.

The map-estimation module predicts a robot-centric binary obstacle map without receiving camera pose or intrinsics, and a small policy trained with PPO navigates from the estimated map and a goal coordinate relative to the robot. We only require that the robot and its heading be visually identifiable in the image; in our setup, we use two colored markers on top of the robot so that this information can be recovered from the low-resolution image. The two stages are trained separately and do not share gradients, so the map-estimation module can be retrained for a new domain while the policy is recycled. The agent scales to multiple cameras with partial views and has been transferred zero-shot to a real robot, where a camera is placed at different positions and orientations and the obstacle layout varies across trials (Figure 1). Figure 2 shows a diagram of the architecture. Our main contributions are the following:

A new problem for the robot navigation literature, where an algorithm must navigate a robot using unknown and uncalibrated exocentric cameras;

A new problem for the robot navigation literature, where an algorithm must navigate a robot using unknown and uncalibrated exocentric cameras;

The ROMUX architecture, which can navigate the proposed setup.

2. The ROMUX architecture, which can navigate the proposed setup.
