title: LAGR: Language-Aware Grasp Re-Ranking for Task Oriented Grasping
authors: Manav Kulshrestha,Shreyans Jain,Apoorva Vashisth,Ankush Gupta,Damon Conover,Aniket Bera
comment: Manav Kulshrestha and Shreyans Jain contributed equally to this work
abstract:
Grasping is a fundamental capability for robotic manipulation, with the appropriate grasp depending on the downstream task.
For example, a hammer should be held by its handle for hammering but by its head when it is handed over.
Selecting such a grasp requires consideration of two criteria: physical feasibility on the object and suitability for the task.
Developing such an approach requires dense grasp labels with both feasibility and task scores on real observations, but existing task-oriented grasping datasets are small, synthetic, or costly to annotate.
To address this gap, we construct a dataset of 2.682.68 million scored 55-DoF grasp annotations over 100,911100,911 image-task pairs from 1717 object categories.
Additionally, we introduce LAGR, a task-oriented grasp detection method that explicitly addresses both these challenges.
Given vision-language inputs, LAGR first generates task-independent grasp proposals along with a physical feasibility score, and then scores the generated grasps with a language-conditioned re-ranker that reasons over all proposals jointly.
Experiments show that LAGR outperforms the next best method by 9.39.3 percentage points.
We further validate LAGR on real objects by executing task-oriented grasps with a Franka Research 3 robot.
introduction:
Autonomous robots [23, 24, 9] have the potential to transform everyday life by assisting humans in a wide range of physical tasks.
A fundamental requirement for such autonomy is robotic manipulation [10, 8], which enables robots to interact with objects in their surroundings.
Central to successful manipulation is task-oriented grasping [25], where robots must select grasps that are not only physically stable but also appropriate for the intended task, making it a particularly challenging problem.
This challenge is further compounded by the lack of large-scale datasets that can provide task-conditioned grasp supervision.
Existing datasets [6, 3, 11, 26, 18] often suffer from limited object and task diversity, sparse grasp annotations, or focus on affordance masks that do not explicitly capture grasp geometry and physical feasibility.
Moreover, manually annotating grasps in this manner is labor-intensive, making it difficult to construct comprehensive datasets for learning task-oriented grasping.

Existing grasp detection methods [16, 17, 5, 4, 30] focus on physical grasp quality without explicitly considering task intent.
Task-oriented and language-guided approaches [19, 7, 22, 25, 14] incorporate semantic and functional reasoning to identify task-appropriate grasps.
However, these methods do not consistently distinguish task-independent physical feasibility from task-dependent grasp suitability, limiting their ability to explicitly evaluate and compare feasible grasp configurations under different manipulation goals.
While affordance learning methods [28, 15, 31] focus on identifying task-relevant object regions, they do not consider physical feasibility of grasp configurations.
Existing grasp datasets [6, 3, 11, 26] provide extensive geometric supervision but largely lack task annotations, while task-oriented datasets [18, 21, 20] often suffer from limited object–task diversity and sparse grasp-level supervision.
Furthermore, partial observations introduce uncertainty in 3D 6-DoF grasp estimation, motivating image-space 5-DoF representations grounded in visible geometry.
These limitations highlight the need for large-scale, language-conditioned grasp annotations that jointly capture geometric feasibility and functional suitability.

To address this limitation, we introduce a large-scale dataset of 2.68 million scored grasps across 100,911 image–task pairs.
Additionally, we build upon this dataset and propose LAGR, a multimodal grasp generation framework that explicitly decouples physical feasibility from task-dependent grasp selection.
LAGR first generates a shared set of physically plausible grasp proposals from visual observations, then employs a language-conditioned reranker that jointly reasons over proposal geometry, visual context, and task intent to select the most appropriate grasp.
Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

Our dataset comprises 2.682.68 million scored grasp annotations across 100,911100,911 image–task pairs, with each annotation providing explicit grasp geometry, a physical feasibility score, and a task-compatibility score conditioned on the corresponding natural-language instruction.

We propose LAGR, a multimodal architecture that separates task-independent physical grasp proposal generation from language-conditioned selection, leveraging joint reasoning over candidate grasps to identify functionally appropriate grasp configurations.

We demonstrate that LAGR achieves 85.9%85.9\% task-conditioned grasp accuracy on our dataset, outperforming the strongest baseline by 9.39.3 percentage points.

1. Our dataset comprises 2.682.68 million scored grasp annotations across 100,911100,911 image–task pairs, with each annotation providing explicit grasp geometry, a physical feasibility score, and a task-compatibility score conditioned on the corresponding natural-language instruction.

2. We propose LAGR, a multimodal architecture that separates task-independent physical grasp proposal generation from language-conditioned selection, leveraging joint reasoning over candidate grasps to identify functionally appropriate grasp configurations.

3. We demonstrate that LAGR achieves 85.9%85.9\% task-conditioned grasp accuracy on our dataset, outperforming the strongest baseline by 9.39.3 percentage points.

title: RePlan-VLA: Progress-Aware Replanning for Long-Horizon Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Apoorva Vashisth,Manav Kulshrestha,Damon Conover,Zachary Kingston,Aniket Bera
comment: Apoorva Vashisth and Manav Kulshrestha contributed equally to this work. Prof. Zachary Kingston and Prof. Aniket Bera jointly advised this work
abstract:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose robotic manipulation, yet their performance often degrades on long-horizon tasks that require multiple interdependent manipulations.
Instead of burdening the VLA policies with long-horizon reasoning, memory, action generation, progress tracking, and error recovery, we argue for leveraging their short-horizon manipulation capabilities within an execution-aware framework.
To this end, we introduce RePlan-VLA, a VLA-agnostic framework that translates a VLA’s short-horizon capabilities into reliable long-horizon execution.
RePlan-VLA explicitly monitors the robot’s motion for progress evaluation, and adaptively revises the future plan based on observed outcomes.
We preserve the underlying VLA policy entirely, requiring no additional fine-tuning.
Experiments on RoboCasa365 and CALVIN benchmarks show an improvement of 21.9%21.9\% and 10.4%10.4\% in success rate over the next strongest baseline.
We also validate our approach for real-world deployment on a Franka Research 3 robot.
introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models [27, 29, 11, 23, 15, 8] have made significant progress toward developing generalist robotic policies capable of performing diverse manipulation tasks.
Despite their performance on short-horizon tasks (e.g. ‘Pick up the straw and place it in the cup.’), these models often struggle with reliable execution of long-horizon instructions (e.g. “Open the drawer, pick up the straw, navigate to the cup, and place the straw in the cup”).
This can be attributed to their inability to coordinate simultaneous progress tracking and execution of the long-horizon tasks, allowing small errors to propagate and cause downstream failures.
Towards this end, we propose decoupling of long-horizon reasoning, action generation, progress tracking, and error recovery from a single-VLA policy to a VLA-agnostic framework, retaining the VLA policy only as a reliable executor of short-horizon tasks.

Recent approaches improve long-horizon manipulation through complementary mechanisms: leveraging future prediction [10, 36, 5], persistent action memory [20, 31, 10], and action prediction [17].
Progress-aware approaches [34, 32, 14], either leverage progress estimates as monotonically increasing rewards for computationally intensive policy training, do not consider explicit failure diagnosis and recovery, or overlook the compositional structure and interdependencies of long-horizon tasks by treating them as monolithic execution problems.
Consequently, missed prerequisites and incorrectly assumed completions propagate through subsequent manipulations, motivating the need for an execution-grounded framework capable of handling task dependencies, progress monitoring, execution awareness, and failure-conditioned replanning.

To address these challenges, we propose a VLA-agnostic framework for long-horizon task execution.
Our approach integrates language-based task decomposition, visual progress monitoring, and failure-conditioned re-planning into a closed-loop execution pipeline.
We evaluate our approach on the RoboCasa365 [22] composite-task benchmark and a focused subset of challenging CALVIN’s [21] long-horizon task sequences.
In summary, our main contributions are threefold:

We introduce RePlan-VLA, a VLA-agnostic framework that enables policies to reliably execute long-horizon tasks without requiring further VLA fine-tuning.

We develop a fine-tuned progress-monitoring VLM that grounds sub-task progress estimation and failure diagnosis via visual observations to guide adaptive re-planning.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of RePlan-VLA on challenging long-horizon manipulation benchmarks, improving average task success rate from 40.6%40.6\% to 62.5%62.5\% on RoboCasa365 composite tasks, and from 3.58/53.58/5 to 4.10/54.10/5 on CALVIN ABCD→\rightarrowhardD.

1. We introduce RePlan-VLA, a VLA-agnostic framework that enables policies to reliably execute long-horizon tasks without requiring further VLA fine-tuning.

2. We develop a fine-tuned progress-monitoring VLM that grounds sub-task progress estimation and failure diagnosis via visual observations to guide adaptive re-planning.

3. We demonstrate the effectiveness of RePlan-VLA on challenging long-horizon manipulation benchmarks, improving average task success rate from 40.6%40.6\% to 62.5%62.5\% on RoboCasa365 composite tasks, and from 3.58/53.58/5 to 4.10/54.10/5 on CALVIN ABCD→\rightarrowhardD.

title: Estimation-Aware Reachability
authors: Himanshu Paudel,Javier Borquez
abstract: Hamilton–Jacobi Reachability computes the states from which a system can be kept safe under worst-case disturbances, but it assumes the state is known exactly, whereas real robots act on noisy estimates whose uncertainty evolves with their motion. We extend Hamilton–Jacobi Reachability to the robot’s belief, estimate and uncertainty, treating unexpected measurements as a bounded adversary and enlarging the unsafe set by the current uncertainty, so that certified states are safe with a prescribed probability. The formulation is compatible with existing solvers. In simulation, the resulting safety filters nearly eliminate the collisions of certainty-equivalent HJ and are less conservative than equally safe uncertainty-padding baselines. The implementation code is available at :https://github.com/HimanshuPaudel/Estimation-Aware-Reachability.
introduction:
Ensuring safety for autonomous and robotic systems operating under uncertainty has motivated a broad family of set-based safety filter approaches. Some of the popular approaches include Control Barrier Functions (CBFs), [1, 2] Zonotope-based methods[3, 4, 5], and Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability analysis [6, 7]. HJ reachability analysis is of particular interest as it provides a general pipeline to compute the maximal safe set for the system, that is, the largest set of states from which the system can be kept safe for a future time horizon while providing the corresponding optimal control policy to avoid that keeps the system in this safe set, without requiring a hand designed safety certificate and naturally handles disturbances.

Classical HJ reachability formulation assumes perfect state observability, an assumption that rarely holds in real hardware setups of autonomous systems, where state estimation is generally used to infer the true state from the noisy measurements. The mismatch between the assumption of full information setting and practical state estimation setting motivates the need for reachability methods that accounts for estimation uncertainty. Doing so, increases the complexity of the underlying problem, further straining classical grid-based HJ reachability solvers that scale poorly with problem size due to the curse of dimensionality. Several lines of work address this scalability challenge such as decomposition methods[8] and learning based approaches. Learning based approaches approximate the reachable sets[9, 10] without explicitly solving the Hamilton-Jacobi equations over the grid, and there has been some recent developments to provide formal assurances to such learning based approaches [11, 12].

We propose an estimation aware reachability framework that augments the system state with the estimator’s mean and covariance. This is generally avoided in the literature due to the curse of dimensionality but recent approaches such as DeepReach [9] make high-dimensional problems tractable. Specifically, we bound the measurement innovation by the instantaneous covariance, and let this bound enter the reachability computation as a worst case disturbance the value function must remain robust to. This yields a value function and safety filter that is aware of and adapts to the system’s real-time estimation confidence, rather than treating estimation error as a static, decoupled quantity layered on top of a reachable set computed with the assumption of perfect information of states.

We validate this formulation on three case studies: the Air3D pursuit-evasion problem with a continuous-time EKF (CT-EKF), a planar quadrotor with a continuous-time extended H∞H_{\infty} filter, and a Dubins car whose full state is estimated by a CT-EKF from position measurements of a beacon whose noise grows with distance. In each, the estimate is augmented with the filter’s Riccati state: the covariance Σ\Sigma for the CT-EKF, and the H∞H_{\infty} bound PP on the error covariance for the H∞H_{\infty} filter. We analyze how the resulting Backward Reachable Tube (BRT) changes with the estimator’s uncertainty, which provides a concrete testbed for the estimation-aware formulation and a way to visualize the coupling between state uncertainty and the guaranteed safe set.

Our contributions are:

An estimation-aware HJ reachability formulation over a belief-augmented state in which the measurement innovation acts as an adversarial input.

An uncertainty-inflated target set with point-wise probabilistic safety guarantees.

A formulation directly compatible with existing state of the art pipelines for reachable set calculations.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on reachability under state uncertainty. Section 3 reviews HJ reachability DeepReach, and the CT-EKF and H∞H_{\infty} filters. Section 4 formulates the problem and Section 5 presents the estimation-aware reachability formulation, including the augmented state dynamics, the bound on the measurement innovation via the instantaneous covariance, and the probabilistic guarantee. Section 6 applies the formulation to the three systems and describes the DeepReach-based training procedure and the safety filter implementation. Finally, Section 7 concludes and outlines directions for future work.

1. An estimation-aware HJ reachability formulation over a belief-augmented state in which the measurement innovation acts as an adversarial input.

2. An uncertainty-inflated target set with point-wise probabilistic safety guarantees.

3. A formulation directly compatible with existing state of the art pipelines for reachable set calculations.

title: RoboDx: Repair and Diagnosis of Faults in Robot Software
authors: Soham Dan
abstract:
A patch to a robot’s navigation software can pass every unit test and still drive the robot off its path.
Checking how the repaired robot drives catches such patches.
It does not show that the agent found everything that was wrong.
We introduce RoboDx, a generator of repair tasks for simulated robot navigation software with known injected faults.
A hidden verifier marks a repair as verified only if the robot then drives correctly in hidden scenarios, which the agent never sees.
A second track hides the code and asks the agent to pick the cause from a list of hypotheses.
A task with two faults can contain a quiet fault, a fault that makes no hidden scenario fail unless the other fault is also present.
On our set of 100 tasks, RoboDx-Hard-100, almost every repair by Claude Opus 5.5 with standard coding tools is verified.
We analyse 94 of the tasks, 44 with one fault and 50 with two.
On the 50 two-fault tasks, only 17 of Opus’s 49 verified repairs remove both injected edits.
Most faults left behind are configuration constants whose correct value the task’s documentation does not state.
Opus names both faults on 10/50 of these tasks when it cannot see the code.
We then give four current models the same measurements of each faulty robot, picked so that, in the simulator, only the true cause produces all of them.
The models name the cause on at most 38 of 94 tasks.
They are right on almost all when they also get the simulator’s output for every hypothesis.
Their own predictions of that output give no detectable gain.
On 97 tasks from real bug-fix pull requests, Claude Haiku 5.5, the weakest model on the generated tasks, scores lowest, and the other three models are not ordered.
introduction:
A coding agent is asked to repair a robot that drives off its route. The robot’s navigation software has two faults. One line sets the heading gain ten times too low. The heading gain controls how hard the robot steers back toward its route, so the robot now turns sluggishly and misses waypoints, the points along its route. The other fault is a deleted speed cap. Without the cap the robot no longer slows down while it turns. With a correct heading gain the robot turns quickly, so alone the missing cap makes no test mission fail. The agent restores the gain. The robot then completes every test mission, and the repair counts as solved. The speed cap is still missing from the code (Figure 1).

Robot software holds much code like the speed cap. Speed caps, timeouts and safety stops do nothing until something else fails, so a check of the robot’s behaviour can miss them. Coding agents are now applied to robot software [34, 37, 72], and finding the cause of a robot’s misbehaviour is a research problem of its own [46, 44, 58]. The closest benchmark for robot repair holds 33 real defects [104]. With real defects only the reported fault is known, so a fault that a repair leaves behind cannot be counted.

Benchmarks built from repository issues, such as SWE-bench, grade a fix with the repository’s unit tests [52, 114]. Unit tests accept wrong patches [92, 82, 110, 5]. Table 1 sets a RoboDx task beside such a task. (i) The fix is graded by how the robot drives, because a wrong line can pass every unit test and still send the robot off its route. Faulty patches for robotic vehicles have been found by their effect on physical behaviour [63]. (ii) Every fault is known, because we inject it, so we can count the faults a repair leaves behind. That count matters because a fault can cause no failure unless a second fault is present, as with the missing speed cap. (iii) The cause is asked for directly. A second track hides the code and asks the agent to name the cause from measurements of the robot.

We introduce RoboDx, a generator of such tasks and the hidden verifier that grades them (Figure 2). The generator injects faults into correct navigation software that runs in a robot simulator. Each fault is a small edit of one of 143 kinds, such as a wrong change of coordinates or a wrong configuration value. A repair is verified if the robot passes every hidden check, among them 21 hidden scenarios, simulated missions that the agent never sees. A quiet fault is an injected fault that fails no hidden scenario unless the task’s other fault is also present. RoboDx-Hard-100 is our set of 100 generated tasks. We analyse 94 of them, 44 with one fault and 50 with two. A companion real set has 97 tasks from merged bug-fix pull requests of three open-source robot projects.

A verified repair often leaves a fault in place. With standard tools, Opus has a verified repair on 98 of the 100 tasks. On the 50 two-fault tasks, only 17 of its 49 verified repairs remove both faults (Section 4.1).

A verified repair often leaves a fault in place. With standard tools, Opus has a verified repair on 98 of the 100 tasks. On the 50 two-fault tasks, only 17 of its 49 verified repairs remove both faults (Section 4.1).

Opus often does on single-fault tasks and rarely on two-fault tasks. It names both faults on 10/50 of the two-fault tasks. A reference procedure that picks its measurements at random, and is given the simulator’s output for each hypothesis, is right on 47/50 (Section 4.2).

Our evidence suggests that they lack the simulator’s output for each hypothesis. Shown the same measurements of the faulty robot, and choosing none themselves, four current models are right on 27 to 38 of 94 tasks. Adding that output raises them to 89 to 94, and their own predictions of that output give no detectable gain (Section 4.3).

The real tasks separate the agents only in part. On the 97 tasks of the real set, Claude Haiku 5.5 scores lowest and the other three models are not ordered (Section 4.4).

A verified repair rate near 1.00 can make repair look solved. Of Opus’s 49 verified two-fault repairs, 32 still hold a fault. A benchmark that reports only the verdict does not count these faults. Opus, when it may ask a simulator what a hypothesis would show, names the cause on every task we analyse. This suggests that diagnosis agents need a way to simulate their hypotheses.

A benchmark generator. RoboDx builds robot-software repair tasks with known injected faults, and its verifier grades a repair by how the simulated robot drives.

Two additions to the verified repair rate. The full-repair rate is the share of verified two-fault repairs that remove both faults. The diagnosis track asks for the cause without the code and is scored against reference procedures that are given the simulator’s output.

Two task sets. RoboDx-Hard-100 has 100 generated tasks and the real set has 97 tasks from real bug-fix pull requests.

An evaluation of current coding agents on both sets, which answers RQ1 to RQ4 above.

title: TacPilot: Does Touch Need to Be Everywhere?
authors: Yunzhen Zhang,Yuxiao Zhu,Jie Yang,Yufeng Miao,Bing Luo
abstract:
Tactile feedback helps visual manipulation policies respond
to local contact, but changes in tactile observations do not
always require corrective motion, and sustained corrections
do not always require new tactile features.
We introduce TacPilot, a tactile residual framework that
separates representation updates from action intervention
around a frozen visual policy.
TacPilot uses a perception gate to determine when tactile
features need refreshing and updates only affected regions
while reusing unchanged features.
A separate intervention gate determines whether bounded
Cartesian and gripper residuals modify the nominal visual action.
This separation allows tactile perception and action correction
to follow different spatial and temporal demands during manipulation.
In offline expert-trajectory replay, local feature reuse
reduces encoded regions by 56.4% relative to periodic full
encoding, with essentially unchanged action predictions.
In an exploratory simulation evaluation spanning two cylinder
sizes, TacPilot succeeds in 26 of 30 trials (86.7%).
We further validate TacPilot on OpenArm v2 equipped with
Paxini tactile sensors across four contact-rich manipulation tasks.
introduction:
Vision provides scene context and guides motion toward
a goal, while touch reveals local interactions that
can be difficult to observe under
occlusion [4, 25].
When uprighting a cylinder, for example, a robot may
need to adjust its grasp as the object shifts between
its fingertips. Tactile feedback provides information
about these contact changes that images alone may
not resolve. Recent work incorporates touch through
adaptive tactile injection [14] and
tactile-conditioned residual policies [29, 24, 20], enabling tactile feedback
to complement visual action generation.

Tactile interaction is local in space. In gripper-based
manipulation, contact with the object is concentrated
at the fingertip–object interface, where small changes
in grasp or alignment can determine whether a motion
succeeds [27, 25].
Within this interface, a shift in contact may change
the readings in only part of the sensing surface,
while other regions remain largely unchanged.
This locality suggests focusing corrective learning
on the end-effector interaction and reusing features
from unchanged regions.

The need for tactile feedback also varies over time.
Over a task, contact difficulties may require corrective
motion during some phases, while visual guidance is
sufficient during others. Within a shorter interval,
high-rate tactile sensing can capture contact changes
between successive visual observations, providing
feedback before the next visual update [14].
During stable interaction, however, many successive
tactile samples may carry little new information.
These variations motivate selective processing and
correction that retain access to rapid contact changes.

We study this spatial locality and temporal intermittency
as spatiotemporal tactile sparsity
(Fig. 1).
We introduce TacPilot (Fig. 2), a tactile
residual framework that uses this structure to guide
feature updates and action intervention.
A frozen ACT policy [27] supplies nominal
actions. A perception gate determines when tactile
features need refreshing, and local updates reuse
features from unchanged sensing regions.
An intervention gate controls whether bounded Cartesian
and gripper residuals modify the nominal action.
We express and supervise corrections in Cartesian action
space to focus learning on motion at the
gripper–object interface. The residual and intervention
gates are trained by behavior cloning while the visual
policy remains fixed.

We evaluate TacPilot on simulated cylinder uprighting
with two object sizes and variations in starting position
and grasp orientation. TacPilot succeeds in 26 of 30
development trials (86.7%).
Offline ablations examine tactile refresh, residual
intervention, and input dependence. Selective updates
reduce the number of encoded regions by 56.4% with
essentially unchanged action predictions.
We further validate TacPilot on the OpenArm v2 platform
across four contact-rich manipulation tasks.

Our contributions are threefold:

Spatiotemporal tactile sparsity.
We identify spatial locality and temporal intermittency
as opportunities for selective tactile processing
and action correction.

TacPilot.
We design TacPilot to exploit this sparsity through
event-triggered local feature updates and gated
task-space residual corrections.

Evaluation and real-robot validation.
We evaluate cylinder uprighting with two object sizes,
examine the components through offline ablations,
and validate TacPilot on OpenArm v2 across four
contact-rich tasks.

title: CoT-WAM: Collaborative Training of Vision-Language Models and World-Action Models via Plan Latents
authors: Jinhao Zhang,Yushen Zuo,Ke Rui,Weitao Zhou,Haibao Yu,Honglong Tian,Xiaoheng Ma,Jie Mei,Jiawei Wang,Minglei Li
abstract: General robot manipulation requires both semantic competence and physical foresight. World action models (WAMs) acquire an understanding of and predictive capability over the physical world by jointly modeling visual foresight and action distributions. However, existing WAMs still lack semantic competence: they have limited ability to perform open-world scene understanding, semantic reasoning, and long-horizon planning. Although vision-language models (VLMs) provide these capabilities, effectively integrating their semantic priors into WAM prediction and control remains challenging. To address this challenge, we propose CoT-WAM, a jointly trained WAM–VLM framework. CoT-WAM uses a learnable embedding to exchange information between the VLM and the WAM, which is supervised by textual and goal-image signals during training to encode rich intent information. A tailored two-stage training strategy enables joint optimization and more effective collaboration between the VLM and WAM. We evaluate CoT-WAM on six benchmarks covering control performance, zero-shot generalization, and long-horizon planning. CoT-WAM achieves SOTA performance on LIBERO, CALVIN, and RoboCasa-Kitchen, and demonstrates stronger zero-shot generalization on LIBERO-Plus and LIBERO-Pro without fine-tuning. On RoboCasa365, it further improves long-horizon planning over baselines with and without external planners. Real-world experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in practical deployments.
introduction:
Vision-language-action models (VLAs) have recently emerged as a dominant paradigm in embodied intelligence [3, 11, 2]. By transferring the powerful semantic and scene-understanding capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs) to robot control signals through discrete action tokens or dedicated action experts, VLAs achieve strong generalization. However, their reactive control paradigm cannot model the evolution of the physical world or predict the consequences of actions, both of which are essential capabilities for open-world manipulation agents. World Action Models (WAMs) address this limitation by jointly modeling future visual-state transitions and action distributions [14, 28, 12]. By conditioning action generation on learned world dynamics, WAMs provide a viable paradigm for pretraining on large-scale videos and make it possible to build manipulation agents capable of understanding the physical world.

Despite their ability to predict state evolution, WAMs lack the open-world understanding, reasoning, and planning capabilities provided by a VLM backbone. Existing WAMs, such as Fast-WAM [28], LingBot-VA [12], and DreamZero [27], typically rely on a separate frozen text encoder to provide language grounding. This design is often insufficient for tasks that require open-world scene understanding, semantic generalization and long-horizon planning. Recent works, such as ST-WAM [26] and SG-WAM [7], incorporate VLMs to provide scene-aware semantic guidance for action generation. However, ST-WAM keeps its VLM frozen throughout training, so its semantic representations are not jointly optimized with the WAM. This limits the adaptation of the VLM’s semantic knowledge to the needs of future-state prediction and action generation. SG-WAM jointly trains a VLM-based semantic planner with the WAM, but relies on additional frozen semantic and geometric teachers to supervise future feature prediction.

To address these limitations, we propose CoT-WAM, a framework that seamlessly integrates the rich semantic prior of a VLM into a WAM, thereby equipping WAM prediction and decision-making with open-world understanding and planning capabilities. Building upon Fast-WAM, CoT-WAM replaces its conditioning input with a learnable hidden state produced by the VLM. The VLM is responsible for scene understanding or subtask planning, and conveys its planning intent to the WAM through the latent embedding. Conditioned on this compact yet semantically rich representation, the WAM predicts the corresponding future states and generates control signals. During training, we supervise the learnable embedding with two complementary signals: a discrete textual task signal and a continuous goal-image signal. Consequently, the information transmitted from the VLM to the WAM is no longer restricted to “hard” text, but can encode richer information about the predicted consequences of an intended action. Through a two-stage training strategy, we successfully endow the WAM with stronger understanding and planning capabilities, leading to improved closed-loop control performance.

We evaluate CoT-WAM across six benchmarks covering control performance, zero-shot generalization, and long-horizon planning. For control, CoT-WAM achieves state-of-the-art performance on LIBERO, CALVIN, and RoboCasa-Kitchen without additional embodied pretraining. For zero-shot generalization, the same LIBERO-trained policy substantially outperforms Fast-WAM on LIBERO-Plus and LIBERO-Pro without fine-tuning, while remaining competitive with methods using additional embodied pretraining or supervision from external visual priors. For long-horizon planning, CoT-WAM outperforms baselines with and without external planners on RoboCasa365, a challenging benchmark for mobile manipulation. Beyond these simulation benchmarks, real-world experiments further validate the practicality of CoT-WAM. Together, these results demonstrate that integrating VLM semantic knowledge with world modeling through joint training improves scene understanding, semantic generalization, and long-horizon planning. In summary, our contributions are:

We propose CoT-WAM, a joint WAM–VLM training framework that equips WAMs with scene understanding, semantic generalization, and long-horizon planning capabilities.

We introduce dedicated latent tokens to enable richer and more flexible information exchange between the VLM and WAM, supervised by text and goal images. A staged training strategy enables joint learning and collaboration between the two models.

Experiments across six benchmarks demonstrate that CoT-WAM substantially improves long-horizon planning over the baseline, while achieving state-of-the-art control performance and stronger zero-shot generalization.

1. We propose CoT-WAM, a joint WAM–VLM training framework that equips WAMs with scene understanding, semantic generalization, and long-horizon planning capabilities.

2. We introduce dedicated latent tokens to enable richer and more flexible information exchange between the VLM and WAM, supervised by text and goal images. A staged training strategy enables joint learning and collaboration between the two models.

3. Experiments across six benchmarks demonstrate that CoT-WAM substantially improves long-horizon planning over the baseline, while achieving state-of-the-art control performance and stronger zero-shot generalization.

title: Improve How You Improve: Recursive Policy Self-Improvement for Zero-Shot Open-Vocabulary Multi-Object Navigation
authors: Yang Li,Ziju Han,Aming WU,Zihao Zhang,Sijia Zhang,Yahong Han,Qinghua Hu
abstract:
To advance the development of embodied general navigation, zero-shot open-vocabulary multi-object navigation has attracted increasing attention, aiming to enable robots to efficiently search multiple objects in unseen environments without training.
For this task, the key lies in improving navigation policies from earlier searches to locate subsequent goals more efficiently. Recent methods automate this process through trajectory reflection and rule revision, enabling policy self-improvement.
However, the mechanisms for diagnosing problems and generating revisions are typically designed by humans and remain fixed across iterations. Consequently, the system’s capacity for continued self-improvement remains constrained, even as its navigation policy evolves.
To this end, we propose RPSI-Nav, a
Recursive Policy Self-Improvement
framework for zero-shot multi-object navigation that revises both
the navigation program and its revision mechanism.
RPSI-Nav diagnoses search behavior, requests diagnostic views
when existing observations cannot distinguish competing causes,
and generates targeted navigation revisions.
Feedback from subsequent goal searches is linked to the rules
that produced these revisions, guiding changes to diagnosis,
observation acquisition, and revision planning.
The updated improver governs subsequent navigation improvements, forming a recursive loop in which RPSI-Nav revises its own improvement process.
Across goals, the robot conditionally inherits accepted program updates and spatial memory, enabling search experience to improve both future navigation and adaptation. Benchmark experiments and qualitative real-robot evaluations validate RPSI-Nav’s effectiveness.
introduction:
Zero-Shot Object Navigation (ZSON) is a challenging task in Embodied AI, requiring an agent to navigate to target objects in unfamiliar
environments without training. Unlike conventional object navigation methods that focus on a single target, we consider zero-shot open-vocabulary multi-object
navigation, where a robot must search for and locate multiple
language-specified targets in succession
within the same environment [1, 19].
In this setting, agents can use experience from earlier searches
to refine their navigation strategies and locate subsequent
goals more efficiently. When agents autonomously reflect on
past searches and revise their decision rules, this process
constitutes policy self-improvement.
Related work  [2, 28, 15] explores such self-improvement across navigation settings.

However, their updates primarily concern navigation rules or
decision guidance, while the procedures that generate these
updates remain predefined.
In multi-object navigation, subsequent searches can reveal
whether earlier revisions resolved their intended problems.
However, the observations needed to explain an ineffective
revision may not yet be available, and acquiring them consumes
the same movement budget as navigation.
Later searches can therefore expose omissions in the
diagnostic checks or observation requests that guided
earlier repairs.
If this feedback only triggers further policy updates,
the rules producing these omissions may remain unchanged,
even as the navigation policy evolves.
Figure 1 illustrates why improving navigation
also calls for improving the revision process.
An initial revision adds checks of neglected locations to
S0S_{0}, producing S1S_{1}. Subsequent searches may still yield
redundant observations, revealing that the repair addressed
where to visit without adequately considering what each view
would reveal. The improver uses this feedback to revise its
own diagnosis and repair rules. The updated improver then revises S1S_{1} into S2S_{2}, which
retains useful site checks and selects views that test
multiple object hypotheses.

To this end, we propose RPSI-Nav, a
Recursive Policy Self-Improvement
framework for zero-shot open-vocabulary multi-object navigation. Its improvement program diagnoses
search problems, gathers observations that distinguish
competing explanations, and generates targeted revisions
to the navigation program. For each revision, the system
records its intended behavioral change and actual execution
outcome. Subsequent goal searches test these revisions
and provide feedback on the diagnosis and repair decisions
behind them.
When this feedback exposes limitations in its improvement
rules, the current improver applies those rules to propose
revisions to itself. These changes can alter which causes
are considered, which observations are requested, and
which navigation functions are revised. The accepted
version then governs the next round of navigation revisions,
whose outcomes drive further self-revision, closing the
recursive loop. Conditional inheritance carries accepted
updates into later searches where applicable. We evaluate
RPSI-Nav on public open-vocabulary multi-object navigation
benchmarks, complemented by qualitative real-robot experiments.

title: ZERITH V2.5: From Predictive Power to Policy Learnability
authors: Chenxi Han,Ruby,Epoch,Orion,Luke, Bin,Dusk,Lyra, Cal,Alvin,Hubert,Alex,Jiahe Han,Tao Zhang,Hang Liu,Shoujie Li,Yizhe Li,Bokui Chen,Houde Liu,Guoping Pan,Yi Cheng

abstract: When humans learn to manipulate an unfamiliar object, they may already be able to anticipate how its state will change while still being unable to control it skillfully. This gap between prediction and control motivates us to study how the priors acquired by video generation models can be used effectively by an action policy. We present ZERITH V2.5, a video–action model (VAM) in which the action policy reads intermediate features of a video generation model, and use it to study, under fixed demonstrations and a fixed total number of updates, what kind of predictive training improves subsequent action learning.
introduction:
When humans learn to manipulate an unfamiliar object, they may already adjust their grip force in anticipation of upcoming load changes while their hand still deviates from the target path [1]. Prediction can develop well before skilled control. This motor-learning result suggests a question for video-driven robot learning: what training does the knowledge acquired by a video generation model need before an action policy can use it effectively?

Video generation models learn from large-scale visual data how scenes and objects change over time. Robot learning seeks to use this knowledge to help a policy generate actions from observations and task instructions. Existing methods train video prediction and action generation jointly [2, 3, 4, 5], read intermediate features of the video model [6, 7, 8], or generate future video to support control [9, 10, 11]. Predicting how images change and learning the actions needed to complete a task, however, have different training objectives. A lower video-prediction error, on its own, says little about how well an action policy can use what the model has learned. We therefore ask two questions: how should a video generation model be further trained so that it provides more useful information for action learning, and which part of the model does the resulting gain come from?

We present ZERITH V2.5 (Figure 1), a video–action model (VAM) built on the Wan2.2 video generation model [12], and use differences in performance across training conditions to study how video priors transfer to action ability. The video generation model computes intermediate features from the current observation; the action policy reads these features and combines them with the task instruction, the robot state, and geometric information about the current scene to generate actions. Training has two stages. Stage 1 (S1) further trains the video generation model on target-task video to predict future changes at different noise levels. Stage 2 (S2) adds action learning and optimizes the video-prediction and action-generation objectives together. Each layer of the action policy has the same structure as a layer of the video generation model, so its weights can be copied from either the original or the adapted model. This lets us vary the initialization of each and test how the gain from predictive training reaches the control task.

In controlled experiments, we fix the demonstrations and the total number of updates and compare two recipes: learning prediction and action jointly from the start (direct training), and spending the first 3,000 of 30,000 updates on video predictive training before joint learning. Across three geometric-conditioning settings with three training seeds each, the second recipe raises LIBERO-Plus success by 17.55 to 19.16 percentage points (Section 6.3). The advantage holds at every evaluated budget from 30,000 to 50,000 updates, and direct training at 50,000 updates still scores below the staged recipe at 30,000 (Section 6.5).

To find where this gain comes from, we vary the initializations of the video generation model and the action policy separately. When the video generation model uses the weights after target-domain predictive training while the action policy is still initialized from the corresponding layers of the original pretrained model, LIBERO-Plus success is 19.67 points higher than with direct training. Conversely, when the video generation model starts from the original weights and only the action policy is initialized from the adapted layers, success is 3.94 points below direct training (Section 7.1). These results suggest that the control gain comes mainly from adapting the video generation model to the target domain rather than from the action policy’s initialization.

The noise setting of predictive training also matters. Training across a range of noise levels gives higher control success. Holding the future inputs at pure noise throughout matches the input seen at deployment, yet success is 20.80 points lower (Section 7.2). This suggests that the range of noise levels covered in training matters, and that matching the deployment condition is not enough. Two factors therefore shape the outcome: the predictive supervision the video generation model receives, and the module that receives the adapted weights. A further control shows that action supervision remains useful to the video generation model once joint learning begins: blocking action gradients into it throughout direct training lowers success below standard direct training.

To explain these differences, we analyze the predictive objective and the state of the model when action learning begins. A theoretical analysis shows that, for the predictive objective used here, different noise levels impose different predictive constraints (Section A.1). With the action-policy initialization held fixed, target-domain predictive training reduces the prediction loss of the video generation model 33.9-fold and its gradient norm by 95.2%, while the gradient that the action loss sends into the video model keeps 96.0% of its magnitude (Section 8.1). We hypothesize that predicting the target scene well before action learning begins gives joint training a better starting point, and eases the burden of adapting both models to the target task at once.

At deployment, the action policy reads intermediate features of the video generation model directly, without fully decoding future video frames, and the features from one forward pass are reused across all steps of the action solver. To evaluate the complete system, we pretrain on 10,000 hours of cleaned and selected real-robot data and then adapt to downstream tasks. A single checkpoint of the complete system reaches 98.95% on LIBERO and 93.70% on LIBERO-Plus (Section 5.1), and the complete policy reaches 92.3% on Meta-World MT50. On a real robot, it succeeds in 97 of 100 pick-and-place trials and 8 of 20 bin-lining trials, matching or exceeding π0.5\pi_{0.5} and Fast-WAM on every task (Section 5.2). These system evaluations test the method as a whole, while the controlled experiments with fixed data and update budgets identify the training conditions under which predictive priors transfer.

In summary, this report makes three contributions:

Training conditions for transferring video priors to control. With fixed demonstrations and a fixed total number of updates, we compare training recipes, verify the control gain of target-domain video predictive adaptation, and examine the gain across geometric-conditioning settings and training budgets (Sections 6.1, 6.3, 6.4 and 6.5).

Source of the adaptation gain and the optimization starting point. Branch-initialization and noise-coverage controls separate the role of where the adapted weights are used from the role of the predictive supervision. Together with a theoretical analysis and diagnostics of initial losses and gradients, they offer mechanistic clues to the differences in subsequent action learning (Sections 7.1, 7.2, 8.1 and Appendix A Theoretical Analysis).

A robot control system built on reusable predictive memory. The video predictive representation, current-scene geometry, and action readout are organized as separate modules, and one pass of the video branch supports a multi-step action solve. With pretraining on 10,000 hours of real-robot data, the complete system is evaluated on simulation benchmarks and real-robot tasks (Sections 2 and 5).

title: RecallFlow: Episodic Memory as the Source Distribution of Generative Robot Policies
authors: Xuji Zhang,Qilin Zhong,Zichen Zhang,Wei Zhai,Jian Di,Kun Li,Yang Cao,Wenjun Lv
abstract:
Diffusion and flow-matching policies have become a standard choice for visuomotor imitation learning, owing to their ability to model multimodal action distributions.
In memory-dependent manipulation, the robot must act on information that is no longer visible.
Existing methods feed the observation history to the policy as an additional condition, while action generation still starts from Gaussian noise.
However, the policy must then pick out the relevant target from a long and redundant history, leading to spurious correlations and unreliable decisions as the memory load grows.
Additionally, the initial noise carries no information about what the robot has seen, leaving generation without guidance toward the remembered target.
To address these issues, we propose RecallFlow, a flow-policy framework that builds the source distribution from episodic memory.
Recall–Relocalization relates the memory to the current view through a few recall slots, so that the source reflects where the remembered targets are now.
Recall Anchors then turns each slot into a Gaussian component of the source, enabling generation to start close to the intended action instead of from noise.
The transport network then completes the action from the current observation alone, keeping inference nearly as cheap as a memoryless policy.
We further build a suite of memory-dependent tasks grouped by memory load and compare all policies under a matched protocol.
Extensive experiments show that RecallFlow achieves a state-of-the-art average success rate of 80.4% on the public MIKASA-Robo memory benchmark, and outperforms the strongest baseline by 20.3 points on our suite and by 18.8 points on four real-robot tasks.
introduction:
Visuomotor policies learned from demonstrations now handle a wide range of manipulation tasks [65, 9, 43, 25, 2].
They typically act only on what is currently in view.
Many manipulation tasks, however, depend on memory: the robot must act on information that is no longer visible.
Consider the shell game (Fig. 1): a ball is placed on the table and then covered by one of three identical cups.
Once the cups are down, nothing in view sets that cup apart, yet the robot must still lift it.
Other tasks require remembering which containers have been touched or where an object was picked up [8, 15, 18].
In such tasks, the current observation shows what can be done but not what should be done, leaving memoryless policies to guess.

Most visuomotor policies today are generative.
Diffusion and flow-matching policies [9, 33, 35, 2] transport samples from a simple source distribution, usually an isotropic Gaussian, to the distribution of demonstrated actions, conditioned on the current observation.
To handle memory-dependent tasks, recent methods extend this condition with the past: they feed long observation windows to the policy [39, 57], read the history through gated cross-attention [15], or maintain structured memory states [18, 27, 50].

Despite this progress, two issues remain.
First, memory enters only as an additional condition, so a single network must both pick out the relevant target from a long and redundant history and decide how to move.
This invites spurious correlations [12, 62] and can make such policies fall far below memoryless ones on tasks that need no memory [15].
Second, generation still starts from uninformed noise, leaving it without guidance toward the remembered target.
Learned priors can replace this noise, but existing ones are derived from dataset statistics, the current observation, recent actions, other episodes, or a compressed history [32, 10, 21, 30, 67], not from the targets seen earlier in the same episode.
Together, these issues make history-conditioned policies increasingly unreliable as the memory load grows.

We take a different view and argue that the memory of an episode belongs in the source.
Flow matching can transport any source distribution to the action distribution [33, 35], so the source is free to carry what the robot remembers.
Generation would then start near the remembered target, and the network would only need to refine the motion from the current observation.
However, memory cannot simply be plugged into the source.
What was seen earlier must first be found again in the current view, a problem long studied in video understanding [16, 56, 60, 6, 47].
It must then be expressed as a distribution over actions.

To this end, we propose RecallFlow, a flow-policy framework that builds the source distribution from episodic memory (Fig. 2).
It rests on a division of labor: memory decides where generation starts, and the present decides how to get there.

RecallFlow keeps an episodic memory bank of patch-level tokens from earlier frames.
Memory attention lets the current visual tokens read this bank.
A few learnable recall slots then read both the memory and the current view, so that the source reflects where the remembered targets are now.

Each recall slot is mapped to a Gaussian anchor in action space, and the anchors, together with a standard Gaussian, form a mixture source.
Generation thus starts close to the intended action instead of from noise.
A transport network then completes the action chunk from the current observation alone, keeping inference nearly as cheap as a memoryless policy.

On RecallSuite, our suite of five memory-dependent tasks, RecallFlow improves the average success rate by 20.3 points over the strongest of two memoryless and two history-conditioned policies under the same protocol, with the largest margins where several items must be remembered (64.7% vs. 15.0% on NoRepeat-4).
On the public MIKASA-Robo benchmark [8], it reaches 80.4% average success over five tasks, above the best published result of 75.1% [18].
On RoboMimic [39], where the current observation suffices, it stays on par with memoryless policies, whereas long-history policies degrade.
On a real xArm 7, it improves over the strongest baseline by 18.8 points on four memory-dependent tasks.
Ablations show that forming the source from the episodic memory matches or exceeds conditioning the same transport network on it (97.0% vs. 92.0% on NoRepeat), and that relocalization matters most when the memory load is high.
Our contributions are as follows:

Memory as source. We form the source distribution of a flow policy from episodic memory as likelihood-trained Gaussian anchors, so that generation starts close to the intended action.

Recall–Relocalization. Memory attention and a few recall slots relate the episodic memory to the current view, so that the anchors reflect where the remembered targets are now.

Evaluation. We build a suite of five memory-dependent tasks grouped by memory load. Under a matched protocol, RecallFlow achieves the highest average success rate on it, and it sets the state of the art on the public MIKASA-Robo benchmark.

1. Memory as source. We form the source distribution of a flow policy from episodic memory as likelihood-trained Gaussian anchors, so that generation starts close to the intended action.

2. Recall–Relocalization. Memory attention and a few recall slots relate the episodic memory to the current view, so that the anchors reflect where the remembered targets are now.

3. Evaluation. We build a suite of five memory-dependent tasks grouped by memory load. Under a matched protocol, RecallFlow achieves the highest average success rate on it, and it sets the state of the art on the public MIKASA-Robo benchmark.

title: Improving While Deployed: Learning Proactive End-to-End Driving from Imperfect Human Takeover Data
authors: Yangang Ren,Di Zeng,Jun Li,Zirui Li,Chengjiang Zhang,Xiaoqing Ye,Ji Tao,Chen Lv
abstract: Once deployed on vehicles, end-to-end driving models continuously encounter challenging scenarios, generating valuable human takeover data that capture both model outputs and human behaviors. However, human interventions are often imperfect, as drivers may intervene too late or unnecessarily. Consequently, direct imitation can reinforce late responses or discourage otherwise appropriate maneuvers. To address this challenge, we propose an offline post-training framework that transforms imperfect takeover data into proactive supervision. We first construct diverse trajectory candidates by augmenting the plans of the deployed model and shifting recorded human corrective maneuvers earlier in time. We then train a scene-conditioned trajectory scorer to rank these candidates using expert demonstrations and unpaired preference signals from takeover logs. Using this scorer, we selectively replace pre-takeover training targets with higher-scoring candidates while retaining the original targets in normal driving scenarios. Finally, we distill the resulting targets into the driving model without changing its inference architecture. In closed-loop evaluations using real-world scenarios reconstructed with 4D Gaussian splatting, our method achieves the highest overall success rate, outperforming the deployed model, direct imitation learning and trajectory post-optimization. These results highlight a practical path toward efficient updates of deployed driving models using existing fleet logs.
introduction:
End-to-end (E2E) driving models can still encounter situations that require a driver to take control after deployment on real vehicles [12, 16]. When a driver intervenes, the resulting log records the vehicle’s
motion before takeover, the timing of the intervention, and the
driver’s subsequent response. These records provide feedback for
post-training from the deployed model’s own on-road
experience [36]. A simple way to use these logs is to imitate the recorded trajectories. However, drivers may take over even when the original model plan is reasonable [11, 42], and a necessary correction may begin only after
undesirable behavior has emerged [1]. Direct
imitation can therefore discourage an appropriate maneuver or
reinforce a delayed response. Trajectory post-optimization can
refine the imitation target, but the result depends on predefined costs and constraints [26]. The
challenge is to infer from the driver’s subsequent response whether an earlier plan needed revision and, if so, how it should have changed.

One way to learn from on-road takeovers is to use driving simulators to recreate the traffic conditions that prompted them and train a model to handle similar situations [2, 42]. For example, DRARL identifies likely causes of disengagement and evaluates the updated planner in simulated scenarios. However, the sim-to-real gap can limit how well improvements observed in these environments transfer to real vehicles [39]. A second line of work reconstructs scenes from real driving logs at the sensor level. RAD trains E2E models through closed-loop interaction in scenes reconstructed with 3D Gaussian splatting [8], while SimScale combines real driving data with pseudo-expert demonstrations for synthetic variations of logged scenes [31]. World Engine uses fleet logs to generate safety-critical interactions for post-training and reports improvements in on-road tests [16].
While intervention signals help identify challenging scenarios, these methods primarily rely on simulated rewards or generated demonstrations, rather than directly leveraging human corrections from takeover logs.

In this paper, we propose an offline post-training framework that transforms imperfect takeover data into proactive supervision for E2E driving models. For each driving scene, we construct diverse trajectory candidates by advancing recorded human corrections and augmenting the multimodal plans of the deployed model. A scene-conditioned trajectory scorer learns to rank these candidates through expert trajectory matching and unpaired preference supervision. Unlike prior methods that directly optimize discrete action choices or action likelihoods [20, 33], our scorer evaluates complete trajectories from their continuous waypoint coordinates. We selectively refine pre-takeover supervision targets using its scores and distill the refined targets into the deployed model.
Our main contributions are threefold.

Intervention-aware trajectory augmentation.
We shift recorded human corrections earlier by different time offsets and randomly augment the deployed model’s multimodal plans. The resulting candidates offer earlier responses while retaining alternatives when corrections are unnecessary or unsuitable.

Trajectory-level preference learning.
We train a scene-conditioned scorer using expert trajectory matching and unpaired desirability feedback from takeover logs. It evaluates continuous, long-horizon trajectories without requiring explicit trajectory likelihoods or preference pairs involving unexecuted model plans.

Selective target refinement for offline post-training.
We replace pre-takeover targets only when a candidate scores sufficiently higher than the recorded trajectory and distill the refined supervision into the E2E model. Using 11,162 real-world takeover segments, our method improves the overall closed-loop success rate from 70.87% to 81.60%, compared with 75.30% for direct imitation learning.

1. Intervention-aware trajectory augmentation.
We shift recorded human corrections earlier by different time offsets and randomly augment the deployed model’s multimodal plans. The resulting candidates offer earlier responses while retaining alternatives when corrections are unnecessary or unsuitable.

2. Trajectory-level preference learning.
We train a scene-conditioned scorer using expert trajectory matching and unpaired desirability feedback from takeover logs. It evaluates continuous, long-horizon trajectories without requiring explicit trajectory likelihoods or preference pairs involving unexecuted model plans.

3. Selective target refinement for offline post-training.
We replace pre-takeover targets only when a candidate scores sufficiently higher than the recorded trajectory and distill the refined supervision into the E2E model. Using 11,162 real-world takeover segments, our method improves the overall closed-loop success rate from 70.87% to 81.60%, compared with 75.30% for direct imitation learning.

title: ExecGap: Exploiting Command-Execution Gap for Patch Attacks on Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Keke Tang,Guolin Qiu,Tianyu Hao,Daizong Liu,Yikai Zhang,Peican Zhu,Zhihong Tian
comment: CoRL 2026
abstract:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have become a powerful paradigm for robotic manipulation and show strong promise for real-world deployment, making adversarial robustness critical for reliable robot operation.
Existing adversarial attacks on VLA-controlled robots mainly optimize prediction-level discrepancies or rollout-level deviations to disrupt manipulation.
However, they rarely account for the fact that VLA-predicted commands are not executed directly, but must be realized through downstream control and robot embodiment.
In this paper, we propose ExecGap, an adversarial patch attack framework that exploits this command-execution gap to expose embodiment-specific execution vulnerabilities.
Specifically, ExecGap biases VLA-predicted task-space commands toward low-executability directions, which are estimated from kinematic inefficiency and dynamic weak actuation.
This induces execution degradation, where the predicted command becomes difficult to realize effectively, thereby impairing task completion.
Extensive simulation experiments across multiple VLA policies show that ExecGap induces larger command-execution mismatch and weaker realized execution than existing patch attacks.
Real-robot experiments further validate that the deployed patch can induce execution degradation on physical platforms.
introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for robotic manipulation [1, 2, 3].
By integrating visual perception, language conditioning, and action generation, they enable robots to interpret natural-language instructions and perform diverse manipulation tasks.
As VLA-based robots show growing promise for real-world deployment, their reliability under adversarial conditions becomes a critical requirement for safe operation in physical environments.

Recent studies have begun to examine this concern through adversarial attacks on robotic VLA systems.
Existing attacks mainly optimize visual perturbations or adversarial patches to induce prediction-level discrepancies, semantic confusion, or rollout-level deviations [4, 5, 6].
Typical objectives enlarge the difference between clean and perturbed actions, drive the policy toward erroneous manipulation behaviors, or cause visible deviations over the rollout.
Although effective at task disruption, these methods primarily treat the VLA output or rollout behavior as the attack target, while the physical realization of the predicted command remains less explored.

However, VLA-controlled manipulation is not determined by prediction alone.
A VLA model may output a semantically plausible command, yet this command must still be realized through downstream control and robot embodiment.
As illustrated in Fig. 1, embodied constraints such as position limits, force limits, and kinematic constraints can reshape or attenuate the task-space command before physical execution.
This creates a command-execution gap: a command that appears reasonable at the prediction level may still be difficult to realize effectively, thereby reducing effective task progress and making task completion less reliable.

In this paper, we expose an embodiment-specific attack surface arising from the gap between VLA-issued commands and their physical realization, and study the resulting failure mode termed execution degradation.
Rather than directly maximizing prediction discrepancy or rollout-level deviation, our goal is to enlarge the mismatch between the VLA-predicted task-space command and the realized motion.
To this end, we propose ExecGap, an adversarial patch attack framework that exploits the limited executability of robot motion.
Specifically, ExecGap derives low-executability directions from two factors: kinematic inefficiency and dynamic weak actuation.
By biasing commands toward these hard-to-execute directions, ExecGap increases command-execution mismatch, weakens realized task progress, and degrades task completion.
Extensive simulation experiments on LIBERO suites [7] show that ExecGap effectively disrupts manipulation and induces larger command-execution mismatch with weaker realized execution across OpenVLA [1], OpenVLA-OFT [8], and π0\pi_{0} [3].
Real-robot validation further shows that physically deployed patches can induce execution degradation on robotic hardware.

Overall, our contributions are three-fold:

We identify execution degradation as an execution-side VLA failure mode arising from degraded embodied realization rather than prediction-side discrepancy alone.

We propose ExecGap, a robot-aware patch attack that exploits kinematic inefficiency and dynamic weak actuation to induce low-executability commands.

We validate ExecGap in simulation and on real robots, showing stronger execution degradation in simulation and physical feasibility on real platforms.

1. We identify execution degradation as an execution-side VLA failure mode arising from degraded embodied realization rather than prediction-side discrepancy alone.

2. We propose ExecGap, a robot-aware patch attack that exploits kinematic inefficiency and dynamic weak actuation to induce low-executability commands.

3. We validate ExecGap in simulation and on real robots, showing stronger execution degradation in simulation and physical feasibility on real platforms.

title: Measuring the Conservatism of Latent Safety Filters for World Models
authors: Johannes Mootz,Mani Amani,Reza Akhavian
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
abstract:
A latent safety filter decides from the latent of a world model whether a planned action is safe.
Conformal calibration sets the threshold of the filter so that it accepts an unsafe action only with a small probability.
However, the filter can still be conservative and refuse many safe actions, depending on the latent.
To measure the conservatism that a latent forces on the filter, we group similar latents and actions into cells.
A filter that gives one decision per cell can refuse the unsafe transitions of a cell only by refusing the safe ones in it as well.
We call the share of safe transitions that lie in such cells the overlap.
We prove that the overlap is the minimum share of safe transitions that such a filter has to refuse in order to accept no unsafe transition in the data.
Both the overlap and the conformal calibration can be applied to any latent.
We use this to compare three existing designs, in which the safety labels train a classifier on top of the world model, the world model itself, or a separate encoder beside it.
In a visual navigation task, the separate encoder has the lowest overlap, and at the same conformal level its filter refuses the fewest safe actions and lets the planner reach the most goals of the three.
introduction:
World models let a robot plan from images and proprioception in a learned latent (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018; Hafner et al., 2025; Toso et al., 2026a).
However, they are prone to hallucinations (Hansen and Wang, 2026), and a robot that relies on their predictions outside the training data can execute unsafe actions (Seo et al., 2025; Cao and Bansal, 2026).
To improve safety, safety value functions from Hamilton–Jacobi reachability (Nakamura et al., 2025) and control barrier functions (Nakamura et al., 2026) have been learned in the latent.
These latent safety filters check each proposed action and either switch to a backup policy (Nakamura et al., 2025; Seo et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2025) or correct the action smoothly (Nakamura et al., 2026).

A latent safety filter is itself learned from data, so it is not fully reliable and can accept an action that leads to a failure (Seo et al., 2025).
Conformal calibration sets its threshold so that, under exchangeability, the probability of accepting a failure stays below a chosen level (Kim et al., 2025).
This bound holds on any representation, and how often the filter refuses a safe action depends on the representation (Kim et al., 2025; Feldman et al., 2026).

A filter on a latent can tell apart only what the encoder keeps.
The encoder of a world model is trained to predict the next latent, and this objective can be minimized while the encoder discards every unstable mode of the system (Toso et al., 2026a) or encodes only features that are irrelevant for control (Toso et al., 2026b).
Kim et al. (2025) show that a latent safety filter fails when the latent does not hold the safety-relevant information.
An encoder can map many states to the same latent, so a safe and an unsafe state can share one latent, and the filter then gives both the same decision.
A filter that is calibrated to rarely accept a failure refuses the safe one as well, which makes it conservative.

Reasoning about safety in a latent space is difficult, because a certificate on the latent does not automatically certify the true system.
Lutkus et al. (2025) show that a latent barrier function keeps the true system safe if it keeps a margin to the unsafe set that is proportional to the error of the latent dynamics.
The set of states that an encoder maps to one latent is the fiber of that latent, which is the nested pre-image of the latent under the observation map and the encoder.
Mootz et al. (2026) show that the certificate needs a second margin, the fiber defect, which is how far safety can fall from one state of a fiber to another.
Both margins are computed from the true state, and in practice there are only logged transitions, each labeled safe or unsafe by its outcome.

In this work, we measure the conservatism that a latent forces on a safety filter from these labeled transitions.
On a continuous latent two logged transitions rarely share a latent, so we group similar latents and actions into cells.
A filter that gives one decision per cell treats all transitions of a cell alike.
If a cell holds both safe and unsafe transitions, the filter can refuse the unsafe ones only by refusing the whole cell, so the safe ones are refused with them.
We call the share of safe transitions that lie in such cells the overlap, and we prove that such a filter has to refuse at least this share to refuse every logged unsafe transition.
Figure  shows the cells of the latents of three encoders.

The overlap and the conformal bound can be computed for any latent.
We use this to compare three existing designs of a latent safety filter, which differ in where the safety labels enter.
A classifier (Kim et al., 2025; Nath et al., 2026) or a projector (Agrawal et al., 2026) can be trained on top of the latent of the frozen world model.
The safety labels can be added to the training loss of the world model, so that the planner and the filter share one latent that was also trained to predict safety (Huang et al., 2024; Seo et al., 2025).
A separate encoder can be trained on the safety labels alone and placed beside the world model, which again stays unchanged (Tabbara et al., 2026; Mani et al., 2025).
We build all three for a visual navigation task with a world model and compare them at the same level of the conformal bound by their overlap and their refusals.
Our contributions are:

We define the overlap of a latent using labeled transitions grouped into cells of similar latents and actions. It measures the share of safe transitions whose cell also contains an unsafe transition.

We prove that the overlap is the minimum share of safe transitions that a filter with one decision per cell has to refuse in order to accept no unsafe transition in the data.

We compare three existing designs in visual navigation with a fixed planner and the same conformal level. The separate safety encoder has the lowest overlap, and its filter refuses the fewest safe actions and reaches the most goals.

1. We define the overlap of a latent using labeled transitions grouped into cells of similar latents and actions. It measures the share of safe transitions whose cell also contains an unsafe transition.

2. We prove that the overlap is the minimum share of safe transitions that a filter with one decision per cell has to refuse in order to accept no unsafe transition in the data.

3. We compare three existing designs in visual navigation with a fixed planner and the same conformal level. The separate safety encoder has the lowest overlap, and its filter refuses the fewest safe actions and reaches the most goals.

title: Finetuning VLAs for Dexterous Manipulation: The Right Checkpoint Is All You Need
authors: Artur Kuramshin,Charlotte Cloutier,Michael Przystupa,Kirsty Ellis,Mohammad S. Akhter,Glen Berseth
comment: Accepted to the Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation at CoRL 2026
abstract:
Vision-Language-Action models have demonstrated strong manipulation capabilities. A limitation of VLA models is that most manipulation datasets focus on parallel-jaw gripper systems, making transfer to multi-finger hands challenging, particularly as teleoperation datasets are harder to collect with multi-fingered robots.
In this work, we study how to best adapt VLAs to dexterous hands by pairing supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with diffusion-steering reinforcement learning (DSRL).
Using π0.5\pi_{0.5} and a LEAP hand, we evaluate five fine-tuning recipes across two simulation tasks using only a handful of demonstrations.
Our empirical analysis yields three key insights: (1) SFT success is poorly correlated with post-DSRL success, meaning the best SFT checkpoint is rarely the most effective to steer; (2) freezing the vision-language model (VLM) and tuning only the action expert produces the most steerable policy for both training and out-of-distribution placements; and (3) low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is the least steerable approach. Consequently, we recommend an adaptation recipe that freezes the VLM, fully trains the action expert, and eschews SFT rollout success as a checkpoint selection metric.
introduction:
Vision-Language-Action models (VLA) [5, 4, 3, 17] are largely pretrained on cross-embodiment corpora dominated by parallel-jaw grippers [26, 16]. This confines them to tasks that a two-finger gripper can solve, which excludes many tasks involving tool use and reorientation of the hand [34, 1]. Because multi-fingered hands are scarce in existing pretraining data [35, 21], deploying a VLA on a novel dexterous embodiment necessitates fine-tuning. Furthermore, this adaptation must succeed on a limited number of demonstrations due to the high data-collection cost associated with dexterous teleoperation [30, 6, 12]. In this work, we investigate how to adapt VLA models for tasks with multi-fingered hands on limited data.

How to fine-tune a VLA, meaning which of its parameters to update and at what rate, is already contested: some report that freezing the language model or the vision encoder degrades adaptation [10, 17], others keep action-pathway gradients out of the backbone by default [23, 8]. These conclusions were reached by evaluating adaptation solely based on the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) checkpoint with the highest rollout success. When adaptation pipelines culminate in latent-noise steering [31, 32], the SFT checkpoint merely serves as an initialization. The critical factor is instead whether the frozen model’s noise space admits an actor that succeeds and generalizes beyond its training states.

In this paper, we investigate five SFT recipes to determine which, if any, reliably supports dexterous manipulation transfer when followed by latent steering. Our recipes vary which parts of the VLA we train (action expert only, plus the vision pathway, or the full model) and whether we update the language model and action expert fully or via LoRA [14] adapters. Our analysis applies these combinations to π0.5\pi_{0.5} [4] on a 16-DoF LEAP hand [28] across two simulation tasks. We first compare VLA fine-tuning recipes as initialization for latent steering. Based on our empirical analysis, we provide a concrete recommendation: when SFT is followed by latent steering, freeze the VLM, train the action expert in full, and avoid using SFT rollout success for recipe or checkpoint selection. Furthermore, the choice of checkpoint mattered less than the choice of recipe. Since steerability declines over the course of SFT while motion quality improves, we suggest selecting the earliest checkpoint that qualitatively reproduces the demonstrated skill as the initialization for steering.
