title: Radar-Native Control Barrier Functions: Doppler Range Rate as a Measured Barrier Derivative
authors: Johannes Mootz,Hesam Mojtahedi,Reza Akhavian
abstract:
Safe control around dynamic obstacles requires information about both distance and relative motion. Range-based filters commonly reconstruct the required range rate from successive range measurements or from obstacle-state estimators, which can introduce estimator delay or sensitivity to range noise when obstacle motion changes.
A frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) radar measures radial relative velocity directly through Doppler. We use this measurement as the derivative of an ego-centered range control barrier function (CBF) and obtain a closed-form filter on the robot’s forward velocity.
A measurement margin constructed from sensor error bounds accounts for errors in range, Doppler, ego velocity, and bearing. In 508 paired encounters within the platform’s retreat capability, direct Doppler produces two buffer incursions, compared with 15 for a constant-acceleration and 25 for a constant-velocity Kalman filter.
On a Unitree Go1, the controller stops at 0.777±0.015​m0.777\pm 0.015\,\mathrm{m} against the predicted 0.758​m0.758\,\mathrm{m} and reacts to a farther approaching object while a nearer static return remains.
The guarantee covers the longitudinal range channel under bounded measurement errors and continuously available detections.
Direct Doppler removes the need to reconstruct range rate in the safety loop, reducing the delay between a change in obstacle motion and its effect on the safety command.
introduction:
When a dynamic obstacle starts moving toward a robot, the safety command must respond before the remaining distance becomes too small. This requires information about both distance and relative motion.
The nearest obstacle is not necessarily the one that requires the strongest response: a farther approaching object can require braking or retreat while a nearer object remains stationary.
Control barrier functions (CBFs) provide a way to enforce a distance constraint by filtering the robot’s nominal command under specified conditions [1].

For a range-based barrier, the constraint depends on the range rate. Range-only measurements, such as from conventional LiDAR or depth cameras, do not provide this quantity directly, so it must be reconstructed from successive measurements or obtained from an obstacle-state estimator [2].
When obstacle motion changes, the estimate can take several samples to adjust. Increasing the estimator’s responsiveness also passes more range noise into the control command.
For a safety filter, this tradeoff matters most when little clearance remains and the constraint becomes active.

A frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) radar provides range and bearing information together with radial velocity measured through the Doppler effect [3].
Each detection carries its radial velocity relative to the sensor, obtained within a single frame. For a range barrier, this is the barrier derivative.
The range rate is therefore available without differentiating successive range measurements or estimating an obstacle-velocity state.
To evaluate a candidate velocity command, the contribution of the robot’s current forward motion must first be accounted for.

We present a radar-native CBF formulation that uses this measured range rate and filters the forward velocity command. The relative range dynamics give the correction from the measured ego velocity to a candidate command.
Each retained detection then imposes an upper velocity bound, and the smallest bound determines the safety command. A measurement-error margin accounts for bounded errors in range, Doppler, ego velocity, and bearing. It follows from the sensor configuration and can be checked before deployment, yet still has to be accounted for in the constraint.
The formulation acts on the velocity interface available on many robots [4] and covers the longitudinal range channel under the conditions stated in Section IV-C.

The evaluation examines how the source of range rate affects the safety command after a change in obstacle motion. In 508 paired encounters within the platform’s retreat capability, direct Doppler produces two buffer incursions, compared with 15 for a constant-acceleration and 25 for a constant-velocity Kalman filter.
Hardware tests on a Unitree Go1 examine the predicted static standoff and the response to a farther approaching object while a nearer static return remains. The main contributions are:

A radar-native range CBF that uses FMCW Doppler as its measured derivative and yields a closed-form filter for forward velocity, without an obstacle-velocity estimator.

A radar-native range CBF that uses FMCW Doppler as its measured derivative and yields a closed-form filter for forward velocity, without an obstacle-velocity estimator.

A measurement-error margin expressed in radar and ego-velocity quantities, with explicit conditions for forward invariance.

A paired simulation showing fewer near-boundary incursions than range-based Kalman filters, and hardware tests of predicted standoff and multi-object response on a quadruped.

1. A radar-native range CBF that uses FMCW Doppler as its measured derivative and yields a closed-form filter for forward velocity, without an obstacle-velocity estimator.

2. A measurement-error margin expressed in radar and ego-velocity quantities, with explicit conditions for forward invariance.

3. A paired simulation showing fewer near-boundary incursions than range-based Kalman filters, and hardware tests of predicted standoff and multi-object response on a quadruped.

title: LoRN: Low-Rank Noise Steering for Generative Robot Policies
authors: Wei Liu,Abrar Anwar,Huihua Zhao,Soha Pouya,Yan Chang
abstract:
Noise steering improves pretrained generative robot policies by learning to select their initial noise without updating model weights.
We find that actions in the evaluated world-action models are more sensitive to video noise than action noise, making video noise an expressive input for steering.
However, the noise-steering methods we evaluate, in their published forms, struggle to scale to the high-dimensional noise inputs of large policy classes such as world-action models.
We introduce Low-Rank Noise Steering (LoRN), a reinforcement learning method that scales noise steering to world-action models.
A small steering actor selects a direction through a fixed low-rank random projection, while our norm-controlled construction keeps the resulting noise near the typical scale of a Gaussian sample.
This separates the actor’s control dimension from the full noise dimension, enabling steering of both video and action inputs.
Across three world-action models and ten model–task pairs, video steering improves average success by 26.2 percentage points over the base policy, compared with 7.1 points for DSRL action steering.
For smaller action policies, the same construction achieves comparable final success while generally improving early-training success. Steering actors trained in simulation also transfer to three physical bimanual manipulation tasks across two base policies, without additional real-world training.
introduction:
Large robot foundation models, such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs), can perform a wide range of behaviors.
For these models to reliably succeed on a particular task, they must learn to improve via interaction with their environment.
Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a way to improve their task performance through interaction, but updating large policies can be computationally expensive.
Noise steering has emerged as an approach to guide the denoising process of diffusion and flow-matching policies by replacing the initial noise samples.
However, these methods struggle to scale to high-dimensional noise inputs that are common in large policy classes such as VLAs and WAMs.
This work develops a noise steering method that addresses this challenge, focusing primarily on WAMs.

World-action models couple visual dynamics prediction with action generation.
Their sampling inputs include initial source distribution noise associated with both video and actions, and changing the video noise can also change the actions the model produces.
Existing action-noise steering methods do not exploit this input, and in the implementations and settings we evaluate they give no consistent improvement when applied to the substantially larger video-noise space.
In this work, we find that WAMs’ decoded actions are more sensitive to video noise than action noise, implying video noise may serve as a strong steering modality.

We introduce Low-Rank Noise Steering (LoRN), a method to efficiently train noise steering policies for world-action models.
Recent work has found that selecting the initial noise samples of diffusion or flow matching heads can effectively steer robot policies in a sample efficient manner without requiring any updates to the full model [26].
We find that extending noise steering to large robot foundation models often fails, primarily because their noise inputs are high-dimensional and their sensitivity to it differs sharply between the video and action inputs.

LoRN overcomes these challenges by steering a low-rank projection of the noise distribution.
A steering actor outputs a low-dimensional vector that a fixed random projection lifts to the full noise dimension, which is then rescaled to resemble a Gaussian sample’s norm.
The frozen policy denoises this noise, and the actor is trained with reinforcement learning.
This formulation scales to high-dimensional action spaces and, most surprisingly, enables the steerability of the video noise to improve denoised actions.

Two design choices underlie our approach.
First, the actor controls only a small, low-rank subspace of the noise regardless of the input dimension.
We show that such a low-rank subspace contains directions that improve on the base policy with high probability.
Second, mixing the actor’s direction with a fresh Gaussian sample preserves the expected squared norm of the noise, so the steered noise stays near the typical norm that diffusion and flow-matching policies are trained to denoise.
Because neither choice depends on the structure of the noise input, LoRN can be applied to either the video or the action noise of a WAM.
This flexibility matters in practice: we find that a WAM’s actions are far more sensitive to one noise input than the other, and a probe that needs no reward identifies that input before training.
On the three models we evaluate, it is the video noise, which existing methods do not steer.

We evaluate LoRN on three world-action models, on action-noise steering with π0\pi_{0}, π0.5\pi_{0.5}, and Diffusion Policy, and on a physical bimanual robot station.
In aggregate across three WAMs and ten model–task pairs, DSRL on the action noise improves the base policies by 7.1 percentage points, while LoRN steers the more expressive video noise and improves them by 26.2 percentage points.
We also evaluate LoRN on twelve action-policy simulation tasks, where it generally achieves higher early-training success against DSRL [26] and LP-DS [24].
Finally, we demonstrate that LoRN trained in simulation transfers to three physical bimanual manipulation tasks on two base policies, the released GR00T N1.7 and a π0.5\pi_{0.5} fine-tuned in simulation, without additional training on hardware.

Our contributions are fourfold:

We introduce LoRN, low-rank noise steering for robot foundation models: a fixed random subspace of the noise, mixed with a fresh Gaussian sample, independent of the actor’s output, so that the expected squared noise norm is preserved.

We identify noise-norm preservation as a key requirement for reliable steering, and measure the band of norms that each frozen policy tolerates.

We prove that a random subspace of rank rr misses the high-advantage noise of a state with probability at most (1−p)r(1-p)^{r}, where pp is that noise’s share of the sphere, and that a policy which selects an improving direction in that subspace whenever one exists improves on the base policy.

We provide a practical recipe for steering world-action models, with a reward-free probe that finds which noise input to steer, and evaluate it on three world-action models, twelve action-policy tasks, and a bimanual robot station with two base policies.

title: How Uncertain Is My Action? Self-Correcting Visual Planning with Frozen World Models
authors: Siqing Li,Luming Yang,Yijia Jiao,Junze Deng,Alper Yilmaz
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract:
A frozen latent world model combined with sampling-based model predictive control is a visual planner. At deployment, the executed action can depart from the commanded one, and the frozen model has no way to notice. We show that the model can be run in reverse: for any hypothesized actuation shift, it predicts what it should have observed under that shift, and comparing this prediction with what was actually observed quantifies the shift and lets the planner correct itself. Unlike the residual energy, which mixes the shift with the model’s own error, the score keeps only the part of the residual that a shift can produce. This shift score detects the shift with a locally optimal test, estimates it with Cramér–Rao error bars, names the dominant generator, and compensates the planner once an alarm fires. On PushT, TwoRoom and OGBench-Cube with a frozen latent world model, measured detection follows the prediction to within 0.05 AUROC. Self-correction raises success from 0.650 to 0.862 on PushT and from 0.378 to 0.432 on the harder Cube task, levels with an oracle that is told the true shift at the same block, better than five common test-time adaptation methods. On a real robotic arm, the score identifies a base-joint offset that no joint encoder registers and reduces the reach error from 36 mm to 3–5 mm, and under shifts drawn at random and sealed before the session, estimates recover 92–94% of the error reduction achieved with the true shift.
The broader implication is that a frozen world model can act as a filter by predicting the future, testing action-interface uncertainty and validity, and finally correcting failures.
introduction:
Visual planning often pairs a frozen latent world model (WM) trained on pixels with sampling-based model predictive control (MPC). The planner rolls out candidate action sequences, selects those predicted to reach the goal, and executes the first action block [48, 25, 1, 36]. This uses the model only in the forward direction, predicting future states from observations and commanded actions. At deployment, however, a miscalibrated axis or a slipped joint can silently transform every command. We call this an actuation shift. The frozen model still assumes commands are executed as given, so its preferred plan can drive the robot away from the goal (Fig. 1a). In other words, the model has no notion of execution uncertainty; it assumes every command is executed as given and cannot detect when it is not.

Existing remedies act on the model’s prediction error [14], and test-time adaptation reduces it by updating weights or auxiliary modules [43, 27, 47, 39, 38], without separating an actuation shift from the model’s own error.

Our starting point is that a frozen world model is a counterfactual simulator of its own actions [32, 10, 7]. For each hypothesized shift θ\theta, the frozen model predicts the next latent as if the command were executed through T⁡(θ)T(\theta). Comparing this prediction with the observed next latent reveals which hypothesis best explains the transition, without further training. Inverting the simulator over a Lie group [37] of action transformations turns the question “is the model wrong?” into an estimation problem amenable to the statistical local approach to fault detection [9, 6]. This perspective motivates a filter-like diagnostic: calibrate the prediction residual and test whether it indicates an actuation shift.

Building on this view, we propose Action Uncertainty Self-correction (Actus), which lets a frozen world model quantify its execution uncertainty and correct actuation shifts without any weight update.
At its core is the shift score, which projects the model’s residual onto the directions in which each generator would move the prediction, given by a Jacobian–vector product (JVP) of the frozen model along that
generator. Without a shift, its covariance is the Fisher information (Fig. 1b).
From this single statistic, Actus detects the shift with a locally optimal Rao test, estimates it by Gauss–Newton (GN) with Cramér–Rao error bars, and attributes it to the dominant generator. Once an alarm fires, it compensates for the estimated shift by replanning through its inverse, enabling self-correcting visual planning without updating the world model. Calibration on nominal rollouts accounts for model error and variation across sessions, allowing us to predict detection and estimation performance before a shift occurs.

We conduct experiments with a frozen LeWM [25] on three standard visual planning benchmarks, PushT [11], TwoRoom [36] and OGBench-Cube [31], and demonstrate that Actus detects and corrects actuation shifts without any weight updates. As shown in Fig. 1c, measured detection follows the predicted law across all 254254 shifts. Compensation brings the frozen planner close to an oracle told the true shift at the same block, outperforming all baselines. Actus further transfers unchanged to DINO-WM [48] and remains effective on a real SO-101 robotic arm.

To summarize, our main contributions are:

Inverse counterfactual formulation.
We formulate action shifts as Lie-group transformations of commands. We show that the residual energy is insensitive to shifts at first order and derive a shift score computed with one JVP per generator, whose detection and estimation performance can be predicted from nominal data (Sec. 3 and Sec. 4).

A self-correcting framework.
We propose Actus, which combines calibrated Rao detection, GN estimation with uncertainty quantification, generator attribution, and alarm-gated inverse compensation to correct actuation shifts without updating model weights (Sec. 4).

Empirical validation.
Across 254254 shifts, detection AUROC matches predictions within 0.050.05 and exceeds residual energy by up to 0.380.38. Compensation raises success significantly, matching the same-block oracle and outperforming the adaptation baselines. Actus also transfers to DINO-WM without retuning (Sec. 5).

Real-world Application. We validate Actus on a real robot arm, detecting a base-joint offset invisible to joint readings and reducing reach error from 3636–3838 mm to 3.03.0–5.55.5 mm, matching repeat noise (Sec. 5.6).

title: Recoverability, Not Invariance: Certified Safety for Robots at the Limits of Performance
authors: Thomas A. Berrueta,Joshua D. Ibrahim,Gilchrist X. Johnson,John Lathrop,Soon-Jo Chung
comment: For our supplementary video, seethis https URL
abstract: Safety certification in robotics typically rests on forward invariance of the deployed controller, a property that demands high-fidelity models at the edge of the operating envelope, exactly where models are least reliable and robots perform best. As a result, many of the behaviors we most want robots to run, from learned policies to aggressive maneuvers at the limits of traction, cannot be certified at all. We introduce recoverability, a contraction-theoretic safety concept that resolves this tension by certifying a robot’s ability to reengage a trusted recovery mode rather than the invariance of a deployed behavior. We prove that switching to the recovery mode from anywhere inside a certified tube guarantees exponential convergence, even under disturbances and model error. To decide when to switch, we derive the contraction insertion gradient, the first-order effect of a recovery insertion on the certificate, and embed it in a switching-time program in which feasibility alone guarantees safety and optimality only shapes performance. To supply the certificates, we develop sequential convex synthesis that monotonically grows the certified tube toward the exact viability kernel. We validate our approach in simulated quadrotor flight through uncertain obstacles, where it outperforms invariance-based safety filters, and in hardware deployments aboard a full-scale IndyNXT autonomous racecar, where it repeatedly recovers the car from an aggressive raceline at the limits of handling in the rain. Recoverability provides a certified exit strategy, extending formal safety guarantees to aggressive, learned, and experimental behaviors without requiring their invariance.
introduction:
Robots are increasingly asked to operate near the limits of their capabilities. Legged robots run and recover from falls using policies learned in simulation [1]. Learned controllers race drones past human champions and to the physical limits of the platform [2, 3]. Automated vehicles exploit tire saturation to avoid collisions and to drive at the limits of adhesion [4, 5, 6]. In each case, the most valuable behaviors lie near the boundary of the operating envelope, and improving performance means operating closer to that boundary or expanding the envelope itself, a practice known as envelope expansion. However, conventional safety certification penalizes operation at the boundary, treating peak performance as a hazard to be avoided.

Most formal safety frameworks are based on the principle of forward invariance [7], in which a set of safe states is rendered invariant under the closed-loop dynamics. This principle underlies control barrier functions (CBFs) [8, 9], Hamilton–Jacobi (HJ) reachability [10, 11], viability theory [12], and predictive safety filters [13, 14]. However, establishing forward invariance of the deployed closed-loop system requires a dynamical model that can be trusted throughout the safe set. High-performance operation concentrates the robot in regimes such as tire saturation, contact, and degraded surfaces, where models are least reliable and data are scarce. As a result, these guarantees are weakest where they are needed most. Invariance-based frameworks also impose a direct cost on performance, since safety filters steer the system away from the boundary of the safe set even in minimally invasive formulations [15, 14]. Backup controller methods lighten the modeling burden by certifying a backup policy instead [16, 17], but they retain its filter and cost, and their membership certificates offer no convergence rate or notion of margin.

In this work, we show that robots do not need certified behavior to be certifiably safe. We formalize safety as recoverability, the certified ability of a robot to fall back on a trusted recovery behavior. Recoverability moves the invariance requirement off the deployed controller and onto the recovery mode, so the deployed controller may be aggressive, learned, or experimental, with no contraction, invariance, or modeling requirement. Figure 1 shows the resulting architecture, in which a recoverability monitor hands control from the deployed mode to the recovery mode at a certified time. Using contraction theory, we certify a tube around the recovery reference from which recovery converges exponentially. Monitoring safety then reduces to evaluating a closed-form Riemannian distance, and the guarantee degrades gracefully under perturbations. The contraction insertion gradient then tells the robot when to hand off, scheduling the switch through an optimization whose feasible solutions are all safe. As a result, robots can run behaviors that invariance-based safety cannot certify, requiring only that they are recoverable.

The contributions of this article are as follows.

We introduce recoverability, a contraction-theoretic safety concept that certifies a trusted recovery mode instead of the deployed controller, and prove that switching within a tube yields robust exponential convergence.

We derive the contraction insertion gradient and use it to schedule switches through an optimization in which feasibility alone certifies recovery, and we synthesize certified tubes by sequential convex programming, benchmarking them against exact HJ viability.

We demonstrate recoverability in quadrotor flight past uncertain obstacles, where it outperforms CBFs and backup CBFs, and onboard a full-scale IndyNXT autonomous racecar at the limits of handling in the rain.

The rest of the manuscript is structured as follows: Section II positions recoverability against invariance-based and fallback-based safety. Section III defines the closed-loop modes and recovery tubes. Section IV presents our main results, proving recoverability from the tube, turning the certificate into an optimal switching decision, and evaluating it in quadrotor flight. Section V grows certified tubes through convex synthesis and benchmarks them against exact HJ viability. Section VI deploys the framework onboard a full-scale autonomous racecar, and Section VII concludes.

title: SPICE: Stochastic Policy for Interaction in Cluttered Environments
authors: Nidhi Parayil,Benjamin Greenland,Thierry Peynot,Chris Lehnert
comment: submitted to IEE RAL
abstract: Agricultural tasks such as harvesting and pruning require robots to reach through dense foliage, where contact is often unavoidable and vision is obstructed. Intermittent contact creates an imbalance between free-space and contact-rich observations, complicating the learning of contact-responsive behaviours. We present SPICE, a tactile-conditioned diffusion policy for reaching targets in dense plant canopies using tactile sensing as the sole environmental feedback. SPICE exhibits three behaviours: moving through compliant foliage, manoeuvring around partially obstructing stems, and manipulating branches that block the target path. To the best of our knowledge, SPICE is the first tactile-conditioned diffusion policy for target reaching through physically cluttered plant canopies. Across over 180 real-robot trials, SPICE was evaluated against tactile-conditioned, image-conditioned, and reactive-control baselines. Spatial tactile information and explicit contact conditioning proved important, with SPICE achieving 95%95\% branch-manoeuvring success versus 45%45\% for the strongest tactile baseline. SPICE also achieved branch manipulation beyond the reactive controller and remained effective under visual occlusion, where the image-conditioned DP failed. Zero-shot transfer across 40 trials on unseen tomato and lime plants achieved 87.5%87.5\% success rate. These results demonstrate the potential of tactile-conditioned generative policies for interaction in visually occluded plant environments.
introduction:
Agricultural labour shortages are increasing demand for robotic systems [1], yet many high-value crops, such as sweet pepper, berries, and citrus, remain difficult to automate because of dense, unstructured foliage [2]. Reaching a fruit or pruning site within dense foliage often requires moving through leaves and branches with unknown geometry, stiffness, and compliance. These structures create physical obstruction by restricting access to the target and visual occlusion by blocking the robot’s view. When multiple nearby structures constrain the available path, the environment becomes cluttered, making contact difficult to avoid and requiring the robot to adapt its motion using local physical feedback.
Humans handle such situations naturally by moving through compliant foliage, manoeuvring around partially obstructing stems, and displacing branches when there is insufficient space to move around them. In contrast, robotic interaction often relies on predefined contact responses or interaction models, limiting behavioural flexibility. Learning from demonstrations (LfD) offers a way to acquire diverse behaviours without explicitly modelling each interaction. However, tactile-based LfD has largely focused on gripper-level manipulation tasks such as grasping [3, 4], rather than guiding whole-arm motion through clutter. Extending tactile LfD to cluttered reaching is challenging because contact is intermittent and the required response changes as the robot progresses through the environment.
Existing methods for moving through plant canopies rely mainly on collision avoidance, model-based interaction, or predefined reactive contact responses [5, 6]. Learning multiple contact-responsive behaviours directly from tactile feedback remains underexplored. We therefore introduce SPICE - Stochastic Policy for Interaction in Cluttered Environments, a vision-free, tactile-conditioned diffusion policy for reaching targets in occluded plant canopies. SPICE generates action sequences from tactile feedback and replans as contact evolves, enabling multiple contact-responsive behaviours within a single learned policy. Figure 1 illustrates SPICE displacing an obstructing branch in a tomato plant.

The main contributions of this work are:

To the best of the authors’ knowledge, the first tactile-conditioned diffusion policy enabling multiple contact-responsive behaviours for reaching a target in visually occluded plant canopies.

A tactile-conditioning design for intermittent contact, combining spatial taxel encoding with explicit contact information to generate whole-arm joint-space responses as interaction evolves.

Extensive real-robot validation and zero-shot transfer, comprising over 180 controlled trials against tactile-conditioned DP, image-conditioned DP, and reactive-control baselines, followed by 40 zero-shot trials on unseen lime and tomato plants.

1. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, the first tactile-conditioned diffusion policy enabling multiple contact-responsive behaviours for reaching a target in visually occluded plant canopies.

2. A tactile-conditioning design for intermittent contact, combining spatial taxel encoding with explicit contact information to generate whole-arm joint-space responses as interaction evolves.

3. Extensive real-robot validation and zero-shot transfer, comprising over 180 controlled trials against tactile-conditioned DP, image-conditioned DP, and reactive-control baselines, followed by 40 zero-shot trials on unseen lime and tomato plants.

title: LuxTac: A Flexible, Scalable, and Open-Source Optical Taxel Array with Distributed Three-Axis Force Sensing for Tactile Robot Learning
authors: Md Rakibul Islam Prince,John Pelan,Zhiyuan Zhang,Adyaa Khera,Katherine Pesetski,Adeesh Desai,Akimizu Sugiyama,Minwoo Ki,Benjamin Alan Capelle,Temitope Ibrahim Amosa,Zijie Xu,Yihan Huang,Taehun Chung,Long Wang,Wei Li,Shaoting Lin,Yu She

abstract: Low-cost tactile arrays have made touch a practical input for robot learning, but piezoresistive designs sense only pressure, while camera-based sensors that also resolve shear are too bulky to tile over a gripper. To solve this problem, we present LuxTac, a scalable optical taxel array, about 3.5 mm3.5\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} thick and built from off-the-shelf parts. Each taxel is a digital RGBC light-to-digital converter under a translucent white silicone layer capped by an opaque black film, so the back-scattered LED light falls monotonically with local indentation depth. The same board accepts two interchangeable gel cartridges: a plain one for normal sensing, and one with colored walls that encodes the local shear in the color of the returned light, with no camera, magnets, or bump overlay, making LuxTac, to our knowledge, the first optical taxel array to resolve shear at individual taxels. Characterized with an automated CNC indenter and a six-axis force/torque sensor, the normal cartridge responds linearly to force (R2=0.999R^{2}=0.999) from 104 mN104\text{\,}\mathrm{mN} to at least 5.8 N5.8\text{\,}\mathrm{N}, with 2.0% repeatability, 5.9% hysteresis, and a taxel-to-taxel variation of 6–10% after normalization. With the shear cartridge, per-taxel models estimate the three-axis force at every taxel; across three indenter shapes and nine held-out sessions, the summed estimates reach R2=0.96/0.96/0.92R^{2}=0.96/0.96/0.92 in x/y/zx/y/z, each taxel’s estimate 0.92/0.93/0.940.92/0.93/0.94, and the median shear-direction error is 4.8 °4.8\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree}. Adding LuxTac pressure readings to an Action Chunking Transformer policy substantially improves peg-in-hole success over a vision-only baseline. Design files, code, and videos are available at https://luxtac.github.io.
introduction:
Touch tells a robot what vision cannot: whether it is holding an object, how hard, and where the contact is when the fingers occlude the scene [1]. Even low-cost tactile arrays substantially improve learned manipulation policies when fused with vision [2, 3, 4]. The most widely adopted are piezoresistive: a force-sensitive film between orthogonal electrodes, read as a resistance matrix [5, 2, 3]. They are thin, flexible, and cheap, and their open-source releases have lowered the barrier to tactile learning considerably.

Piezoresistive arrays have two weaknesses that matter once a sensor leaves the bench. Each taxel reports a single number, so they sense pressure but not shear. And that number is a contact resistance through a polymer composite, which drifts, saturates early, depends on the loading history, and differs between pads.

Optical transduction offers a different trade-off. Camera-based sensors such as GelSight [6], DIGIT [7], and TacTip [8] reconstruct the deformation field of an elastomer at high resolution, at the cost of bulk, bandwidth, and high-dimensional observations. Miniaturized designs such as TacScope [9] and MVP-Tac [10] shrink the sensing surface, but the camera’s optical path still makes them thick along the viewing axis. Between these extremes, discrete LED–photodetector pairs embedded in elastomer have been used to sense contact and proximity [11, 12, 13]. Such optical taxels measure a geometric quantity, the deformation of the elastomer above them, through a stable, linear photodetector with an on-chip digital converter.

We develop this idea into LuxTac (Fig. ), a flexible, dense, and scalable tactile array. Each taxel is a commercial light-to-digital converter [14] under a translucent silicone layer and an opaque black film; compressing the silicone moves the absorbing film closer to the detector and reduces the returned light. Because every taxel is an independent digital device on its own bus segment, the same taxel cell tiles into arrays of any size and aspect ratio without changing the readout (Fig. 2). Because each detector also reports color, a second gel cartridge with colored walls adds shear sensing at every taxel without changing the electronics, which makes LuxTac, to our knowledge, the first optical taxel array that resolves shear per taxel. Our contributions are:

An approximately 3.5 mm3.5\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} thick optical taxel array built entirely from off-the-shelf parts on a four-layer flexible PCB, in which every taxel is an independent digital RGBC detector on its own I2C bus segment, with no analog front end, so the same cell tiles into arrays of any size by adding multiplexers and buses (Sec. III).

Two interchangeable gel cartridges: the shear cartridge encodes the local shear above each taxel in the color of the returned light, so the same board senses either normal deformation, or normal deformation and shear, at every taxel (Secs. III-C and IV-C).

Characterization over 240 normal presses and shear tests with three indenter shapes in nine sessions, evaluated at contact positions and in sessions held out from training; sim-to-real alignment of contact patterns; and two real-world tasks, peg-in-hole insertion and cube sorting, with an Action Chunking Transformer policy (Secs. IV–VI).

title: Panini- Feasible Grammar For Robot Designs
authors: Mayukh Debnath,Manan Roy Choudhury
abstract: Symbolic approaches to robot design provide interpretable rules but often overlook continuous geometry, while learned approaches handle geometry but offer limited explanations of their decisions. We introduce a typed production grammar that connects the two through a shared representation of robot skills and morphologies. Its rules use Fillmore-style case roles, parameter inheritance, and specificity-based arbitration, while a geometric realization map translates rule composition into transformations in S​E​(3)SE(3). This allows a single grammar to describe both manipulation skills and robot bodies. We show that the grammar is substantially more compact than an untyped alternative and that its rule arbitration can be recovered from learned geometric containment, achieving 0.905±0.0620.905\pm 0.062 decision agreement across 10 seeds, compared with 0.611±0.0900.611\pm 0.090 for a Euclidean control. We also characterize how inheritance affects the compositional properties of the geometric realization map by measuring its homomorphism defect. For morphology optimization, we introduce PĀṇini (Production-rule And role-typed compositioN for Intelligent, Novel robot desIgn), a cross-entropy search method operating directly on the grammar’s typed genome. Across 30 methods and 24 seeds, PĀṇini achieves the best mean rank, but is statistically indistinguishable from strong generic optimizers, including IPOP-CMA-ES, CEM, PSO, and TuRBO. Evaluating final designs with reinforcement-learning-trained controllers leads to a similar conclusion: the grammar-based search does not consistently outperform generic optimization. Further search mechanisms designed to exploit grammar structure also fail to establish a general advantage. A curriculum over grammar depth is a promising exception, becoming significantly better than six of seven strong baselines at 48 seeds, although this result requires caution because multiple variants were explored. The grammar’s main advantage is therefore not superior optimization performance, but structured and feasible design generation. Every generated candidate satisfies the grammar’s structural constraints, whereas unstructured methods achieve legality rates of only 0–82%. Coordinated limb placement maintains 95% joint feasibility in a highly constrained design space, compared with 55% for range-constrained resampling and no feasible designs from 6,000 flat-parameter samples. The grammar also supports designs with different limb counts, which the compared alternatives do not reach. We further examine the limits of these guarantees: structural legality does not ensure locomotion, and geometric feasibility does not reliably predict simulator failure. Together, these results establish typed production grammars as a compact, interpretable, and constraint-aware framework for robot skill and morphology generation, while showing that their structural advantages do not automatically translate into better black-box optimization. Codes for every experiment in this paper are available at https://github.com/mdebnath22/panini.
introduction:
Black-box optimizers are routinely applied to structured design spaces such as robot bodies, where each candidate must be both good and legal. Unconstrained continuous or graph-based parameterizations can express a wide range of bodies, but whether a body is valid must be checked after it is generated rather than guaranteed by construction. This also affects recent LLM-based low-level design editors (Qiu et al., 2025; Song et al., 2025; Qiu and Cygan, 2025). The alternative is to represent a body as a structured object governed by a discrete, checkable grammar (Sims, 1994), echoing the older trade-off in planning between explainable symbolic operators (Fikes and Nilsson, 1971) and reactive loops that gain robustness by dropping explicit structure (Brooks, 1991). This raises a question that is rarely separated empirically: when a black-box optimizer searches a structured space, does the structure help it find better designs, or only restrict which designs it can propose?

Existing grammar-based approaches address parts of this. RoboGrammar (Zhao et al., 2020) and GLSO (Hu et al., 2022) use graph grammars to constrain robot morphology, but their rules lack checkable geometric semantics and are typed only by graph adjacency. Region and order embeddings show that asymmetric relations such as entailment or default-versus-override can be represented geometrically as containment (Vilnis and McCallum, 2015; Vendrov et al., 2015; Ren et al., 2020; Ganea et al., 2018), but to our knowledge this has not been tested as a way to resolve competing rules inside a grammar.

We build a typed production grammar that combines semantic roles, parameter inheritance, and specificity-based rule arbitration. For manipulation, rules carry Fillmore-style case roles (Fillmore, 1968) (Agent, Patient, Instrument, Location, Source, Goal); for robot morphology, a separate structural role set (Root, Limb, Segment, Joint, Terminal). A geometric realization map turns every valid derivation into a sequence of rigid-body transformations in S​E​(3)SE(3). Rather than assuming that this map preserves the algebraic structure of rule composition, we measure its composition error over sampled rule pairs and longer chains. We then evaluate the grammar as a search space for morphology optimization, asking two separate questions: does it make search find better bodies, and does it make the bodies it proposes structurally valid? The answers differ, and we report both as measured.

Only the grammar reaches designs that require a different limb count.

title: Learning the Dynamics of Deformable Linear Objects Through Coupled Oscillators for Bimanual Robotic Manipulation
authors: Iván López-Broceño,Maximilian Stölzle,Daniel Feliu-Talegon,Daniela Rus,Cosimo Della Santina
abstract:
Many learning-based approaches for deformable linear objects (DLOs) rely on simplified deformation models that neglect dynamic effects and the mechanical response of the objects, limiting their applicability to lightweight, compliant objects and slow motions.
Inspired by recent advances in learning physically structured dynamics with coupled oscillator networks (CONs), we propose Φ\Phi-CON for learning force-driven DLO dynamics.
The model combines a floating-base coupled oscillator network (FBCON), whose latent potential energy depends only on the DLO’s shape, with a learned affine diffeomorphism Φ\Phi between observed positions along the DLO and latent coordinates.
Its shape dynamics are stable by construction, and its Lagrangian structure yields explicit expressions for kinetic and potential energy.
We exploit this structure to design a model-based proportional-derivative (PD) controller that compensates for the learned potential forces, thereby establishing closed-loop stability guarantees and ensuring convergence.
We evaluate the approach on four simulated DLOs and a real bimanual robot setup.
In simulation, Φ\Phi-CON achieves prediction accuracy comparable to neural ordinary differential equation (NODE) models and Lagrangian neural networks (LNNs), with 97.2%97.2\% and 90.2%90.2\% fewer parameters, respectively.
Relative to a model-free PD baseline, the proposed controller reduces mean endpoint regulation error by 97.597.5–99.7%99.7\% in simulation and achieves a mean per-target reduction of 27.9%27.9\% across both endpoints in real-world experiments, demonstrating the importance of explicitly accounting for the mechanical response of stiff and heavy objects.11

introduction:
As robots are increasingly adopted across a wide range of activities, they are required to interact with a more diverse set of objects.
Manipulating  DLO (DLO) such as cables, wires, or tree branches is key to applications like electrical installation, cable routing, and automated harvesting, yet it remains challenging (Billard and
Kragic, 2019; Zhu et al., 2022; Caporali et al., 2026): DLO are high-dimensional, underactuated during manipulation, and often stiff and heavy enough that their physical response cannot be neglected, particularly during rapid motions.
A main body of existing work relies on simplified deformation models of the DLO, namely quasi-static assumptions (Bretl and McCarthy, 2014) and kinematic descriptions, usually through Jacobian-based deformation estimation (Yu et al., 2025) or visual servoing (Shetab-Bushehri et al., 2022; Cao et al., 2024), instead of its full dynamics.
Such simplifications are hard to justify for stiff and heavy DLO, whose physical response cannot be neglected, especially under rapid motions.

Recent approaches to DLO manipulation learn motion models from data using LSTMs (Yang et al., 2022), GNNs (Wang et al., 2022; Chu et al., 2024), or recurrent state-space models (RSSMs) (Missal et al., 2026) to predict shape changes from past states and control inputs.
Such architectures can require millions of learned parameters (Missal et al., 2026).
Using position or velocity commands as inputs assumes that the manipulator can impose the commanded endpoint motion regardless of DLO reaction forces, limiting applicability to lightweight, compliant DLO.
Moreover, deploying these learned models for control typically requires numerical optimization at runtime and yields no analytical closed-loop guarantees.

Among learning methods that preserve physical structure (Stölzle, 2025), LNN (Cranmer et al., 2020) have been applied to modeling the dynamics of soft robots (Liu et al., 2024) and deformable objects (Zhong et al., 2021; Friedl et al., 2025; Pierallini et al., 2026).
However, evaluating their forward dynamics requires runtime differentiation of the learned Lagrangian, including second-order derivatives, which incurs substantial computational cost (Cranmer et al., 2020).
Moreover, Lagrangian structure alone does not guarantee stability of the learned dynamics (Müller, 2023) or the resulting closed loop (Liu et al., 2024).
\AcpCON combine Lagrangian structure with provably stable latent dynamics and explicit expressions for model-based control (Stölzle and
Della Santina, 2024).
However, their strictly convex latent potential does not accommodate the translational freedom of floating-base DLO, while their separately learned observation and input mappings do not enforce consistency between physical and latent forces under the principle of virtual work.

To address these limitations, we propose 𝚽\mathbf{\Phi}-CON for learning force-driven DLO dynamics and enabling closed-form control of bimanual manipulation.
We extend CON to floating-base systems through a  FBCON (FBCON), whose latent potential depends only on shape, accommodating base translation while retaining stable shape dynamics.
A learned affine diffeomorphism Φ\Phi connects observed marker positions to latent coordinates and determines the corresponding force transformation through the principle of virtual work.
The resulting Lagrangian structure enables us to explicitly account for the object’s physical response and design a PD model-based controller using the learned potential forces, without requiring runtime optimization.

Our contributions are:

Closed-form, force-based bimanual regulation of DLO through learned potential-force compensation and PD feedback, with closed-loop stability guarantees in observation space for compatible target equilibria of the learned model.

FBCON: an extension of CON to floating-base systems with explicit kinetic and potential energies and open-loop stability guarantees for the shape dynamics.

Φ\Phi-CON: joint learning of FBCON dynamics and an affine diffeomorphism that consistently transforms coordinates and forces, preserves Lagrangian structure, and transfers shape-stability guarantees to observation space.

title: RESCUE Jumper: A Centimeter-Scale Rolling and Jumping Robot for Search and Rescue
authors: Kiran Marques,Shashwat Singh,Ben D'Ambrosia,Zeynep Temel,Melisa Orta Martinez
comment: IEEE International Symposium on Safety, Security, and Rescue Robotics 2026, Best Paper Award
abstract:
Centimeter-scale robots are promising for urban search and rescue because they can enter confined spaces that are inaccessible or unsafe for humans. However, their small size limits obstacle traversal after deployment. This paper presents the RESCUE Jumper, a 125 g mobile robot with a 6.2 cm width and 6.2 cm diameter wheels that combines ground rolling with jumping to traverse steps and gaps that exceeds its rolling capability. The RESCUE Jumper uses its two actuators for both rolling mode and jumping by reversing the direction of wheel motion. Forward wheel motion enables rolling, while reverse wheel motion winds a spring steel tail to store elastic potential energy and release it for jumping. The RESCUE Jumper varies tail winding speed to control jump direction, transitioning from backward to forward jumps as winding speed increases from 0.75 rad/s to 8.73 rad/s. The launch angle of the jumps ranges from 45∘
to -11∘ with respect to the vertical axis, reaching a maximum height of 9.2 cm and a maximum lateral displacement of 11.2 cm. We model the winding speed-dependent jumping behavior in three phases: tail release to determine the contact point and robot orientation, tail straightening until liftoff, and ballistic flight to predict jump height and lateral displacement. Finally, qualitative tests highlight the robot’s locomotion in cluttered, real-world environments. The model and experiments presented in this work can inform future designs of space-constrained jump mechanisms in centimeter-scale robots for search and rescue and inspection in unstructured environments.
introduction:
Urban search and rescue (USAR) requires exploring collapsed, cluttered, and confined environments where human access is dangerous [1, 2]. Centimeter-scale mobile robots are well suited to these settings because they can pass through narrow openings, move within confined voids, and provide information from inaccessible regions [3, 4]. Their small size limits their ability to traverse through unstructured terrain like debris, steps, gaps, and other terrain features encountered after deployment [5, 6, 7]. Improving the mobility of these robots is important for extending their usefulness in search-and-rescue deployments.

One approach to improving mobility at centimeter scales is to use ground-contact mechanisms such as whegs [8], C-shaped legs [9], and compliant legs [10]. Whegs combine the continuous rotation of wheels with leg-like spokes, allowing small robots to interact with rough terrain through simple geometry [8]. Similarly, C-shaped legs can provide legged locomotion at small scales with relatively simple actuation, while compliant wheels can passively deform to increase contact area and adapt to uneven terrain [9]. These mechanisms can improve obstacle interaction and rough-terrain traversal compared with conventional wheels. However, because they rely on continuous or repeated ground contact, their performance remains limited by body size, available traction, and the geometry of the locomotor mechanism [10].

Reconfigurable swarm robots can improve mobility by forming larger structures that bridge gaps, climb obstacles, or traverse rough terrain [11, 12, 13]. However, these approaches often require reliable coupling, accurate alignment, and coordinated motion, which can be difficult to achieve in cluttered and time-sensitive USAR environments. In addition, once individual robots separate from the group or operate locally, they must still overcome nearby obstacles using their own mobility capabilities. This motivates improving single-robot mobility while preserving the compact form factor needed for deployment in confined spaces.

Jumping is one way to improve single-robot mobility beyond the limits of continuous ground-contact locomotion. By temporarily leaving the ground, centimeter-scale robots can clear discrete obstacles and traverse distances larger than their body length. Existing jumping robots use springs [14], combustion [15], or pneumatics [16], but require a dedicated actuator, latch, or winding system. For deployable centimeter-scale robots, these components add mass, volume, and electrical and mechanical complexity. For compact deployable mobile robots, this creates a need for a jumping mechanism that improves vertical mobility without adding a separate jump actuator.

This paper presents RESCUE Jumper, a centimeter-scale, two-actuator mobile robot that combines rolling with repeatable forward and backward jumping (Fig. 1). The robot uses two independently driven wheel actuators for ground locomotion and steering during normal operation. When the wheels rotate in reverse, the same actuators are repurposed to wind and release a spring-steel flexure tail through a passive unidirectional gate mechanism. As the tail unlatches, the stored elastic energy is released, launching the robot for a jump. By changing the reverse winding speed, the robot changes its launch direction, enabling forward or backward jumps. The contributions of this work are: (1) a compact two degree of freedom robot that combines rolling locomotion and active jumping; (2) a passive flexure-gate mechanism for reverse drive tail winding and forward rolling; (3) a three-phase model of the tail release, pre-liftoff tail extension, and ballistic flight; and (4) experimental validation of direction-dependent jumping across multiple tail winding speeds.

title: RageVLA: Augmentation-Trained Perception and Action for State-of-the-Art Robustness on LIBERO
authors: Amrit Lal Singh,Smarak Kanjilal
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models look saturated on LIBERO, yet most of them fall apart on LIBERO-PRO as soon as an object moves or the instruction asks for something new. We argue that what is missing is not scale but decoupling. In these policies, what to do is tied to where things were during training, to the scene around them and to the wording of the instruction. We cut these ties in two places. In the data, LIBERO demonstrations are re-arranged by general rules: every object and fixture is moved and rotated, tasks are carried into other environments and onto other surfaces, and every instruction is paraphrased. In the policy, a perception engine on frozen DINOv3 features, trained on this augmented data, hands the action model the scene in decoupled form: a list of objects with their positions, and a compact code of what the gripper is looking at, next to image and instruction embeddings from TinyCLIP. A flow-matching diffusion transformer, trained from scratch, acts on this view. We call this combination of Robust Augmentation and Grounded Encoding RageVLA. With 0.21 billion parameters, RageVLA sets a new state of the art on LIBERO-PRO among VLA policies, scoring 0.72 against 0.53 for the best published model, and a larger variant reaches 0.73. Two further tests on LIBERO-Object show that the policy acts on what it perceives. When the object positions it is given are shuffled while the camera images stay correct, its success falls from 0.965 to 0.215. When the target object is displaced by 28 cm, it still succeeds in 0.865 of the episodes, where π0.5\pi_{0.5}, run through the same harness, succeeds in 0.105.
introduction:
LIBERO [1] has become the default benchmark for vision-language-action (VLA) policies, and its four evaluation suites are now saturated: recent models report average success well above 90% [2, 3, 4]. LIBERO-PRO [5] asks what these numbers measure. It keeps LIBERO’s scenes and perturbs one factor at a time: object appearance (Obj), initial positions (Pos), instruction wording (Sem), the task itself (Task) and the table (Env). Strong LIBERO models collapse under two of these. On the LIBERO-PRO leaderboard, OpenVLA [6], π0\pi_{0} [7], MolmoAct [8] and NORA [9] score zero on almost every Pos and Task cell, and the best model, π0.5\pi_{0.5} [10], averages 0.11 over them. The models have learned to replay trajectories.

The benchmark’s headline number hides this. LIBERO-PRO summarizes a model by its mean over all cells, but Obj and Sem leave both the layout and the task unchanged, so a model that replays its training trajectories still scores highly on them. OpenVLA, for example, has a total of 0.52 while solving none of the position-perturbed or task-changed tests. Fig. 1 separates the two readings.

This paper takes a simple position: these policies fail because what they do is coupled to things it should not depend on. Each LIBERO task is demonstrated 50 times in almost the same layout, so the identity of an object is tied to where it stands, the motion is tied to the scene around it, and the instruction is tied to one wording and one initial layout. A policy trained on such data has no reason to separate them, whatever its size. Robustness under perturbation requires decoupling these factors, and it has to happen in two places at once.

The first is the data. We re-arrange LIBERO’s demonstrations by general rules. Re-placing every object and fixture at a random position and orientation decouples what an object is from where it is. Carrying tasks into other environments and onto other surfaces decouples the manipulation from its background. Paraphrasing decouples the task from its wording. The second is the policy’s input. Variation in the data helps only if the policy can read it, so a perception engine hands the action model the same factors in separated form: a list of objects with their classes and global positions, a wrist code of the surfaces and depths in front of the gripper, and one image and one instruction embedding. With accurate object positions as an input, the policy does not need to recall a trajectory; it can act on the scene in front of it. The two parts are designed for each other: without varied data the position input carries no information that the policy needs, and without the position input the variation has to be recovered from pixels. We call the resulting system RageVLA, for Robust Augmentation with Grounded Encoding.

Our contributions are as follows.

A general augmentation pipeline for LIBERO-style demonstrations. Every object and fixture is re-placed at a random position and orientation, tasks are transplanted into LIBERO’s other environments and onto its other surfaces, and every instruction is paraphrased (Sec. III). The rules are general: no layout, object pair or instruction is taken from LIBERO-PRO.

RageVLA, an object-centric flow-matching policy. Small perception adapters on a frozen DINOv3 backbone [11] produce an object list and a wrist-view code, TinyCLIP [12] provides one image and one text embedding, and a diffusion transformer trained from scratch produces actions (Sec. IV).

State-of-the-art LIBERO-PRO results among VLA policies on the full protocol, with 0.21 billion parameters in total (Sec. V).

Direct evidence that the policy acts on perceived positions. Changing the object positions given to the policy at inference changes its behaviour even in LIBERO’s original layouts, and under LIBERO-PRO’s graded object displacement the policy degrades far more slowly than π0.5\pi_{0.5} evaluated in the same harness (Sec. V-D).

title: Learning and Control in Physically Coupled Dynamical Systems
authors: Bao Trung Truong,Dat Thanh Nguyen,Thinh T. Doan
abstract: We introduce TAG (Testbed for Autonomous Games), a compact, low-cost robotic platform for studying learning and control in physically coupled dynamical systems. TAG combines an actively tilted and steered ball-in-maze board with a top-mounted rotary inverted pendulum. The pendulum’s reaction torque and vibration disturb the board and marble, while the board’s tilt, driven by the maze-solving policy, simultaneously disturbs the pendulum’s balance. The main challenge in learning control policies for each subsystem is accounting for the impact of one subsystem’s dynamics on the other’s learning process. To address this challenge, we present complementary reinforcement learning paradigms, leveraging model-based and model-free approaches to learn the control policies for the maze and pendulum, respectively. Our key finding is that introducing the pendulum causes an immediate, sharp drop in the maze policy’s success rate, but the policy adapts online and recovers to its pre-coupling performance within a small number of learning episodes. Experimental results show that both policies, trained independently, successfully control the maze board and the pendulum despite their physical coupling.
introduction:
Many real-world robotic systems are not single, monolithic plants, but composed of physically coupled subsystems. These subsystems must be sensed, controlled, and often learned jointly. A prominent example is the humanoid robot, where legs and arms are physically coupled. Locomotion must account for arm-manipulation dynamics, and vice versa. Designing control and learning algorithms for such coupled systems is difficult and costly. A poorly designed controller can damage the hardware, while exploratory actions during real-time learning can break robot components. This risk grows when a fault in one subsystem propagates through the coupling and destabilizes another. High-fidelity simulation offers a safer alternative, but policies trained purely in simulation often lose performance when transferred to real hardware [1]. This sim-to-real gap remains a central challenge in robot learning. Thus, there is a need to develop a simple, low-cost, and safe testbed to study learning and control for physically coupled systems. Such a testbed would enable researchers to iterate and validate learning and control algorithms quickly on real hardware, before moving to more complex and expensive coupled robotic systems.

Motivated by this observation, we introduce a new compact robotic platform to study learning and control in physically coupled dynamical systems. We name our testbed TAG: a Testbed for Autonomous Games, illustrated in Figure 1. TAG combines two classic benchmark systems, a ball-in-maze board and a rotary inverted pendulum, into a single physically integrated system. The pendulum is mounted directly atop an actively tilted and steered maze board. As the pendulum balances, its reaction torque and vibration are transmitted directly into the board’s dynamics, and in turn into the motion of a marble navigating the maze under overhead visual tracking. Conversely, the board’s own movement, driven by the maze-navigation task, perturbs the pendulum’s balance. Each subsystem has its own controller, and its design must account for the presence of the other.

To learn control policies for TAG, we develop complementary model-based and model-free learning algorithms, one for each subsystem. The maze-navigation subsystem uses DreamerV3 [2], a model-based algorithm well suited to costly real rollouts. DreamerV3 was previously used for autonomous maze-solving in CyberRunner [3], but without coupling to a second physical subsystem. We build on this by extending to a physically coupled system. For the pendulum, we instead use the model-free TQC algorithm [4], trained entirely in simulation and deployed as a fixed policy on hardware. Our experiments test whether these two separately optimized controllers remain effective when operating together on the same mechanically coupled platform. Our experimental results show that the pendulum policy sustains high success across a wide range of board disturbances, degrading gracefully and being more sensitive to disturbance dimensionality than to speed. On the other hand, the maze policy suffers a sharp but transient drop upon pendulum activation, recovering within a small fraction of the episodes required for initial learning. Our key finding is that independently-trained policies, with no shared model of one another, can each remain effective despite continuous, physically transmitted interference from the other.

Physically coupled robotic systems. A growing body of work studies robots whose subsystems are mechanically coupled and must be controlled jointly. Quadrotors carrying suspended payloads exhibit strongly coupled, underactuated dynamics that motivate controllers modeling the full vehicle-payload system [5]. In legged manipulation, pairing a model-based arm controller with a separate RL-based locomotion controller, treating manipulator motion purely as a disturbance to the base, lets each subsystem perform well individually, but the two controllers can only passively adapt to one another [6]. Humanoid robots exhibit a more bidirectional coupling: momentum from leg motion affects whole-body dynamics, while coordinated arm motion can generate opposing momentum, improving disturbance recovery over a fixed-arm baseline [7]. Free-floating space manipulators show a still more fundamental case, where momentum conservation dictates that manipulator motion necessarily induces spacecraft attitude reaction, a coupling studied since [8] and sometimes exploited deliberately for propellant-free attitude control rather than merely rejected. TAG is motivated by the same phenomenon, but isolates it in a compact, fully-observable tabletop platform rather than a full-scale legged, aerial, or orbital system, making the coupling itself easier to vary and study systematically.

Benchmark testbeds for learning-based control. Ball-in-maze and rotary inverted pendulum systems are long-standing benchmarks for control and reinforcement learning individually. Maze-navigation benchmarks typically use a force-actuated ball reaching a target within a closed maze [9], while ball-in-maze systems on tip-tilt platforms have separately been proposed as physical RL benchmarks for their rich dynamics and ease of construction [10]. The rotary inverted pendulum is a standard underactuated benchmark, used to evaluate both model-free and model-based RL for swing-up and stabilization [11, 12]. In both lines of work, disturbances are typically exogenous and unstructured, rather than the controllable byproduct of a second, independently actuated subsystem. More broadly, most learning-based control is validated primarily in simulation, and resulting policies often fail to transfer due to the sim-to-real gap [1], motivating low-cost, reproducible physical benchmarks such as robotic arm cells [13], legged platforms [14], and miniature driving benchmarks [15]. TAG follows this same low-cost, reproducible philosophy, while specifically targeting physically coupled dynamics rather than a single subsystem.

Model-based and model-free learning for control. We will leverage complementary reinforcement learning paradigms. The model-based Dreamer family learns a compact latent world model and trains policies through imagined rollouts [2]. DreamerV3 has been applied to autonomous maze-solving on a physical ball-in-maze platform [3], which we build on and extend to a physically coupled setting. Model-free off-policy actor-critic methods are widely used for underactuated balancing [12]; we specifically use Truncated Quantile Critics (TQC), whose distributional, truncated critic is designed to reduce overestimation bias in continuous control [4]. Together, these paradigms let us match each subsystem’s learning algorithm to the structure of its dynamics, without either policy requiring a model of the other.

title: BiCAT: Bimanual Coordination Action Tokenization
authors: Xuanwei Liu,Guipu Cao,Zhongyi Luo,Jiafei Duan
abstract: Autoregressive vision-language-action (VLA) models predict discrete action tokens with the next-token objective of their vision-language backbone, so the action tokenizer defines the interface between the policy and the robot. In bimanual manipulation, the two arms share a repertoire of movements yet coordinate through complementary roles, and an action representation should capture both. However, most existing tokenizers encode both arms as a single concatenated action vector, in which motion patterns common to the two arms are not shared and cross-arm dependencies remain entangled within each token. The policy must therefore learn both aspects implicitly. We propose Bimanual Coordination Action Tokenization (BiCAT), which shares one motion representation across arms while conditioning each arm’s tokens on its partner through symmetric cross-arm attention and a joint decoder. The policy then predicts all tokens of each arm in parallel, generating the left arm first and the right arm conditioned on it. Across ten RoboTwin 2.0 tasks and six real-world tasks on three embodiments, BiCAT achieves the highest success among the compared tokenizers. In simulation, it improves mean success by 17.6 percentage points over the strongest of eight baselines, with the largest gains on tasks that require close coordination between the arms, while requiring only 40.5 ms per action chunk. These results suggest that the action tokenizer is a natural place to model bimanual coordination.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models extend pretrained vision-language models to robot control (Zitkovich et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Qu et al., 2025; Black et al., 2025b; Black et al., 2025a; NVIDIA et al., 2025; Fang et al., 2026). A common design keeps the autoregressive next-token prediction of the backbone: an action tokenizer discretizes continuous action chunks into tokens, which the policy generates either one token at a time (Brohan et al., 2023; Zitkovich et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Pertsch et al., 2025; Qu et al., 2025) or in blocks of tokens predicted in parallel (Liu et al., 2026a; Jawaid and Xiang, 2026; Dong et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026b). The action tokenizer thus determines what the policy learns to predict and how errors in those predictions affect the resulting robot motion (Pertsch et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026a; Dong et al., 2026). Existing tokenizers have explored frequency-domain compression (Pertsch et al., 2025), learned temporal abstraction (Mete et al., 2024), vector quantization (van den Oord et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2024b; Wang et al., 2025), and coarse-to-fine coding (Liu et al., 2026a; Jawaid and Xiang, 2026), but they treat an action chunk as a flat vector and do not model how its dimensions are organized across the arms of the robot.

This limitation is especially consequential in bimanual manipulation, where successful execution depends on coordinated motion across both arms. Tasks such as handing over objects, folding fabric, and carrying large objects often require two arms (Smith et al., 2012; Krebs and Asfour, 2022), and VLAs are increasingly being applied to these tasks (Liu et al., 2025; Black et al., 2025b; NVIDIA et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026). However, most general-purpose action tokenizers concatenate both arms’ actions into a single vector, a formulation we call joint tokenization. Although this formulation can capture cross-arm dependencies, it leaves the structure of bimanual coordination to be learned implicitly.

Human bimanual manipulation illustrates two useful aspects of this structure: the arms share a repertoire of movements, yet adapt their actions to complementary roles (Guiard, 1987). During a handover, for example, one hand presents and releases the object while the other reaches to receive and secure it. For robots with matching arm kinematics, this suggests an action representation that captures both reusable motion patterns across arms and task-dependent coordination between them. Joint tokenization does not explicitly distinguish these two aspects, leaving the policy to learn both shared motion structure and cross-arm dependencies from the concatenated representation.

Making this structure explicit raises a design question. One option, which we call per-arm tokenization, splits the action by arm and tokenizes each arm separately, as in ℳ2\mathcal{M}^{2}Tok (Xu et al., 2026), leaving coordination to the policy. Per-arm tokenization yields arm-indexed tokens and lets both arms reuse one motion representation, but it removes partner context from each arm’s codes; in our experiments, such a tokenizer performs no better than the strongest joint tokenizer (Sec. 4.2). This paper therefore asks: once the arms are tokenized as separate streams, how should the streams interact to yield a better interface for bimanual policies?

Our key insight is that arm-indexed tokens need not be arm-independent: each arm’s tokens can be computed with access to its partner while the two streams remain separate. We build on this insight in Bimanual Coordination Action Tokenization (BiCAT), a per-arm tokenizer that restores partner context. Its design follows one principle: share the motion representation across arms while conditioning discretization on the partner arm. For the shared motion patterns, BiCAT exploits the mirror-image mounting of the arms: it maps the right arm into the left arm’s convention, so that mirrored motions share one canonical trajectory, and encodes both arms with one shared causal temporal encoder. For the cross-arm coordination, symmetric cross-arm attention adds partner context to each stream before shared finite scalar quantization (FSQ) (Mentzer et al., 2024), and a joint decoder reconstructs both trajectories from temporally paired codes. Trained by reconstruction alone, BiCAT produces separate tokens for each arm, which the VLA predicts in two successive blocks: the tokens of each arm are generated in parallel, and the right arm is conditioned on the left.

We compare BiCAT with eight baselines from seven tokenizer families under a common VLA training protocol. On ten RoboTwin 2.0 tasks (Chen et al., 2026), BiCAT improves mean success by 17.6 percentage points over the strongest baseline, with a gain that grows from 1.5 points on single-arm tasks to 21.3 on tightly coupled ones, and on six real-world tasks across three embodiments it succeeds in 113 of 150 trials, compared with 74 for OAT (Liu et al., 2026a). Two-block prediction keeps policy latency at least 5.6×5.6\times lower than token-by-token decoding. Ablations show that the gain requires both the tokenizer and the prediction schedule: removing cross-arm interaction or predicting both arms in one block leaves BiCAT no better than the strongest baseline.
