title: NereidVLA: Learning to Understand and Navigate the Underwater World
authors: Chenjie Zhao,Zhiliang Zhu,Quan Chen,Yuquan Xue,Xingxue Shi,Puyue Wang,Zhiqiang Zhao,Kangye Zheng,Boyang Xu,Mingwei Lin,Dejun Li
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Underwater navigation requires translating visual spatial cues into motion, yet marine vision-language datasets rarely include paired robot trajectories.
We present NereidVLA, a vision-language-action model that transfers marine spatial knowledge to language-conditioned 3D navigation.
We first train Sea2Know on approximately two million marine examples to learn target grounding, spatial relations, and scene structure without paired robot-motion supervision.
We then adapt it using expert trajectories executed under simulated underwater vehicle dynamics.
Given RGB histories and a language instruction, NereidVLA predicts discrete motion tokens that decode into local 3D trajectories for closed-loop tracking.
Evaluation combines an independent six-dimensional underwater navigation understanding benchmark with offline prediction and closed-loop navigation.
Under matched navigation training and execution settings, marine spatial pretraining increases simulation success from 72.4% to 84.4%.
Without fine-tuning on the real test environment, NereidVLA achieves 78.75% success in laboratory-pool robot trials, compared with 47.50% for InternVLA-N1.
These results show that marine spatial supervision can support downstream motion learning and physical underwater navigation.
introduction:
Language-guided underwater navigation requires robots to interpret a goal
in the context of three-dimensional scene geometry. Following a pipeline
requires understanding its direction and the obstacles nearby, while cave
navigation depends on recognizing entrances and the geometry of traversable
passages. These decisions involve changes in depth as well as horizontal
motion: recognizing the target is only one part of determining how to reach
it. Turbidity, light scattering, changing illumination, and occlusion further
complicate these spatial judgments [1].

Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual understanding and language
to robot behavior [35, 13, 22],
and recent work has begun to explore this connection in underwater
environments [25, 9, 29].
Meanwhile, marine vision-language datasets provide rich annotations for
objects, spatial relationships, and scene structure [28, 34]. These resources offer an opportunity to learn about the
underwater world, but rarely include paired robot trajectories.
Collecting underwater navigation demonstrations remains costly and difficult
to scale, and spatial understanding alone does not specify how a robot
should move. We therefore investigate a central question:
Can spatial knowledge acquired from large-scale marine observations
be transferred to language-conditioned 3D underwater navigation?

We propose NereidVLA, an underwater VLA model that connects marine
spatial learning with trajectory-supervised navigation adaptation
(Figure 1). The first stage establishes spatial knowledge
before learning robot motion. Using available annotations and question-answer
formats from NAUTILUS [28] and
USI-Brain [34], together with underwater simulation data,
we construct approximately two million marine spatial-understanding examples.
We use these examples to train Sea2Know, built on
Qwen3-VL-8B [4], to learn target grounding, spatial
relationships, and scene structure. This stage makes marine observations
useful for navigation preparation without requiring paired robot-motion
annotations.

The second stage turns this spatially informed model into a trajectory
predictor for closed-loop navigation. Using 573 simulated scenes in
MarineGym [7], we collect 5,117 expert demonstrations
and derive approximately 100,000 navigation examples spanning obstacle
avoidance, target search, pipeline navigation, and cave navigation.
An expert controller executes geometric reference plans under simulated
vehicle dynamics, and the resulting robot motion supplies the trajectory
targets. We use these demonstrations to adapt Sea2Know into NereidVLA,
encoding local body-frame displacements as motion tokens.
Given RGB histories and language instructions, the model autoregressively
predicts local 3D trajectories, which a low-level feedback controller tracks
as visual observations are updated and the trajectory is replanned.

Our evaluation examines both the spatial knowledge learned in the first
stage and its value for navigation. On a six-dimensional underwater
navigation understanding benchmark strictly disjoint from the spatial
training data, Sea2Know outperforms its backbone across all six dimensions.
NereidVLA improves offline trajectory prediction over
SimpleVLN [11] in unseen scenes.
Under matched downstream training and execution settings, Sea2Know
initialization increases closed-loop simulation success from 72.4% to
84.4% compared with direct navigation fine-tuning of Qwen3-VL-8B.
On a BlueROVHeavy robot, NereidVLA achieves a 78.75% task success
rate in laboratory-pool trials without fine-tuning on the test environment,
compared with 47.50% for InternVLA-N1.

Our main contributions are as follows:

We propose NereidVLA, a two-stage underwater VLA framework that
transfers marine spatial knowledge to language-conditioned local
3D trajectory prediction and closed-loop navigation.

We construct a diverse underwater navigation dataset from expert
demonstrations executed under simulated vehicle dynamics, and introduce
an independent six-dimensional underwater navigation understanding
benchmark.

We demonstrate improvements in offline trajectory prediction and
closed-loop navigation in simulation and on a real robot.
Matched comparisons establish the benefit of marine spatial pretraining,
while laboratory-pool trials demonstrate transfer to physical execution
without test-environment fine-tuning.

title: Does the Action Matter? Probing Action-Conditioned Semantic Forecasting as a World Model for Autonomous Driving
authors: Binay Kumar Singh,Niels Da Vitoria Lobo
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)
comment: . Accepted at the WAM-AD Workshop, WACV 2027. Code:this https URL
abstract:
World models are increasingly used in autonomous driving to predict how a scene
evolves under the ego vehicle’s actions, supporting counterfactual reasoning and
model-based planning.
However, existing evaluations focus on prediction fidelity and planning
performance, and rarely verify that the predictions depend on the conditioning
action.
In this paper, we study action dependence in action-conditioned semantic
forecasting, which predicts future semantic segmentation from past segmentations
and the ego action.
We compare a forecaster with feature-wise and input-level action conditioning
against an identical model without action input, and measure action dependence
with test-time action interventions scored by standard segmentation metrics.
The evaluation is validated in a synthetic environment with known
action-dependent dynamics and applied to Cityscapes and BDD100K, both within
each dataset and across the two vehicle platforms.
Experiments show that the executed action improves mid-term mIoU by at most 2.5
points on Cityscapes and 0.6 points on BDD100K, whereas a wrong action reduces it by
up to 23.2 and 7.0 points, below the model without action input.
On real data, feature-wise conditioning depends 1.6 times more on the action than
input-level conditioning at similar accuracy, whereas both depend on it equally in
the synthetic environment, where the history does not determine the action.
These results show that an accuracy gain indicates that a driving world model uses
its action, but not how strongly its forecasts depend on it.
Code is available at https://github.com/binayksingh/does-action-matter.
introduction:
World models have become a central component of autonomous driving research.
By predicting future scene states conditioned on ego actions, they support
counterfactual reasoning, closed-loop simulation and model-based planning.
Recent driving world models synthesise future video conditioned on ego
trajectories or high-level commands [11, 22, 7],
and planning-oriented approaches learn latent or occupancy dynamics jointly with
a driving policy [10, 26].

Existing evaluations of these models focus on the fidelity of the generated
futures or on downstream planning performance, and rarely verify that the
predictions depend on the conditioning action.
Over short horizons, however, ego motion is strongly autocorrelated, so the
observed history already encodes much of the information carried by the future
action.
A model trained on logged driving data can therefore attain high forecasting
accuracy while making little use of its action input, a failure mode analogous to
the inertia and copycat problems reported for imitation-learned driving
policies [2, 23, 4].
An accuracy gain over a model without action input shows that the action is used,
but not how strongly the forecasts depend on it, since on logged data the executed
action and the action implied by the history largely coincide.
How strongly action-conditioned forecasters trained on real driving data depend on
the ego action, and whether this dependence holds across vehicle platforms,
therefore remains largely unexplored.

To address these questions, we study action dependence in semantic
forecasting [12], which predicts future semantic
segmentation from past observations and has an established evaluation protocol
on Cityscapes [3].
Conditioning this task on future vehicle odometry has been proposed
before [1], but whether the forecaster uses the
odometry was not examined.
We condition on the ego action, represented by speed and yaw rate, and
compare a U-Net forecaster with feature-wise linear modulation
(FiLM) [16], input-level conditioning, and no action input.
The rationale is that semantic forecasting has a compact output space and
standard metrics, so each variant can be trained with several seeds at modest
cost and its use of the action can be measured without new evaluation criteria.
To assess whether the findings transfer across vehicle platforms, we define an
equivalent protocol on BDD100K [25], which differs from
Cityscapes in camera, ego-motion sensing and driving environment.

To measure action dependence, we evaluate each trained model under test-time
action interventions, in which the executed future action is replaced by the
action of a sample from another sequence, by zero yaw rate, by a stop command, or
by the training-set mean action.
All conditions are scored with the standard mIoU and MO-mIoU
metrics [12].
Before applying this evaluation to real driving data, we validate it in a
synthetic driving environment whose dynamics depend on the action by
construction.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We present an action-conditioned semantic forecasting framework that
compares FiLM, input-level and no action conditioning within a single
U-Net forecaster under identical training.

We develop a test-time intervention protocol that replaces the executed
future action with shuffled, zero-yaw, stop and mean actions, and
measures action dependence with established segmentation metrics only.

We validate the interventions in a synthetic driving environment with
action-dependent dynamics and a negative control trained on shuffled
actions, which shows whether a model uses or ignores its action input.

We provide a cross-platform evaluation on Cityscapes and BDD100K with
GPS-derived ego actions, both within each dataset and across the two
platforms.

1. We present an action-conditioned semantic forecasting framework that
compares FiLM, input-level and no action conditioning within a single
U-Net forecaster under identical training.

2. We develop a test-time intervention protocol that replaces the executed
future action with shuffled, zero-yaw, stop and mean actions, and
measures action dependence with established segmentation metrics only.

3. We validate the interventions in a synthetic driving environment with
action-dependent dynamics and a negative control trained on shuffled
actions, which shows whether a model uses or ignores its action input.

4. We provide a cross-platform evaluation on Cityscapes and BDD100K with
GPS-derived ego actions, both within each dataset and across the two
platforms.

title: Counterfactual World Models: JEPAs That Reason About "What If"
authors: Randall Balestriero,Yann LeCun,Kerda Varaku
subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO); Machine Learning (stat.ML)
abstract:
World models operate in a world they cannot fully observe.
When a hidden disturbance, such as a current pushing a boat, changes the outcome of an action, a counterfactual question follows: what would have happened under a different action, subject to the same disturbance? Its answer separates bad decisions from bad luck.
We prove that world models trained on factual transitions cannot answer it on their own, whatever their data or capacity.
For many physical systems, the observed outcome and a simple property of the dynamics suffice: natura non facit saltus, nature makes no leaps.
When actions and disturbances act as separate forces, their interaction is second-order in time, so the counterfactual outcome is, to first order, the observed outcome plus the difference between the world model’s predictions under the alternative and factual actions.
This yields a counterfactual world model with no counterfactual data, extra parameters, or retraining.
For transitions of duration hh, we prove an O⁡(h2)O(h^{2}) bound on the counterfactual error relative to the disturbance variance, establish a matching minimax lower bound from unpaired factual data, and characterize failures at discontinuities, coordinate folds, and disturbances that scale the command.
We validate these predictions from pixels with JEPA world models on frozen DINOv2 and masked autoencoder (MAE) encoders.
On four rendered simulators, our approach improves counterfactual R2R^{2} from 3838–46%46\% to 8686–96%96\% with the same world models; on a fifth, an underwater vehicle, it reaches 9090–94%94\% with sixteen times more factual data.
Four further frozen encoders, DINOv3, SigLIP 2, CLIP and EVA-02, give 8181–95%95\% on the same simulators.
In hindsight planning, it finds the action that would have reached the goal in 3535–69%69\% of events, against 1414–23%23\% for an oracle planner that knows the simulator but not the outcome.
introduction:
World models predict the consequences of actions and are becoming a core component of agents that interact with the world. From latent dynamics models for control
[17, 18, 19, 20, 53, 21]
to joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) that predict in the feature space of self-supervised encoders
[28, 3, 7, 4, 64, 57],
they allow agents to anticipate outcomes before acting.

Yet the real world is never fully observed. Consider the boat of : it picks a heading while an unseen current pushes it. Before acting, no world model can know the current it is about to meet, so the best it can do is predict where the boat ends up on average over currents (green). The observed outcome (diamond) lands elsewhere, and in doing so reveals how far the current actually pushed the boat. A new question then arises: where would the boat have ended up under a different heading, in that same current? (dotted). This is an individual counterfactual. Asked about another heading, a standard world model returns the average over currents again (green) and discards what the outcome revealed. The same question arises whenever a gust of wind or a miscalibrated actuator alters an outcome. Its answer is what one needs to debug a failure, to tell a bad decision from bad luck, to assign credit to an action, and to find in hindsight the action that would have reached the goal, which we call hindsight planning.

This question is fundamentally different from factual prediction: as we prove, a world model trained on factual transitions cannot answer it on its own. A world model learns the conditional consequences of actions from observed transitions, whereas an individual counterfactual asks about an alternative action under the same hidden disturbance. An unpaired factual dataset does not record outcomes under two actions for the same initial state and realized disturbance. Consequently, even a perfect model of factual transitions does not determine how alternative outcomes are coupled, i.e., which outcome under the alternative action belongs to the observed event: distinct counterfactual worlds can induce exactly the same factual distribution ( and ). Neither a more accurate predictor nor a more expressive generative model resolves this ambiguity, and no factual test can reveal it. Without additional structure, individual counterfactuals are not identified.

For many physical systems, nature provides this structure. Natura non facit saltus: nature makes no leaps. When the action and the hidden disturbance enter as separate forces, as the boat’s propulsion and the current do, each changes the state gradually, and each alters the effect of the other only through the change of state it has already caused. Their interaction, i.e., how much the effect of changing the action depends on the disturbance, is therefore second-order in the transition duration. To first order, changing the action changes the outcome by the same amount in every event, and this amount is what a factual world model predicts between the two actions. Separate channels are an assumption on how the disturbance enters, not a consequence of smoothness: a worn actuator whose effect grows with the command is smooth, yet it interacts with the action at first order (), and we test this failure in . Under separate channels, this observation leads to a simple construction. Let zt=f⁡(ot)z_{t}=f(o_{t}) denote the representation of an observation, and let μ⁡(zt,a)\mu(z_{t},a) be a factual world model trained to predict the next representation under action aa. Given an observed transition (zt,at,zt+1)(z_{t},a_{t},z_{t+1}), we estimate the outcome under an alternative action a′a^{\prime} by

In additive worlds, residual reuse is the unique counterfactual rule that is exact for every factual transition (). Outside this regime, its error is governed by the interaction between actions and hidden disturbances, quantified by the mixed derivative of the dynamics (). For short physical transitions with separate action and disturbance channels, this interaction is second-order in the time step hh, leaving only an O⁡(h2)O(h^{2}) fraction of the disturbance uncertainty unexplained ( and ). This guarantee extends through smooth representations and to systems with hidden velocities (). The rate cannot be uniformly improved: we establish a matching minimax lower bound, with the sharp leading constant, for estimators using unpaired factual transitions and one observed outcome (). Residual reuse therefore achieves the best possible asymptotic rate under the stated information and physical assumptions. How short is short enough depends on the system, and we measure it (). The same analysis identifies the limits of residual reuse: disturbances that scale the command, discontinuous contacts, and folded representations can invalidate it.

Residual correction is familiar in control theory, where disturbance observers, offset-free model predictive control, and iterative learning control reuse errors from observed trajectories
[39, 35, 41, 2, 11].
Likewise, additive-noise structural causal models provide a classical route to individual counterfactuals
[44, 45].
What has remained unclear is why this construction should be justified for learned world models, what can be recovered without paired counterfactual observations, and whether the principle survives nonlinear representations learned from pixels. Our analysis connects the identification problem of causal inference, the disturbance structure of control, and the representations of modern world models. In particular, factual training of the predictor is sufficient under the stated shared-input conditions, without additional propensity weighting or encoder retraining
(,  and ).

We test these claims using rendered physical simulators and frozen self-supervised image encoders, DINOv2 [40] in two sizes and masked autoencoders (MAE) [23], and repeat the main comparison with four further frozen encoders, DINOv3 [56], SigLIP 2 [58], CLIP [50] and EVA-02 [16]. We score predicted physical quantities, such as joint angles and positions, by their R2R^{2} against the true counterfactual outcome, i.e., the fraction of its variance they explain (physical counterfactual R2R^{2}). On four environments, with DINOv2 and MAE, counterfactual world models improve physical counterfactual R2R^{2} from 3838–46%46\% to 8686–96%96\% using the same factual predictors, with the correction applied after a readout of these quantities fitted on factual frames; applied to the image features themselves, which needs no state labels, it reaches 7373–94%94\%. On the fifth, the BlueROV2 underwater vehicle, they reach 9090–94%94\% with sixteen times more factual data. They outperform even an oracle predictor that knows the true simulator and its full state, but not the disturbance that occurred, and therefore predicts the average outcome. With the four further encoders, correction after the readout reaches 8181–95%95\% on the first four environments. In hindsight planning, the counterfactual model reaches the goal in 3535–69%69\% of events, compared with 1414–23%23\% for the true-simulator planner without access to the observed outcome. The experiments also recover the predicted failure modes, including contacts, folded coordinates, and disturbances that multiply the command. These results demonstrate that the observed outcome can be more informative for individual counterfactual reasoning than an otherwise perfect predictive model.

Our contributions are threefold.

First, we establish the nonidentification of individual counterfactuals from factual world models, including a minimax impossibility result and an explicit gauge ambiguity that persists even with exact factual likelihoods: the latent noise of a generative model can be relabeled separately for each action without changing any factual prediction ().

Second, we derive residual reuse from the short-time structure of physical dynamics, prove its exactness under additivity, characterize its interaction error and failure modes, and establish its minimax rate-optimality from unpaired factual data ( and ).

Third, we validate the resulting counterfactual world models from pixels, across seven frozen image encoders, physical disturbances, hindsight-planning tasks, and controlled violations of the assumptions ().

title: DRIFT: Detachable Reasoning for Runtime-Flexible and Efficient End-to-End Driving
authors: Emad Aghajanzadeh,Bethany Anne Wong,Leonhard Kunze,Moritz Thoma,Maximilian Forstenhäusler,Nael Fasfous,Manoj Rohit Vemparala,Pierpaolo Mori,Christos Anagnostopoulos,Daniel Mueller-Gritschneder,Ulf Schlichtmann
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)

abstract:
The integration of vision-language models (VLMs) into end-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving has demonstrated strong potential by providing scene description and reasoning capabilities. However, VLMs are computationally expensive, and switching language reasoning on and off at runtime without hurting closed-loop performance has not been demonstrated, which hinders practical adoption. To address these issues, we propose DRIFT, an E2E autonomous driving framework that integrates a lightweight language model (LM) for visual question answering and action commentary. By efficiently projecting intermediate driving representations into the language embedding space, we demonstrate that a compact LM (<<150M parameters) can achieve strong scene description and action commentary. Furthermore, we introduce a runtime-flexible planning module that is trained on surrogate reasoning features distilled from the LM and can be conditioned on either the LM or the surrogate reasoning features at inference. This design enables bypassing the LM entirely when required by deployment constraints, without sacrificing driving performance.
With only 255M parameters, DRIFT reaches up to a Driving Score (DS) of 97.03 and a Success Rate of 89.39% (mean over three runs) on Bench2Drive by interleaving its LM and surrogate reasoning at a chosen reasoning rate. This is on par with the strongest non-language models while being far more compact than existing VLM-based models. DRIFT further achieves competitive results on the real-world NAVSIM and AlpaSim benchmarks at significantly lower computational cost than existing VLM-based approaches. introduction:
End-to-end (E2E) driving models [13, 16] achieve promising driving performance, but they lack interpretability and high-level semantic reasoning. To address these limitations, recent works have integrated vision-language models (VLMs) into the driving pipeline, enabling visual question answering (VQA) [32, 34] and language-guided reasoning [32, 8].
Despite their success, existing VLM-based E2E methods typically improve language performance by scaling up the language models (LMs), incurring substantial computational overhead. Approaches such as DriveVLM [34], ORION [8], and AdaThinkDrive [25] employ models exceeding 7B parameters, making real-time deployment on edge hardware increasingly challenging. This motivates us to study how strong language reasoning can be achieved with a significantly smaller LM.

A second limitation is that these frameworks couple language reasoning tightly to the driving pipeline, requiring LM inference throughout deployment. To reduce this cost, some models run separate fast (standard E2E) and slow (VLM-based) branches and switch between them at runtime [30, 10, 41], while others switch a single VLA between thinking and non-thinking modes [25, 45], but most of them still rely on a large model in complex scenes. Others distill the LM into the driving model, such as DiMA [11], VLM-AD [38], and VERDI [7], but language only shapes the planner during training, and the planner cannot take reasoning as input at inference. DiMA’s Dual variant is the only one of them that is able to run the LM at inference, but it is evaluated only in open-loop settings, leaving the switching of the LM on and off in difficult closed-loop driving unexplored.

We argue that efficiently integrating a language model into E2E driving requires two properties: compactness, so that the LM adds little computational cost, and detachability, so that the LM can be removed at runtime without degrading driving score. We propose DRIFT, an E2E driving framework that realizes this paradigm.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

Efficient driving VQA and action commentary with a compact LM: by aligning dense driving representations with the language embedding space, a 135M-parameter LM achieves competitive VQA and action commentary at an edge-compatible latency on a Jetson AGX Orin. Additionally, as an interesting finding, we show that language training also enriches the shared backbone features.

Detachable LM reasoning: we distill the LM’s reasoning into a lightweight surrogate module, so that a single planner can run on either reasoning source and the LM can be enabled or detached without degrading driving score.

Extensive closed-loop experiments on Bench2Drive show, first, that language training improves driving over the language-free base model (+0.5 DS), and second, that combining the LM and surrogate reasoning at a chosen reasoning rate reaches 97.03 DS (+1.8 over TFv6/LEAD [27]). On the real-world NAVSIM benchmark, DRIFT is competitive with much larger VLM-based planners, and on AlpaSim it is comparable to the LTFv6 and TransFuser-K1 baselines. Moreover, similar to Bench2Drive, enabling the LM on these benchmarks does not degrade planning performance, which shows that the detachable design carries over from simulation to real-world data.

title: ALIVE: Bring Foundation Features to Life with Events
authors: Rong Zou,Haiqing Hao,Davide Scaramuzza
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Visual foundation models provide powerful representations for diverse tasks, but their features become stale as visual content changes between image observations. Refreshing them requires new frames and repeated runs of a computationally expensive image encoder.
We introduce ALIVE, an event-based method that incrementally updates native foundation model features between image observations. Given an anchor image, ALIVE uses subsequent events to transport and correct existing multi-layer features extracted by a frozen DINOv3 encoder. Its lightweight updater is trained end-to-end using only synthetic data, without downstream task supervision, and transfers directly to real-world event streams without any adaptation.
Across three real-world datasets and five task–dataset settings spanning object detection, semantic segmentation, and depth estimation, ALIVE outperforms all evaluated event-based methods in every metric. On DSEC, when the anchor frame is 200 ms old, ALIVE improves over anchor-image predictions by 30.9 mAP in detection, 11.6 mIoU in segmentation, and 15.9% in depth AbsRel. Compared with image re-encoding, ALIVE reduces FLOPs by 82.4% and latency by a factor of 2.5.
Code will be released.
introduction:
Visual foundation models (VFMs) provide general-purpose features that a single frozen backbone can share across many tasks through lightweight heads [33, 29, 21, 37].
However, these features are computed from a single image and describe the scene only at the moment it was captured.
Between frames, they stay fixed while the scene keeps changing, and every prediction derived from them grows stale.
This staleness limits applications that must respond quickly, such as autonomous driving and robotics [13, 23].

With a conventional camera, one must choose between two unsatisfactory options.
At a low frame rate, predictions remain stale until the next image arrives, and at a high frame rate, the VFM must run on every image at a high computational cost.
Event cameras offer a way out of this dilemma.
They report per-pixel brightness changes asynchronously with microsecond resolution [11].
Paired with a frame camera, either on the same chip [6, 2, 22, 17] or as a separate sensor [14, 49, 50], they observe precisely the interval in which VFM features go stale.

The question then becomes how to use events to keep perception up to date.
Most event-based methods train dedicated networks with task labels, e.g., detection [31, 16, 18], segmentation [1, 38], or depth estimation [12].
Event-guided feature propagation [43, 41] keeps the features of task-specific networks up to date between frames but is likewise trained with task supervision.
Each new task thus requires new labels and new training.
Task-agnostic alternatives avoid task labels, but each falls short in efficiency or accuracy.
Reconstructing images, from events alone [35, 9] or from events and frames [48], and encoding them with the VFM brings back the cost of running the VFM on every image.
Warping features with event-based optical flow [15, 25] only moves existing content and cannot account for changes that motion does not explain.
Mapping events directly into the feature space of a VFM [8, 32] discards the rich visual information already captured by the latest frame.
What remains missing is a task-agnostic update that builds on the latest frame, accounts for changes beyond motion, and costs only a fraction of re-encoding.

Our key insight is that such an update should act on the features of the frozen VFM and can be supervised by the VFM itself.
These features are the common input of all heads, and updating them refreshes all predictions at once.
Encoding a later frame with the same VFM yields the features that the update should produce.
The update can therefore be learned without any task label.
Based on this insight, we propose ALIVE, a lightweight event-driven updater that keeps the features of a frozen VFM up to date between frames ().
We instantiate it with DINOv3 [37].
Starting from the multi-layer features of the latest frame, ALIVE updates them with each incoming packet of events (Fig. 2): it moves existing content along the motion observed by the events and corrects the changes that motion cannot explain.
At inference, parameter-free moment matching aligns the updated features with the statistics of the latest frame.

We train ALIVE solely on synthetic RGB–event sequences [42, 40] and apply it zero-shot to three real-world datasets, DSEC, DDD17, and CoSEC [14, 5, 30], which cover object detection, semantic segmentation, and metric depth estimation in five task–dataset settings.
In each setting, a frozen head trained only on DINOv3 features of real RGB images reads the updated features.
ALIVE outperforms all compared event-based methods in all five settings.
On DSEC, when the latest frame is 200 ms old, it improves over reusing that frame’s features by 30.9 mAP in detection, 11.6 mIoU in segmentation, and 15.9% in depth AbsRel (Fig. 3).
ALIVE has only 2.5M parameters, and each update requires 82.4% fewer FLOPs than re-encoding a frame with DINOv3 and runs 2.5×2.5\times faster, which makes it the only evaluated method fast enough to update at 200 Hz.

In summary, our contributions are:

We propose to keep the features of a frozen VFM up to date with events between frames, which refreshes all downstream heads at once and lets the VFM itself supervise the update without task labels.

We present ALIVE, a lightweight recurrent updater that transports and corrects multi-layer VFM features with events, together with a parameter-free moment matching that aligns its output with the latest frame.

We show that a single ALIVE updater trained only on synthetic data transfers to real data without any adaptation, outperforms all compared methods in all five settings, and is the only one fast enough to update at 200 Hz.

1. We propose to keep the features of a frozen VFM up to date with events between frames, which refreshes all downstream heads at once and lets the VFM itself supervise the update without task labels.

2. We present ALIVE, a lightweight recurrent updater that transports and corrects multi-layer VFM features with events, together with a parameter-free moment matching that aligns its output with the latest frame.

3. We show that a single ALIVE updater trained only on synthetic data transfers to real data without any adaptation, outperforms all compared methods in all five settings, and is the only one fast enough to update at 200 Hz.

title: Allocentric Memory, Egocentric Acting: A Dual-Frame VLA for Urban Aerial Navigation
authors: Haotian Xu,Yue Hu,Zhengqiu Zhu,Tuo Feng,Wenguan Wang,Quanjun Yin
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: Language-goal aerial navigation requires a UAV to reach a destination specified in natural language using observations collected during flight. A key challenge is linking changing egocentric perception with spatial evidence anchored to stable locations for long-range navigation. We propose CityNav-VLA, a dual-frame vision-language-action model for urban navigation integrating dynamic egocentric context with persistent allocentric spatial memory. The UAV incrementally accumulates visual observations on a fixed north-up map initialized with geographic and landmark priors, preserving evidence across viewpoint changes. A dynamic query conditioned on the instruction, current observations, UAV state, and motion history retrieves relevant memory evidence to predict a map-frame target. A deterministic controller converts this target into body-frame commands using the UAV’s current pose, connecting global reasoning with egocentric execution. To reduce target fluctuations over long horizons, early goal commitment (EGC) fixes the execution target to the coordinate-wise median of the first KK predictions without extra trainable parameters. On Test Unseen, CityNav-VLA reduces NE by 21.2% and improves SR and SPL by 15.8% and 30.9%, respectively. It also reduces NE by 6.2% and improves SR and SPL by 5.6% and 23.2%, respectively, relative to the former SOTA after dataset refinement. Cumulative ablations show that navigation-map features yield the largest gains, while metric coordinates further improve endpoint accuracy. With a 4B-scale backbone, inference averages 0.68 s per decision with 8.6 GB peak memory on a single A100, presenting remarkable model efficiency.
introduction:
Language-goal aerial navigation (LGAN) [16, 6, 21] requires a UAV to reach a destination specified by a natural-language instruction, typically describing its appearance, surrounding landmarks, and spatial relations. Because the target often lies outside the current field of view, the policy must relate local observations to spatial evidence accumulated along the flight path. Existing approaches mainly follow two paradigms: LLM-driven egocentric planning [12, 45, 2] and map-based navigation policies [43, 34, 4], as illustrated in panels 1 and 2 of Fig. 1. The former reasons over observations that change with the UAV’s viewpoint, making it difficult to maintain consistent spatial references over long trajectories. The latter preserves environmental information in maps, yet typically fuses map features implicitly within black-box policy networks without explicit spatial reasoning over long-range targets. Recently, vision-language-action (VLA) models [46, 13] have offered a unified framework for learning perception-to-action mappings. However, applying VLA models to city-scale navigation still requires a way to retain spatial evidence across changing viewpoints and use it for long-range target prediction.

The central challenge lies in connecting two complementary reference frames. In the egocentric frame, perception and actions are relative to the UAV’s current position and heading, so the same landmark appears at different relative positions during flight. An allocentric map instead provides a fixed reference for organizing landmarks and accumulated observations. Yet a global map alone is insufficient: the UAV must identify the instruction-specified target and determine how to approach it from its current pose. Because this pose continuously changes, even a fixed map-frame target requires different body-frame commands. Navigation therefore requires a connection between first-person perception, global spatial reasoning, and local execution.

To this end, we propose CityNav-VLA, a dual-frame VLA architecture for city-scale aerial navigation (Fig. 1, panel 3). Unlike prior map-based methods that rely on implicit feature fusion (Fig. 1, panel 2), our dual-frame design explicitly decouples allocentric spatial memory from egocentric execution, anchoring visual evidence to metric coordinates for explicit target grounding. Inspired by findings that navigational strategies shape hippocampal spatial representations [8], our design assigns complementary roles to these frames: allocentric memory anchors environmental evidence to fixed locations for long-range reasoning, while egocentric context supports perception and action from the current UAV pose.

To ground target prediction, we develop persistent allocentric memory with explicit metric grounding. A fixed north-up map is initialized with landmark priors, then accumulates newly observed RGB regions, exploration masks, and flight trajectories at corresponding map locations. Its position, orientation and scale remain fixed throughout an episode, making previously observed regions accessible even after they leave the current field of view. At each step, visual tokens from observed map imagery are aligned with navigation-map features on a shared spatial grid. Learned positional embeddings and metric coordinate encodings anchor cell to a fixed physical location, preserving visual evidence and spatial relations across viewpoint changes.

A frozen pretrained multimodal backbone encodes the instruction, current observations, and accumulated map imagery. The resulting context feature is combined with UAV state and motion history to form a dynamic navigation query. Through cross-attention, the query retrieves relevant memory evidence and predicts the destination as a map-frame waypoint. To mitigate target fluctuations over long navigation horizons, we further introduce early goal commitment (EGC), a lightweight strategy that takes the coordinate-wise median of the first KK predictions as a fixed execution target, without introducing additional trainable parameters. A deterministic controller then transforms this target into body-frame commands based on the UAV’s current position and heading, enabling adaptive egocentric execution while maintaining a stable global target.

On Test Unseen, CityNav-VLA reduces NE by 21.2% and improves SPL by 26.1% on CityNav, with corresponding gains of 6.2% and 23.2% on refined CityNav, respectively, relative to the best prior results for each metric. Ablations highlight navigation-map features as the primary source of performance gains, with metric coordinates and EGC providing further improvements.

title: TrajWAM: Trajectory-Conditioned Future Learning for Vision-Language Driving
authors: Xuerui Fang,Gulimila Kezierbieke,Chen Wangxing,Hui Li
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)

abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) connect future scene prediction with action planning for autonomous driving. Driving records pair executed trajectories with observed futures, leaving alternative trajectory queries unlabeled. We present TrajWAM, a trajectory-conditioned WAM that improves vision–language driving through auxiliary bird’s-eye-view (BEV) future learning. An ego-trajectory query conditions DINOv3-aligned BEV predictions from shared planner representations. Training combines factual reconstruction under the executed trajectory with one-sided feature separation under an unlabeled perturbed trajectory. Joint optimization with waypoint supervision transfers these auxiliary learning signals to the shared planner. Native inference directly generates waypoints and bypasses the auxiliary future-prediction branch. On all 220 Bench2Drive routes, TrajWAM achieves 91.53 Driving Score and 75.45% Success Rate, exceeding a schedule-matched planning-only fine-tuning baseline by 5.31 Driving Score points and nine successful routes.
introduction:
Autonomous driving requires recognizing the current scene and anticipating its evolution under ego actions. World Action Models (WAMs) connect observations and actions with future scene representations [27, 32]. Driving systems learn video, latent, or bird’s-eye-view (BEV) futures to support planning [28, 11, 13, 40]. When future prediction and planning share parameters, observed futures also supervise the driving policy during training. This coupling supports direct waypoint generation at deployment.

Representation-space supervision provides a compact interface for this coupling. DeepSight supervises DINOv3-aligned BEV futures within a driving VLM [36], and Latent-WAM trains auxiliary latent dynamics alongside a driving policy [26]. We study how an explicit future-trajectory query can strengthen this auxiliary supervision.

Trajectory-agnostic supervision predicts future features from scene states. A future-waypoint query explicitly links these predictions to ego motion (Figure 1(a)). The resulting training problem has asymmetric supervision: driving records supply the observed future for the executed trajectory, while alternative queries have unobserved outcomes. Our central question is: How can trajectory queries and observed futures jointly improve a vision–language driving policy?

We introduce TrajWAM, a trajectory-conditioned WAM that trains a Qwen2.5-VL-3B driving planner with auxiliary BEV future supervision [1]. A four-waypoint ego trajectory modulates the shared VLM’s future-query states through feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM) [17]. A frozen readout maps these states to DINOv3-aligned features at the current anchor and four future times [20]. The trajectory enters the readout after planner-logit computation, and the auxiliary losses backpropagate into shared planner layers. Native inference retains the fixed future-query tokens and directly generates reasoning and waypoints.

Our joint objective combines factual reconstruction and perturbed-query separation (Figure 1(b)). Factual reconstruction aligns the executed-query prediction with observed DINOv3 targets. One-sided separation uses this prediction as a detached reference and encourages a distinct prediction under the perturbed query. Both objectives update the shared planner, coupling observed-future supervision with trajectory-query sensitivity.

On all 220 Bench2Drive routes [7], TrajWAM achieves 91.53 Driving Score and 75.45% Success Rate. It improves on schedule-matched planning-only continuation by 5.31 DS points and nine successful routes. Matched two-seed controls on 120 routes show gains from trajectory conditioning and separation. Correct trajectory pairing improves DS by 4.25 over shuffled pairing. Prediction diagnostics on newly collected episodes connect these controls to reconstruction quality and executed-query benefits.

Our contributions are:

Trajectory-conditioned auxiliary training for vision–language driving. An external waypoint query conditions shared future-query states, coupling BEV supervision with a policy that directly generates driving waypoints.

Joint learning from factual and unlabeled trajectory queries. Factual reconstruction anchors the observed outcome, and one-sided separation trains the readout to respond to changes in the trajectory query.

Closed-loop gains supported by matched training controls. Full-set evaluation establishes planning performance; two-seed controls quantify the gains from trajectory conditioning, separation, and correct query pairing. Joint planning–prediction diagnostics relate these gains to reconstruction quality and query responses.

title: Adaptive Action Horizon Selection via Flow-Field Uncertainty
authors: Idan Ben-Ami,Arnon Netzer,Sarah Keren,Idit Diamant
comment: IEEE IROS 2026 Workshop
abstract:
Reliable uncertainty estimates are important for adaptive execution in
vision-language-action (VLA) models. Existing approaches such as
Adaptive Action Chunking (AAC) estimate action entropy from multiple sampled action chunks, introducing additional inference cost and capturing both uncertainty within an action trajectory and diversity across alternative strategies. We introduce Divergence-based Uncertainty-aware Adaptive Action Chunking (DUAC), a post-hoc method that extracts trajectory-conditioned predictive uncertainty from the vector field of a pretrained VLA. Building on a closed-form flow-posterior covariance formulation, DUAC derives action-level uncertainty scores from a single generated chunk using Jacobian–vector products, without retraining or multiple endpoint samples. DUAC strongly correlates with AAC, while capturing distinct information: AAC measures global dispersion across sampled chunks, whereas DUAC measures local uncertainty around the trajectory selected for execution. Consequently, DUAC is less sensitive to diversity among distinct but valid action strategies.
Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Pro, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboCasa, DUAC-based adaptive horizon selection performs favorably among the evaluated methods, combining strong task success with low uncertainty-estimation latency.
These results establish
the flow vector field as an efficient, trajectory-conditioned source of
predictive uncertainty for robot decision making.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have emerged as a general approach to robotic manipulation, mapping visual observations, language instructions, and robot state into executable actions [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. Many recent VLAs generate continuous action chunks with diffusion or flow-matching action heads [4, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13]. Starting from noise, these policies repeatedly evaluate a learned vector field to transform a latent variable into a coherent action trajectory. Despite the inherently iterative nature of this computation, the internal flow trajectory is usually treated only as a mechanism for producing the final action, rather than as a source of information about the reliability of that action.

Reliable estimates of predictive action uncertainty are particularly useful when action chunks are executed in closed loop [14, 15, 16]. Longer execution horizons preserve temporal consistency and reduce the frequency of policy inference, but limit the policy’s responsiveness to new observations. Shorter horizons permit frequent replanning, but can produce discontinuous or overly reactive behavior. Adaptive Action Chunking (AAC) [15] addresses this trade-off by sampling multiple candidate action chunks, estimating the entropy of the resulting action distribution at each predicted step, and shortening the execution horizon when this entropy increases. While effective, the quality and stability of its estimate depend on the number of sampled chunks, and obtaining multiple complete action trajectories introduces additional inference-time computation and memory.

These limitations motivate using the local geometry of a flow-matching policy to estimate predictive action uncertainty without sampling multiple terminal action chunks. Xing et al. [17] derive a closed-form expression that relates the conditional posterior covariance of a flow-matching model to the divergence of its learned vector field. However, the utility of this formulation for VLA action generation remains unexplored, including whether it can provide uncertainty for individual actions within a predicted chunk and support adaptive action horizon execution.

We introduce Divergence-based Uncertainty-aware Adaptive Action Chunking, DUAC , a post-hoc method that extracts predictive uncertainty from the vector field of a pretrained flow-matching VLA. We adapt the flow-posterior covariance formulation to VLA policies and derive an action-wise uncertainty signal for generated action chunks. At an intermediate state of the flow process, DUAC estimates the dispersion of terminal actions associated with that local flow state. When nearby action trajectories converge toward similar terminal actions, the prediction is more certain. When they remain dispersed, the terminal action is less determined. Unlike entropy-based uncertainty in AAC [15], which summarizes variability across independently sampled action chunks, our score is conditioned on the intermediate state of the specific trajectory being generated. It therefore provides a local, trajectory-specific uncertainty estimate for the action chunk selected for execution. Figure 1 illustrates this signal, showing higher uncertainty during later stages of unsuccessful rollouts.

We compare DUAC with the sampling-based action entropy used by AAC [15] and observe strong correlations in both their per-action uncertainty profiles and selected execution horizons. Nevertheless, the two methods capture different information: AAC measures global dispersion across sampled action chunks, whereas DUAC measures local uncertainty around the particular trajectory selected for execution. Consequently, DUAC is less sensitive to variability among distinct but valid action strategies and avoids treating such diversity as uncertainty in the selected trajectory. Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, LIBERO-Pro, and RoboCasa, DUAC improves performance while substantially reducing uncertainty-estimation latency relative to entropy-based AAC.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We introduce Divergence-based Uncertainty-aware Adaptive Action Chunking (DUAC), which adapts the closed-form flow-posterior covariance to VLA action generation and derives per-action uncertainty scores from one generated action chunk using Jacobian–vector products.

We provide a sampling-efficient alternative to entropy-based AAC that requires one generated action chunk and achieves substantially lower uncertainty-estimation latency in our implementation.

Since DUAC captures local uncertainty around the selected action trajectory, we show that it is less sensitive than AAC’s entropy to variability among distinct but valid action strategies, reducing unnecessary replanning.

We apply DUAC to adaptive horizon selection, achieving improved performance over the evaluated methods.

1. We introduce Divergence-based Uncertainty-aware Adaptive Action Chunking (DUAC), which adapts the closed-form flow-posterior covariance to VLA action generation and derives per-action uncertainty scores from one generated action chunk using Jacobian–vector products.

2. We provide a sampling-efficient alternative to entropy-based AAC that requires one generated action chunk and achieves substantially lower uncertainty-estimation latency in our implementation.

3. Since DUAC captures local uncertainty around the selected action trajectory, we show that it is less sensitive than AAC’s entropy to variability among distinct but valid action strategies, reducing unnecessary replanning.

4. We apply DUAC to adaptive horizon selection, achieving improved performance over the evaluated methods.

title: Object Pose: The Link between Weak Perspective, Paraperspective, and Full Perspective
authors: Radu Horaud,Fadi Dornaika,Bart Lamiroy,Stephane Christy
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Recently, DeMenthon & Davis [4], [5] proposed a method for
determining the pose of a 3-D object with respect to a camera from 3-D to
2-D point correspondences. The method consists of iteratively improving the
pose computed with a weak perspective camera model to converge, at the
limit, to a pose estimation computed with a perspective camera model.
In this paper we give an algebraic derivation of DeMenthon and Davis’ method
and we show that it belongs to a larger class of methods where the
perspective camera model is approximated either at zero order (weak
perspective) or first order (paraperspective).
We describe in detail an iterative paraperspective pose computation method for
both non coplanar and coplanar object points.
We analyse the convergence
of these methods and we conclude that the iterative paraperspective method
(proposed in this paper)
has better convergence properties than the iterative weak perspective
method. We introduce a simple way of taking into account the orthogonality
constraint associated with the rotation matrix. We analyse the sensitivity
to camera calibration errors and we define the optimal experimental setup
with respect to imprecise camera calibration. We compare the results
obtained with this method and with a non-linear optimization method.
introduction:
Recently, DeMenthon & Davis [4], [5]
proposed a method for
determining the pose of a 3-D object with respect to a camera from 3-D to
2-D point correspondences. The method consists of iteratively improving the
pose computed with a weak perspective camera model to converge, at the
limit, to a pose estimation computed with a perspective camera model.
To our knowledge, the method proposed by DeMenthon & Davis is among one of the first attempts
to link linear techniques, associated with the weak perspective camera model,
with non-linear techniques, associated with a perspective camera model. Indeed, on one
side, linear resolution methods can be used but the solution thus obtained is
just an approximation and, on the other side, non linear resolution methods
lead to a very accurate solution but proper initialization is required.

One possibility could be to use a robust numerical method to perform the non
linear minimization that is initialized with the solution obtained by a linear
method. However, there are several drawbacks. First, such an approach does not take into account the simple
mathematical link that exists between the perspective model and its linear
approximations. Second, the linear approximation may be quite faraway from the
true solution and a large number of iterations would be required before the
non-linear minimization process converges to a stable solution. For example,
as it will be described below, a non-linear method requires 10 times more
iterations than the method of DeMenthon & Davis and than the method described in
this paper.

The perspective projection is modelled by a projective transformation mapping the
3-D projective space to the 2-D projective plane. Weak perspective is just an
affine approximation of full perspective. More precisely, it may well be viewed as a zero-order approximation: 1/(1+ε)≈11/(1+\varepsilon)\approx 1. Paraperspective
[1]
is a first order approximation of full perspective: 1/(1+ε)≈1−ε1/(1+\varepsilon)\approx 1-\varepsilon. The method proposed by DeMenthon & Davis starts with computing the pose of an object using weak perspective and after a few iterations
converges towards a pose estimated under perspective. The method is very
elegant, very fast, and quite accurate. It is however limited to situations
where the weak perspective approximation is valid. If the object is close to the camera and/or at some distance away from the optical axis then the pose algorithm of DeMenthon & Davis either converges very slowly (100 iterations rather
than 5 to 10) or it doesn’t converge at all.

In this paper we show how the initial method proposed in [4] and [5] may be extended to paraperspective. More precisely, we describe a method for computing object pose with a paraperspective model and we establish the link between paraperspective pose and perspective pose.
We show that the case of a coplanar set of object points is somehow more
complex than the case of a non coplanar set of object points and we describe a
method which can deal with both cases.
We show both theoretically and experimentally that our method has better convergence properties than the method proposed by DeMenthon & Davis. Moreover we introduce a simple computational way of taking into account the orthogonality constraint associated with the 3×\times3 matrix describing the
orientation between the 3-D object and the camera.
Indeed, the linear pose algorithms using weak perspective and paraperspective do not guarantee that this matrix is orthogonal. The orthogonalization method that we describe below computes the best rotation in close form using unit quaternions. This orthogonalization method considerably increases the accuracy of the method at the cost of very few extra computations. We characterize the best experimental setup that allows one to compute a precise pose even in the presence of camera calibration errors. Finally we provide a comparison between the results obtained with this method and the results obtained with a non-linear minimization method
[14], [15].

The problem of object pose from 2-D to 3-D correspondences has received a lot
of attention both in the photogrammetry and computer vision literatures.
Haralick et al. [10] cites a German dissertation from 1958
that surveys nearly 80 different solutions from the photogrammetry literature.
Various approaches to the object pose (or external camera parameters) problem
fall into 2 distinct categories: closed-form solutions and numerical
solutions.

Closed-form solutions may be applied only to a limited number of
correspondences [8],
[11], [6]. Whenever the number of
correspondences is larger than 4 then
closed-form solutions are not efficient any
more and iterative numerical solutions are necessary [18],
[12], [10]. These approaches are, in general, very
robust but they converge towards the correct solution on the premise that a good
initial estimate of the true solution is provided. Phong et al.
[15] describe a method that uses trust-region optimisation and
that is less sensitive to initialisation than other minimization methods.
However, the method of Phong et al. performs well for a relatively large
number of correspondences. Whenever the number of correspondences is between 3
and 10, then the trust-region minimization method either requires a large
number of iterations or doesn’t converge towards the correct solution. From a
practical point of view, it is important to have available an object pose algorithm
which doesn’t necessarily require a large number of correspondences and which
doesn’t suffer from the limitations that are inherent to closed-form methods.

The method recently proposed by DeMenthon & Davis
[4], [5] requires an arbitrary
number of point correspondences. The 3-D points must be in
general position
(i.e., non coplanar)
and there should be at least 4 point correspondences. The
method is fast and it is robust with respect to image measurements and to
camera calibration errors. However, the object pose algorithm as suggested by
DeMenthon and Davis has convergence problems if the object is too faraway from
the optical axis of the camera — a limitation that can be overcome as
explained farther in this paper. The method of DeMenthon & Davis was extended
to the case of a coplanar set of points by Oberkampf, DeMenthon, and Davis
[13] and by DeMenthon [3].

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we briefly recall the perspective camera model and two possible
approximations of this model, weak and paraperspective.
Section 3 describes the iterative weak
perspective algorithm as it has been proposed in [5].
Section 4 describes the new iterative paraperspective
algorithm that we propose as well as how to compute the object
pose from a paraperspective approximation.
Section 5 provides details for
solving the linear equations associated with pose computation in the case
of both non coplanar and planar sets of object points.
Section 6 analyses the convergence of both the
iterative weak and paraperspective
algorithms and Section 7
shows how to improve the pose algorithms using a simple and straightforward
formulation of the orthogonality constraint. Section 8 analyses the sensitivity of both algorithms with respect to camera
calibration errors, and Section 9 provides an experimental
comparison of the two methods described in this paper together with a
comparison of these methods with a non-linear minimization method.
Section 10 shows many examples of application of pose
computation.
Finally, Section 11 provides a discussion and gives directions for
future work.

title: AeroRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement for Aerial Vision-Language Navigation
authors: Shiwei Wu,Yuwen Pan,Zhi Li,Yaowen Li,Yan Zhou,Xuemiao Xu,Yu Liu
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Robotics (cs.RO)
comment: 8-page main paper with references and supplementary material (); 5 figures, 13 tables. Code:this https URLProject page:this https URL
abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to follow natural-language instructions, yet still fail frequently in closed-loop flight.
Correcting these failures requires repairs, i.e., actions that avoid them at the states the policy itself reaches, which human pilots cannot label at scale and rule-based planners cannot supply reliably.
In this paper, we present AeroRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework in which an aerial navigation policy iteratively learns from its own failures.
Our key insight is that a failing policy should judge its own repairs by flying on from them.
Judged in this way, its sampled actions and even rule-based proposals that hurt it when imitated directly become reliable supervision.
Moreover, an episode terminates at its first failure, concealing subsequent failures until the earlier ones are repaired.
AeroRSI thus renews its supervision in every round, anchoring the failures of the current policy, verifying repairs by its continuation, and distilling them while keeping its behavior elsewhere.
On TravelUAV, three rounds raise the success rate of a supervised 2B-parameter policy from 46.4% to 67.5% and reduce collisions by half, surpassing the previous state of the art by 10.6 points from the same initialization without extra human labels or inference cost.
introduction:
Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) that follow natural-language instructions could inspect infrastructure, search for people, and deliver goods without a human pilot.
Toward this goal, recent vision-language-action (VLA) models for aerial vision-language navigation (VLN) [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] directly map visual observations and instructions to flight actions [8, 9, 1, 10, 11], mirroring their success in robotic manipulation [12, 13, 14, 15, 16].
Despite this progress, existing aerial agents [8, 1, 17, 9, 18] still fail frequently in closed-loop flight, often due to collisions with obstacles.
Since a single wrong action can terminate an entire flight, such failures severely limit their reliability.

These failures stem from a well-known mismatch in imitation learning [19, 20, 21], as a policy trained on demonstrations reaches states that the demonstrations never cover and accumulates errors along the flight.
Correcting them requires repairs, namely actions that avoid a failure at the states the policy itself reaches, and existing approaches differ mainly in who judges such an action.
Interactive imitation learning [21, 22, 23, 24] queries an expert for corrective actions, but human annotation is extremely expensive at scale, and rule-based planners [25, 26] ignore the language instruction.
Automatic correction methods [1, 27, 28] avoid human labeling by deriving corrections from collision rollbacks, reference paths, or auxiliary teacher policies, yet they do not consider whether the policy can actually execute these corrections.
Reinforcement learning [18, 29, 30, 31] instead relies on episode-level rewards, which indicate whether a flight fails but not which action should have been taken.
As a result, annotation-free, action-level supervision that the policy itself can execute remains missing.

Recursive self-improvement offers a promising route toward such supervision.
It has recently achieved remarkable success in language models [32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 37], where a model learns from its own verified outputs, and has begun to extend to robotics and navigation [38, 39, 40, 41, 42, 43, 28].
However, closed-loop flight poses three challenges that answer-level self-improvement leaves open.
First, an answer can be verified on its own, whereas the value of a flight action depends on the subsequent flight of the policy, which calls for step-level values as in process supervision [44, 45].
Second, a language model learns from a fixed set of problems, whereas a flight terminates at its first failure, so later failures remain hidden until earlier ones are repaired.
Third, self-improvement in language models mainly reinforces answers that the model can already produce [46, 47], whereas a failing flight policy often cannot sample the action it needs, even though simple physical priors, such as climbing or detouring around obstacles, can readily propose one, as rationalization does in STaR [32].

These challenges lead to our key insight that a failing policy should judge its own repairs.
By continuing its flight after each candidate action, the current policy estimates the value of the candidate under its own behavior, which is what approximate policy iteration requires [48, 49, 50].
This self-verification turns weak sources into reliable supervision.
Actions sampled from the policy often contain a repair, and rule-based proposals that degrade the policy under direct imitation become its most effective supervision once verified, whereas checking only the next few actions often favors candidates that fail later (Fig. 1(a)).
It also reveals how failures evolve.
Verified repairs remain valid for subsequent policies, while new failures emerge elsewhere on the same routes (Fig. 1(b)), so supervision must be renewed in every round.
Moreover, actions learned from rule-based proposals in one round appear among its sampled actions in the next, indicating that the loop expands what the policy can do rather than reinforcing existing behavior.

Based on these insights, we present AeroRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework that repeats three steps in every round.
First, adaptive failure anchoring (AFA) collects the states leading to each failure of the current policy at multiple time scales, so that supervision follows the failures as they are revealed.
Starting from these states, continuation-verified repair (CVR) builds candidates from actions sampled from the policy and from rule-based proposals, and accepts a candidate only if the original action fails again from the same state or falls clearly behind the best candidate, and the policy completes the candidate again in an independent re-flight.
Finally, retentive repair learning (RRL) distills these verified repairs into the policy while keeping its behavior on states that need no repair.

Extensive experiments on the TravelUAV benchmark [3] demonstrate the effectiveness of AeroRSI.
Starting from a supervised policy, AeroRSI improves the success rate from 46.4% to 67.5% in three rounds and reduces collisions by half (Fig. 1(c)), outperforming the previous state-of-the-art method [1], which is trained from the same policy, by 10.6 points.
When built upon the stronger policy of this method, AeroRSI further improves the success rate to 69.9%, establishing a new state of the art without additional human annotation or inference cost.

In summary, our contributions are as follows.

We identify three challenges of self-improvement in closed-loop flight and show that letting a failing policy judge its own repairs turns its sampled actions and even rule-based proposals into reliable supervision.

We reveal that verified repairs remain valid while new failures emerge elsewhere on the routes, and that actions learned from rule-based proposals enter its sampled actions, which together make recursion essential.

We propose AeroRSI, which anchors the failures of the current policy, verifies candidate repairs by its own continuation, and distills them while keeping its behavior elsewhere, achieving state-of-the-art results on TravelUAV with no extra annotation or inference cost.

1. We identify three challenges of self-improvement in closed-loop flight and show that letting a failing policy judge its own repairs turns its sampled actions and even rule-based proposals into reliable supervision.

2. We reveal that verified repairs remain valid while new failures emerge elsewhere on the routes, and that actions learned from rule-based proposals enter its sampled actions, which together make recursion essential.

3. We propose AeroRSI, which anchors the failures of the current policy, verifies candidate repairs by its own continuation, and distills them while keeping its behavior elsewhere, achieving state-of-the-art results on TravelUAV with no extra annotation or inference cost.

title: Control-Aware Separating Hyperplanes for Control Barrier Functions in Planar Navigation
authors: Aadarsh Ramachandiran,Rachel Kalpana Kalaimani
abstract: Separating hyperplanes are widely used in Control Barrier Function (CBF)-based collision avoidance, yet their orientations strongly govern control intervention—the deviation of the applied control from the robot’s nominal command. Existing methods typically select hyperplane orientations from geometry alone. Jointly optimizing orientations and control yields a continuous, non-convex problem in which local nonlinear solvers suffer from initialization sensitivity, local minima, and unpredictable latency, while discretized orientation grids scale exponentially with obstacle count. For planar navigation of a polygonal robot among polygonal obstacles, we present a solver-free, control-aware separating hyperplane selection method that directly computes a global optimum of this joint problem at each step whenever it is feasible. Exploiting the geometry of Minkowski difference polygons, we reduce this continuous non-convex optimization to evaluating a polynomial-size set of candidate control interventions via closed-form algebraic checks, selecting the feasible candidate of minimum norm. Across 250 simulated navigation scenarios, our method reduces cumulative intervention cost by 3.6% at the median and 27.3% at the 90th percentile compared to a local nonlinear solver, and completion time by 0.6% and 5.6%, respectively. In scalability benchmarks, it achieves a 6.1×\times per-step speedup at 16 simultaneous obstacles.
introduction:
Autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) deployed in warehouse intralogistics must navigate confined spaces while tracking their desired motion and avoiding collisions with dynamic obstacles [1]. Control barrier functions (CBFs) enforce safety constraints while minimally modifying the nominal command [2, 3] with high-order CBFs (HOCBFs) extending this framework to higher relative degree systems, such as acceleration-controlled robots [4, 5].

Geometric safety constraints also depend on how robot and obstacle footprints are modeled. Simplified primitives such as points, circles, or ellipsoids [6, 7, 8] inflate true footprints and add conservatism, whereas polygonal representations preserve shape fidelity for CBF-based collision avoidance [9, 10, 11].

Separating hyperplanes provide a convenient means of enforcing collision avoidance between polygonal footprints [6, 7, 8]. The choice of hyperplane orientation strongly governs how restrictive the resulting control constraint is. Existing approaches generally select this orientation using either closest-point methods, which align the normal vector along the line joining the nearest points of the robot and obstacle [12], or geometric optimization methods, which explicitly maximize spatial separation [6, 13, 14]. However, neither accounts for the robot’s nominal command. Consequently, maximizing geometric separation does not necessarily keep small the resulting control intervention Δ​u=u−unom\Delta u=u-u_{\mathrm{nom}}—the deviation of the applied control uu from the nominal command unomu_{\mathrm{nom}} required to satisfy the safety constraint.

The least-restrictive hyperplane (LRH) CBF [15] jointly selects the separating hyperplane orientation and control input at each step to minimize the control intervention. However, this per-step joint problem is continuous and non-convex. Existing LRH implementations therefore rely on discretized orientation grids, which scale exponentially with obstacle count, or local nonlinear solvers, which suffer from initialization sensitivity, local minima, and unpredictable latency.

We present Exact LRH (ELRH), which adopts the least-restrictive-hyperplane idea of [15] for polygonal footprints and solves the resulting joint hyperplane–control problem exactly, without numerical solvers, for planar navigation among dynamic polygonal obstacles. By exploiting the geometry of Minkowski difference polygons, ELRH reduces the continuous non-convex problem to evaluating a polynomial-size set of candidate control interventions via closed-form algebraic checks. This yields a bounded worst-case runtime without any numerical optimization solver, attractive for resource-constrained hardware, while provably recovering a global optimum of the per-step problem whenever it is feasible.

Our main contributions are:

Joint Hyperplane-CBF and Control Formulation: We address planar navigation among dynamic polygonal obstacles via a separating-hyperplane control barrier function, jointly selecting the hyperplane orientation and control input to minimize the norm of the control intervention Δ​u\Delta u.

Joint Hyperplane-CBF and Control Formulation: We address planar navigation among dynamic polygonal obstacles via a separating-hyperplane control barrier function, jointly selecting the hyperplane orientation and control input to minimize the norm of the control intervention Δ​u\Delta u.

Solver-Free Method: We develop ELRH, an algebraic procedure that constructs a polynomial-size set of candidate control interventions and selects the feasible candidate of minimum norm without numerical optimization.

Theoretical Optimality and Safety Guarantees: We prove that evaluating this finite candidate set recovers a global optimum of the per-step problem whenever it is feasible, and derive an explicit time-step bound under which the chosen hyperplane and Zero-Order Hold (ZOH) control guarantee safety throughout each step.

Benchmark Validation: Across 250 simulated dynamic navigation scenarios, ELRH achieves lower cumulative intervention cost and faster completion time than a local nonlinear solver, while runtime benchmarks confirm its scalability with increasing obstacle counts.
