title: RoboBuilder: Agentic Robot Co-Design with Real-world Video Feedback in the Loop
authors: Ghadi Nehme,Dahyun Nam,Akshay Govind Srinivasan,Faez Ahmed
subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: Can AI agents design robots that work in the real world? We introduce RoboBuilder, a benchmark in which coding agents co-design a robot’s hardware and program from standard parts, motors and a custom 3D-printed part, and every design that passes in simulation is built and tested on a physical course. Simulation alone is not enough: under public part data, none of 15 initial passing designs crossed the real course, so an agent learns the simulator from measurements it requests and videos of real runs. Across four frontier coding agents, ten obstacles at three difficulty levels, 16,427 simulations of 12,774 distinct robots and 135 physical robots built in an estimated 240 hours, agents solve nearly all easy obstacles and invent mechanisms our search baselines do not reach, but falter at harder levels, when one robot must cross every obstacle, and in the real world, where 66% of simulated passes hold across all levels. Closing the loop helps: shown a video of its real failure, an agent redesigns the robot, sometimes correcting its simulator, and removes 72% of level-1 and level-2 failures. RoboBuilder measures progress toward agents that engineer real machines. Project Page: https://ghadinehme.com/robobuilder.github.io/
introduction:
Engineering design is a loop: build a prototype, test it, learn why it failed, and iterate. Coding agents have mastered this loop for software, where a test runs in seconds and its verdict is exact. For a machine, the test is a physical build, and the simulator that stands in for it is wrong in ways only real runs reveal. We ask whether agents can run the full loop for functional robots: designing assemblies that achieve a task under constraints and objectives, and closing the sim-to-real gap the way engineers do, by building and testing.

Agents became capable engineers through executable feedback: writing code, running the tests and reading the failure [32, 90, 75]. The same recipe now produces CAD models [50, 33, 54, 55], robot code [40] and machines in physics sandboxes [93, 88]. These works judge geometry, or judge function in a simulator whose verdict is taken as truth. A functional assembly is held to more: it must achieve its task within the parts on hand, with joints that hold, gears that mesh and motors that can drive it, often as light or fast as possible, and only the physical world can confirm it.

Simulation alone does not suffice. With a simulator built from public data for our parts, none of 15 initial robots that passed in simulation crossed the real course: tyres slipped, joints pulled apart, gears walked out of mesh and loads shifted. Sim-to-real methods calibrate a model of a fixed robot from real data [80, 78, 9]; in co-design the robot changes with every iteration, so the simulator must hold for designs nobody has built yet. A simulator never checked against reality rewards agents for exploiting it.

We introduce RoboBuilder, a benchmark for agentic robot co-design under constraints and objectives whose verdict is grounded in the real world (). Agents design a robot and its open-loop program from an inventory of real parts, motors and a custom 3D-printed part (up to four copies), under building rules, to cross ten obstacles at three levels. They must pass each obstacle, pass with a printed part if needed, then make the design lighter or faster, and build one robot that crosses every obstacle (Figure 3). The design space is vast. With 132 part types and about 3,000 parts in stock, a rough count gives about 106810^{68} assemblies of only 25 pieces, while passing robots use a median of 114; each motor program adds about 101610^{16} timings, and the printed part can be any shape an agent can write as CAD code (Sec. H.4). Agents also close the sim-to-real gap themselves. An agent (Opus 5.5) first learns the simulator, requesting measurements and adjusting the physics until simulation matches training and validation videos of real runs. Every design that passes a task is then built and tested, and each real failure returns to its agent as video, which redesigns the robot, correcting its simulator where the video shows a modelling error, before the redesign is built again.

Four frontier coding agents pass 98% of level-1 tasks where search over the full inventory passes none, and invent whegs, printed hoops, cable cars and walkers that our search baselines, with the same budget but without prior knowledge, do not find (Figure 2; more in Appendix A). Their success rate drops sharply at harder levels and when one robot must cross every obstacle. Iterating in simulation is essential, since a single call without it passes almost nothing, but more exploration does not predict better designs: the strongest agent passes with its first idea in over half its runs, suggesting that the agent’s built-in engineering knowledge is its main edge. In the real world, 73% of level-1 and level-2 simulated passes cross with the learned simulator, and 93% after agents redesign from their failures.

Contributions.

RoboBuilder-Bench. Functional robot co-design under constraints and objectives: ten obstacles at three levels, four tasks plus integration, and a real-part inventory.

RoboBuilder-Sim and RoboBuilder-Loop. Simulator learning from requested measurements and real videos, and a protocol that turns each real failure into simulator and design adjustments that are built and tested again. At levels 1 and 2, 73% of simulated passes cross for real, and 93% after the loop.

Analysis of Agentic Design. Performance and optimization, iteration in simulation, the distribution, novelty and diversity of designs (two to three times as diverse as search), how agents explore ideas, and how easily the designed robots can be assembled by hand.

RoboBuilder-Lab and Dataset. 135 robots built by hand in an estimated 240 hours, 16,427 simulations of 12,774 robots, and 461 paired real videos.

Simulator learning from requested measurements and real videos, and a protocol that turns each real failure into simulator and design adjustments that are built and tested again. At levels 1 and 2, 73% of simulated passes cross for real, and 93% after the loop.

3. Analysis of Agentic Design. Performance and optimization, iteration in simulation, the distribution, novelty and diversity of designs (two to three times as diverse as search), how agents explore ideas, and how easily the designed robots can be assembled by hand.

title: Learning Martial Arts Motion Skills for Animating Opponents in VR Sparring Games
authors: Jiqing Wen,Qixuan Shi,Robert LiKamWa,Pavan Turaga
subjects: Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Multimedia (cs.MM); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: Animating virtual opponents is an important yet challenging task in game development. In martial arts games, opponent motions must not only be physically plausible but also exhibit appropriate technique, timing, transitions, and target-directed intent. Traditional game animations often rely on handcrafted clips, state machine transitions, and procedural adjustments, which can be labor-intensive and may limit the behavioral diversity of non-player characters. This paper presents a martial arts motion skills learning framework for character animation in virtual sparring games. Inspired by Tang Soo Do, we collected a martial arts motion capture dataset containing isolated attacking and defending techniques, technique combinations and transitions, and contextual sparring variations. We first pretrained a reusable repertoire of martial arts motion skills from the captured data using reinforcement learning (RL) with adversarial style rewards, and then adapted these skills with task-specific rewards for target-directed striking and threat-aware evasion. We evaluated the motions generated by the learned policy through a user study, in which participants assessed their physical plausibility, smoothness, and martial arts form. To demonstrate their applicability to interactive gameplay, we developed a VR sparring prototype for Meta Quest headsets. The prototype combines policy-generated motion clips with lightweight state-based control to support interactive opponent behavior. Together, these findings support the feasibility of using a learned martial arts skill repertoire as a motion foundation for animating opponents in VR sparring games.
introduction:
Traditional animation production involves multiple stages, including character design, 3D modeling, rigging, and keyframe-based motion authoring. While modern game engines such as Unity and Unreal provide animation systems to manage logic and state transitions, most game animations are still manually scripted and require substantial human effort. Moreover, unlike film animation with fixed timelines, interactive applications demand animations to adapt dynamically to real-time events, further increasing development complexity and cost. Direct mocap manipulation is also not enough, because it can preserve capture noise, marker errors, or self-collision caused by the differences in body proportions between human performers and virtual characters.

Deep learning-based animation synthesis has greatly improved real-time character animation by replacing hand-authored state graphs with data-driven or neural motion generators [28, 29, 27]. However, many of these methods are still primarily kinematic: they synthesize visually plausible motion, but they do not necessarily guarantee physical interaction, task success, balance under contact, or adaptive opponent behavior.

Recent advances in robotics and physics-based humanoid control provide a promising direction for addressing these limitations. Instead of treating character animation only as pose generation, physics-based learning formulates motion as a control problem, where an embodied agent must generate actions that satisfy both stylistic and task-driven objectives. Generative motion models further expand this possibility by reducing repetitive manual authoring effort while increasing the range of behaviors that virtual characters can produce. More importantly, learned motion policies can generate adaptive, varied, and less predictable behaviors through motion priors and emergent motion combinations, rather than relying solely on fixed animation sequences. Beyond increasing behavioral diversity, task-specific training examines whether the learned repertoire can be adapted to functional combat objectives, such as striking a target or evading an incoming threat. Together, these capabilities can support more realistic and varied opponent behaviors, with the potential to provide human players with less predictable and more challenging sparring experiences.

Motivated by these advances, we propose a skill-based learning framework for generating physically plausible, martial arts-specific character motions. Figure 1 presents the broader vision of a virtual martial arts game that connects offline motion learning with online interactive gameplay. Within this vision, the present work focuses on the offline training pipeline, which uses martial arts demonstrations to learn a reusable repertoire of movements and subsequently adapts the learned repertoire for target-directed striking and threat-aware evasion. We evaluate the resulting motions through task performance measures and a user study of their perceived motion quality. To explore their potential for interactive gameplay, we retarget motions generated by the learned policies as animation clips and integrate them into a lightweight Unity sparring prototype. Predefined movement thresholds recognize the player’s controller gestures and determine the requested action state, after which a motion is selected from the skill library associated with that state. The player-controlled character spars with a virtual opponent fully governed by the game logic and the retargeted clips. The player receives game feedback such as distance visualization, health bars, sound effects, and event logs. The prototype therefore serves as a proof of concept for integrating the learned motions into virtual sparring; executing the learned policies online to support physics-based interaction remains future work.

Learning-based control for humanoid robots often builds on imitation learning (IL) [38, 26], where the goal is to map states to actions based on expert demonstrations. Behavioral Cloning (BC) provides a straightforward approach to this by treating the problem as supervised learning; however, it often suffers from distributional shift when the robot encounters unseen states. To overcome these limitations, researchers have turned to RL combined with generative models to create more robust controllers. For instance, the pioneering work AMP [22] employs a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) to produce style rewards, allowing the agent to bridge the gap between rigid imitation and flexible RL by learning from motion priors. Building upon this, ASE [21] scales the approach by encoding vast datasets into a latent space, which can then be sampled to synthesize complex behaviors. In this study, we utilized Tang Soo Do as a representative model for martial arts movement. We incorporated the Tang Soo Do training progression and technical hierarchy into our humanoid training paradigm and the gaming system’s scoring mechanism. We improved the training flow by decomposing the complex combat behavior into two foundational subtasks: 1. target-directed striking, in which the humanoid learns to strike virtual targets using punches and kicks; and 2. threat-aware evasion, in which the humanoid learns defensive movements to avoid incoming threats. In this way, we can produce more realistic martial arts motions.

Our contributions include the following:

We collected a Tang Soo Do-inspired motion capture dataset using a structured three-phase protocol that includes isolated techniques, short combinations and transitions, and contextual sparring variations.

We developed a staged ASE-based training pipeline that combines adversarial motion pretraining with task-specific adaptation, enabling physics-based humanoid agents to perform target-directed strikes and threat-aware evasions while retaining the learned martial arts motion characteristics.

We evaluated the learned motions through a practitioner user study and demonstrated their applicability in a lightweight Unity prototype, showing their potential for physically plausible character animation that is recognizable as martial arts motion in virtual sparring games.

title: LightSEAD: Lightweight SE(3)-Aware Keypoint Detector through Selective Knowledge Distillation
authors: Mayowa Adebambo,Alexander D. Rast,Andrew Bradley
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
The pursuit of improved performance in deep learning has often been accompanied
by increasing architectural complexity and computational demands. We explore an
alternative direction: achieving more with less through structured
supervision. We introduce LightSEAD, a lightweight SE(3)-aware keypoint detector
initialised with calibrated Harris pseudo-labels and enriched through
viewpoint-aware and appearance-aware supervision and selective knowledge
distillation. LightSEAD comprises only six convolutional layers and 84,289
learnable parameters, achieving competitive repeatability across HPatches, KITTI
06 and 4Seasons while demonstrating its downstream applicability to relative
pose estimation on MegaDepth-1500. Further optimised for mixed-precision
inference, LightSEAD Coarse achieves approximately 909 FPS on an NVIDIA RTX 4090
and 139 FPS on a Jetson Orin Nano Super.
introduction:
Real-time visual perception requires accurate features within limited compute
budgets. Repeatable geometric keypoints support image matching, camera calibration
and robotic applications such as simultaneous localisation and mapping (SLAM).
Handcrafted detectors, including Harris [7],
FAST [16] and ORB [17], use explicit
gradient or intensity criteria with low computational requirements, but their
repeatability can deteriorate under viewpoint and appearance variations.

Learned detectors such as DISK [19] and
R2D2 [15] optimise repeatable image locations through data-driven
supervision. XFeat [14] demonstrates that learned local features
can also prioritise computational efficiency. These advances motivate using
richer supervision to improve geometry without increasing inference complexity.

This motivates our central question: can structured geometric supervision
enable a compact learned keypoint detector to achieve competitive repeatability
and low inference latency without increasing architectural complexity?
Figure 1 shows why architectural
compactness, runtime and repeatability must be considered separately: Key.Net [2]
has only 5,873 learnable parameters yet substantially higher measured latency,
whereas mixed-precision LightSEAD balances compactness, repeatability and
latency. We propose LightSEAD Full and LightSEAD Coarse as two inference
configurations of the same compact student trained with structured supervision.

The main contributions of this work are:

Competitive geometry with compact inference. A six-convolution
detector preserves network-input resolution using dilated convolutions.
Its 84,289 parameters and 168.6 kB FP16 weights support competitive repeatability.

Calibration-guided pseudo-label supervision. Known synthetic
corners calibrate Harris parameters to provide structured pseudo-labels,
initialising K from random weights over 20 epochs.

Geometrically informed knowledge distillation. We present a pair-based teacher
that uses viewpoint, appearance, and geometric verification signals to supervise
a single-image student. At inference, the student requires no paired frames,
depth, pose, or temporal history. We evaluate the training signals through the K
→\rightarrow KV →\rightarrow KVA progression.

Efficient cross-domain and embedded detection. We evaluate
LightSEAD on KITTI 06, 4Seasons and HPatches, testing transfer from driving-oriented
training to indoor scenes and less constrained viewpoints. Mixed-precision
LightSEAD Coarse achieves 7.206 ms per
image (about 139 FPS) on KITTI 06 with a Jetson Orin Nano Super.
